civility.statement: We must call out those members of this House who collude and collaborate with the very protesters targeting politicians’ homes. Do they have no shame?
civility.explanation: Imputes collusion with people who target politicians' homes to named-but-unnamed colleagues and asks whether they have any shame. That is an attack on the members' character rather than on any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Those extremists, including those in this House, are entitled to go off the deep end and preen hysterically and monomaniacally about a single conflict overseas while many others rage in other parts of the world.
civility.explanation: 'Preen hysterically and monomaniacally' and 'go off the deep end' are mockery of other members' mental state and motives, not of their position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it because they’re black that you don’t care, or what?
civility.explanation: Accuses the member of racial indifference to victims in Sudan and Myanmar. This goes to the person's character, not to anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They refused it because they’re virtue signallers—they are performative; they aren’t real.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the motives and sincerity of the flotilla participants rather than on the merits of the voyage.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, knackering is that member’s specialty.
civility.explanation: A play on the member's surname used as a personal jibe in reply to her interjection; it engages nothing she said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister has had countless opportunities to show moral clarity on Palestine; each time, he has chosen delay, equivocation, or inaction.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person — 'equivocation' imputes evasiveness rather than disagreement — but it stays on the Prime Minister's conduct on a policy question rather than his character or competence generally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is not leadership to watch atrocities unfold on our screens and say, “Let’s review it again in a month or a year.” It is not leadership to wait for coalition partners to stop squabbling before deciding to do nothing.
civility.explanation: Mockery: a fabricated quotation put in the Prime Minister's mouth, plus 'squabbling', which imputes pettiness to the coalition rather than engaging its stated reasoning.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member can sit opposite me and critique, but given the only policy she’s talked about so far is a higher target for inflation and more tax, I’d suggest she’s got more homework to do.
civility.explanation: 'She's got more homework to do' is condescension directed at the member rather than at the policies just described — it casts her as unprepared rather than wrong.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Those extremists, including those in this House, are entitled to go off the deep end and preen hysterically and monomaniacally about a single conflict overseas while many others rage in other parts of the world.
focus.explanation: Characterises opponents as extremists; the only near-policy content is the gesture at other conflicts, with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t.
focus.explanation: It bears on the named policy (recognition) but the content is the record of the other parties rather than the case for or against recognising Palestine now.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is not leadership to watch atrocities unfold on our screens and say, “Let’s review it again in a month or a year.” It is not leadership to wait for coalition partners to stop squabbling before deciding to do nothing.
focus.explanation: The recognition decision sits behind it, but the content delivered is about the Prime Minister's leadership and the coalition's internal state, not about what recognition would or would not achieve.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To the Minister, does he agree with the hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens in this country that the Government of New Zealand needs to take more action, like sanctions, in response to the unfolding genocide by the Government of Israel against innocent and defenceless Palestine civilians?
focus.explanation: Puts a specific instrument — sanctions — to the Minister on the matter of his statement. This is scrutiny directed at a named policy option, not at the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the Minister's stated rationale for the recognition decision — the measure actually at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have to say is that condemning the flotilla is then condemning any efforts that we’re trying to humanely do to get aid into a nation of people who are enduring the most inhumane suffering disproportionately—disproportionately.
focus.explanation: Engages the Minister's own stated position on aid delivery, though the argument is carried more by the framing than by any named mechanism or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific tenures (Clark nine years, Ardern five, Hipkins one) and that none of the three Labour Prime Ministers recognised the State of Palestine.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ prime-ministerial terms (Clark Dec 1999–Nov 2008, Ardern Oct 2017–Jan 2023, Hipkins Jan–Nov 2023) and MFAT's record of New Zealand's recognition decisions; true if the stated durations are approximately right and none of the three governments recognised Palestinian statehood, false if any did or if a stated duration is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific polling results: a poll in which 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition, and a Stuff poll running 55:45 against recognition before being manipulated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ polling on recognition of Palestine in 2025 (e.g. Curia, Talbot Mills, Research NZ) and the Stuff online poll he refers to; true if a poll shows ~60% not expressing support and the Stuff poll ran ~55:45 against, false if the published figures differ materially or no such polls exist.

veracity.statement: There was a statement made there about genocide that is not authorised, supported, or precedented by any international court whatsoever, but they make the statement anyway, and, sadly, that’s been far too often the case on this very, very sad issue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at October 2025 no international court had made a finding of genocide in Gaza, or one supporting that characterisation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ICJ docket in South Africa v Israel (provisional measures orders of Jan/Mar/May 2024 and any later ruling) and ICC filings; true if no court has made a determination of genocide, false if any international court has so ruled. A provisional-measures finding of 'plausible' risk is not a determination.

veracity.statement: And might I say, on the so-called aid programme, the flotilla was offered—by the Italian Government—a military ship to take all of their so-called aid on those boats and to make sure they got to the destination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Italian Government offered the Global Sumud Flotilla a naval vessel to carry its aid to its destination, and that the offer covered all the aid aboard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Italian government statements and contemporaneous reporting from late September 2025 on Italy's offer to transfer flotilla aid (via the Italian navy / the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem); true if such an offer to carry the aid was made and declined, false if no offer was made or it did not involve carrying the aid onward.

veracity.statement: Further to the Minister, does the Minister agree that New Zealand was put on notice in 2024 by the International Court of Justice that it had a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, that is not necessary for a definitive determination on genocide to be made before action is taken, and what actions has the Government taken to prevent genocide in Gaza?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2024 the ICJ put New Zealand specifically on notice of a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, and that no definitive determination of genocide is needed before that obligation bites.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ICJ's 19 July 2024 advisory opinion on the occupied Palestinian territory and the provisional-measures orders in South Africa v Israel; true if either addresses third states' obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza, false if the 2024 rulings impose obligations only on Israel or address third-state duties on grounds other than genocide prevention.

veracity.statement: Let us be clear that recognising Palestinian Statehood, the likes of which the Green Party put forward a motion to propose to do exactly that in 2021, was opposed by National and ACT MPs, is an important part of being very clear that Israel must not be rewarded for its genocide.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Green Party moved for recognition of Palestinian statehood in 2021 and that National and ACT MPs opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for 2021: the notice of motion or request for leave on Palestinian statehood, and the record of which parties objected; true if a Green motion was put and National and/or ACT blocked or voted against it, false if no such motion exists or the objection came from other parties.

veracity.statement: Because any world that normalises over 20,000 - plus children’s lives being taken by the violence of Israel, any State—any country—that normalises the intentional killing of doctors and nurses and journalists and the winding back of the health system, surely, that needs to be part of our responsibility.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure of more than 20,000 children killed by Israeli military action in Gaza as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health cumulative casualty data and UN OCHA reporting for children killed as at 7 October 2025; true if the recorded figure exceeds 20,000, false if it is materially below that.

veracity.statement: The Freedom House index, an internationally recognised index, measures democratic process around the world. It has democracies in 19 years of consistent free fall, where now autocratic regimes are more plentiful than democracies that we support; more plentiful than countries that foster and use the democratic process.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two findings to Freedom House: 19 consecutive years of global democratic decline, and that autocracies now outnumber democracies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2025 report; true if it records a 19th consecutive year of decline and reports autocracies outnumbering democracies, false if the run of years differs or the outnumbering finding comes from a different index (e.g. V-Dem) rather than Freedom House.

veracity.statement: We acknowledge the three New Zealanders who were detained by Israel after being illegally intercepted in international waters, because they had the courage to actually do what this Government doesn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three New Zealanders were detained by Israel and that the interception took place in international waters and was unlawful.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT consular statements and contemporaneous reporting on the Global Sumud Flotilla interception of early October 2025 — the number of NZ citizens detained, and the coordinates of interception relative to Israel's 12-mile territorial sea; true if three NZ citizens were detained after interception outside territorial waters, false on either count if the record differs. The 'illegally' element turns on whether a competent legal body has so found.

veracity.statement: As I’ve tried to explain before, when Governments increase spending by 84 percent, that takes inflation up to 7.5 percent and that leads to 12 or 13 interest rate rises, which then puts an economy into recession.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an 84 percent increase in government spending, a resulting inflation peak of 7.5 percent, and 12 or 13 interest rate rises.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses 2017–2023, Stats NZ CPI annual peak (June 2022), and the RBNZ OCR decision record Oct 2021–May 2023; true if spending rose ~84%, CPI peaked at ~7.5% and there were 12–13 OCR increases, false if any figure is materially off.

veracity.statement: We now have $237 billion worth of infrastructure projects in the pipeline; we have $125 billion of them funded; and this is a Government that’s accelerating $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment before Christmas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $237 billion national infrastructure pipeline, $125 billion of it funded, and $7 billion of investment being accelerated before Christmas 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Infrastructure Commission's national infrastructure pipeline data as at late 2025 and the Government's October 2025 infrastructure acceleration announcements; true if the pipeline and funded totals match those figures, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, I mean, the member can play politics with it as much as he likes, but the reality is that the number of New Zealanders leaving New Zealand is the same as it was in the last year that he was Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual departures of New Zealanders are at the same level as in 2023, the last year of the previous Prime Minister's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, NZ-citizen departures, year to September 2023 compared with year to September 2025; true if the two annual totals are within a few percent, false if 2025 departures are materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: As I said in the House a couple of weeks ago, forecasters were predicting a negative GDP result for the June quarter; they got a little more than expected: GDP was reported at negative 0.9 percent for the quarter, following positive growth of 0.9 percent in the previous quarter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a June 2025 quarter GDP contraction of 0.9 percent following March quarter growth of 0.9 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted) for the June and March 2025 quarters as published September 2025; true if the prints are −0.9% and +0.9%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, these comparisons are interesting; however, I note that the member did not make those comparisons in the first quarter of the year when New Zealand’s growth rate was three times the rate of Australia’s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's March 2025 quarter GDP growth rate was three times Australia's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ and ABS quarterly GDP for the March 2025 quarter; true if the NZ quarterly growth rate is approximately three times the Australian rate, false if the ratio is materially different.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister please clearly explain, for the 15,000 young people spending their days filling out job applications, why there are four job seekers for every single job ad; is it because young people should “get off the couch and stop playing PlayStation” or is it because his Government policies have increased unemployment?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 15,000 young people are seeking work and that there are four job seekers for every job advertisement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD jobseeker support numbers for 18–24 year olds and job-advertisement counts (Seek NZ / MBIE Jobs Online) for late 2025; true if the ratio of job seekers to advertised vacancies is around 4:1 and the youth figure is around 15,000, false if either is materially off.

veracity.statement: How exactly does he reconcile his statement to young people “The world doesn’t owe you a living.” with his $3 billion tax cut to landlords?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's restoration of interest deductibility for residential rental property amounts to a $3 billion tax cut for landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / IRD costings for the phased restoration of interest deductibility announced in 2024; true if the forecast revenue foregone is around $3 billion across the forecast period, false if the costing is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Does he accept that there are 36,000 fewer jobs under his leadership than when he started as Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net fall of 36,000 filled jobs between November 2023 and October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly employment indicator (filled jobs) for November 2023 compared with the most recent 2025 release; true if the fall is around 36,000, false if the change is materially smaller, or positive.

veracity.statement: Why did he say that those struggling for work should move to Christchurch, Dargaville, and Hawke’s Bay given that, in the Kaipara district, which includes Dargaville, there are 1,404 jobseeker recipients with 16 vacancies listed; Hawke’s Bay has 7,359 jobseekers with 569 vacancies listed; and Christchurch employers have been reporting over 500 applicants per job?
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific jobseeker and vacancy counts for Kaipara district (1,404 / 16) and Hawke's Bay (7,359 / 569), and that Christchurch employers report over 500 applicants per advertised job.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD regional jobseeker support data for the September 2025 quarter and MSD/Work and Income listed vacancies for those districts; true if the counts match, false if materially different. The Christchurch applicants-per-job claim resolves against contemporaneous employer or recruitment-agency reporting.

rigor.statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
rigor.explanation: The inference slides from 'did not express support' to 'a majority against', which are not the same thing — a respondent with no view is counted as opposition. He also relies on an online poll he simultaneously says was corrupted by repeat voting, then treats the conclusion as 'demonstrably numerically wrong'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They refused it because they’re virtue signallers—they are performative; they aren’t real.
rigor.explanation: Infers motive straight from a single decision: because the offer was declined, the participants must be insincere. No alternative explanation is considered and nothing beyond the refusal is offered to support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow: that Israeli officials welcomed non-recognition does not show the Minister's stated reason was wrong, only that the decision had a beneficiary. It also treats 'not rewarding Hamas' and 'not rewarding Israel' as exhaustive alternatives.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Recognition should be based on clear, democratic principles, not just political pressure or symbolism. A State must have a legitimate, accountable Government; respect for the rule of law; and a commitment to peace. That’s not the case today, with the Palestinian territories divided and part of it controlled by Hamas—a terrorist organisation that rejects democracy and has committed horrific violence.
rigor.explanation: A stated criterion, an application of it to the case, and a conclusion that follows from both. The criterion itself is asserted rather than derived — he offers no reason why these particular tests should govern recognition — which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we have to say is that condemning the flotilla is then condemning any efforts that we’re trying to humanely do to get aid into a nation of people who are enduring the most inhumane suffering disproportionately—disproportionately.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: criticising one particular attempt to deliver aid by sea does not entail opposing aid delivery in general, and the Minister had in the same statement endorsed aid through other channels.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, but I’d just say to that member, who raises that issue regularly, when Kiwis leave and go to Australia, what do they do? They go to oil and mining, they go to gas, and they do a bunch of things over there that he’s refused to create opportunities for here at home.
rigor.explanation: An inference about why New Zealanders emigrate rests on an unevidenced assertion about the sectors they go to, and 'a bunch of things' does the work that data would have to. The conclusion — that the Opposition's resource policy causes the departures — outruns what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No. The economy is recovering from a period of economic management in which the previous Government engaged in reckless increases to Government spending, which drove inflation sky high, which in turn required huge hikes in interest rates, and which then in turn caused a deep, protracted economic downturn.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain, but presented as the sole mechanism: nothing is offered to exclude the global inflation shock of 2021–22, which produced the same sequence in economies with very different fiscal settings. The conclusion is stronger than the single-cause reasoning supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To the Minister, does he agree with the hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens in this country that the Government of New Zealand needs to take more action, like sanctions, in response to the unfolding genocide by the Government of Israel against innocent and defenceless Palestine civilians?
specificity.explanation: Names an actual lever (sanctions) but supplies no target, scope or timeframe: sanctions on whom, of what kind, by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Recognition should be based on clear, democratic principles, not just political pressure or symbolism. A State must have a legitimate, accountable Government; respect for the rule of law; and a commitment to peace. That’s not the case today, with the Palestinian territories divided and part of it controlled by Hamas—a terrorist organisation that rejects democracy and has committed horrific violence.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete tests a state must meet and the fact pattern he says fails them, but no instrument, threshold or timeframe for when recognition would follow.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Freedom House index, an internationally recognised index, measures democratic process around the world. It has democracies in 19 years of consistent free fall, where now autocratic regimes are more plentiful than democracies that we support; more plentiful than countries that foster and use the democratic process.
specificity.explanation: Names the index, the duration and the direction of the trend — a listener can go and check the source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Holidays Act will be repealed and replaced with a simpler, more workable alternative: what will be known as the employment leave bill. The new legislation will be based on hours-based accrual, something I know businesses have been asking for for a long time now.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act to be repealed, the replacement bill, and the operative mechanism (hours-based accrual). No commencement date or transitional detail, which is what keeps it off the top of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve tried to explain before, when Governments increase spending by 84 percent, that takes inflation up to 7.5 percent and that leads to 12 or 13 interest rate rises, which then puts an economy into recession.
specificity.explanation: Three checkable quantities — a spending increase, an inflation peak and a count of OCR rises — attached to a stated causal sequence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We now have $237 billion worth of infrastructure projects in the pipeline; we have $125 billion of them funded; and this is a Government that’s accelerating $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment before Christmas.
specificity.explanation: Three figures, a funded/unfunded split and a deadline. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister please clearly explain, for the 15,000 young people spending their days filling out job applications, why there are four job seekers for every single job ad; is it because young people should “get off the couch and stop playing PlayStation” or is it because his Government policies have increased unemployment?
specificity.explanation: Carries a population figure and a ratio of job seekers to advertised vacancies — precise enough to be checked or rebutted, which is what a specific question looks like.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did he say that those struggling for work should move to Christchurch, Dargaville, and Hawke’s Bay given that, in the Kaipara district, which includes Dargaville, there are 1,404 jobseeker recipients with 16 vacancies listed; Hawke’s Bay has 7,359 jobseekers with 569 vacancies listed; and Christchurch employers have been reporting over 500 applicants per job?
specificity.explanation: Three named regions with exact jobseeker counts and vacancy counts. A precise question, and as checkable as any answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That’s why in the Budget we saw 240,000 new jobs will be created over the next four years and an economy that’s expected to grow about 2.7 percent, on average, each year for the next four.
divination.explanation: Forecasts employment growth of 240,000 jobs and average annual economic growth of about 2.7 percent over the four years from Budget 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS employment levels and real GDP for the four years to mid-2029 against the Budget 2025 baseline; true if employment rises by ~240,000 and average annual real GDP growth is ~2.7%, false if either outturn falls materially short.

divination.statement: On the data available last Friday, it predicts GDP growth of between 0.6 percent and 0.7 percent in the September quarter.
divination.explanation: Relays the Reserve Bank's nowcast model forecast of 0.6–0.7 percent GDP growth for the September 2025 quarter.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release for the September 2025 quarter (published December 2025); true if seasonally adjusted growth falls between 0.6% and 0.7%, false if it falls outside that range.

specificity.statement: The Government has recently introduced legislation that’ll make it a criminal offence to engage in targeted and disruptive demonstrations near residential premises. It targets a narrow range of behaviours where demonstrators cause an unreasonable disruption directed at a person regularly occupying a property.
specificity.explanation: Names the legal instrument, the form of liability (criminal offence), the conduct targeted and the location test. No figures or dates, and 'unreasonable disruption' is left undefined, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government knows that Kiwi families and businesses are feeling the pressure of high power bills. That’s why our energy package tackles the root causes: limited fuel supply, a shortage of back-up generation in dry years, and years of policy uncertainty. The issues add a risk premium of between $240 and $400 annually on Kiwis’ household power bills.
specificity.explanation: Three named causes and a quantified annual cost range per household. No dates or delivery milestones for the package itself, which keeps it off the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I noted before in one of the responses to the questions, our plan will fix the problems in our energy system by securing affordable power, guaranteeing reliability, and restoring investor confidence. This is critical so that Kiwi families and businesses can rely on their lights staying on and their bills going down.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — affordable power, reliability, investor confidence — with no mechanism, figure or timeframe, in an answer where the Minister had his own package's detail available to cite.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many more businesses need to shut their doors, how many more people need to lose their jobs, and how much higher must household power bills soar before his Government will take action to deliver affordable energy for New Zealanders?
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical escalation with no figure, no named firm or closure, and no named alternative measure — where the same point could have carried closure counts or price data. A precise question would have scored high here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This test will consist of two parts: a parental income test and a parental support gap test. The parental income test will determine if a young person’s parents earn above an income, limited to financially support them—this is currently $65,529. The parental support gap test will determine if a young person can reasonably be expected to rely on their parents for support. This would need to be verified through a third party—for example, through evidence from a doctor, counsellor, or other agency.
specificity.explanation: Two named components, the exact income threshold to the dollar, and the verification route including who can supply the evidence. Someone could act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
specificity.explanation: Anchors to the actual threshold, supplies the arithmetic gap in dollars, and names the cost categories the threshold ignores. A precise question, not a precise answer, and scored the same way.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Two quantified anchors — the spending cut and the job loss — and a named agency and sector, making the proposition checkable. No period is stated, which is the missing piece.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The change will save regional and rural Kiwis around $1.8 billion and will breathe life back into communities, with those funds available to be deployed for other purposes where the money otherwise simply would not be available. Dannevirke, Pahiatua, and Woodville will save, respectively, $68 million, $29 million, and $22 million.
specificity.explanation: An aggregate figure plus town-by-town amounts. About as checkable and concrete as a ministerial answer gets.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve. But I, as a Māori, am not willing to enable the department or others to dictate to iwi and Māori what customary rights happen to be.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact change — removing regulation of customary non-commercial fishing — but gives no clause reference, area or consequence for the protections the bill creates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While we have ended up with a situation that is far better than the status quo, and we can and should celebrate the consensus that this House has come to with increasing protection to 6 percent, it is nowhere near the 30 percent that is necessary, that scientists tell us is necessary, but more so that our communities so desperately want, nor does it even touch the sides on the need to ban bottom trawling, for which we have so much evidence and which research tells us releases immense amounts of carbon and poses serious risks, therefore, for us with regard to climate changing emissions.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies both what the bill delivers and the benchmark it is measured against, and names the specific further measure sought. The evidence for the 30 percent target is gestured at rather than sourced.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Everybody should be able to enjoy their privacy at home and be free from unreasonable interference with it. We don’t think it’s acceptable for people to bang pots and pans all through the night or to create an environment of fear and intimidation for individuals, their families, and neighbours. Intimidation has no place in our democracy, and I call upon all members and all parties in Parliament, particularly the Greens but also Labour, to join the Government to defend that principle.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested question with plenty of room to impugn opponents' motives. He names the Greens and Labour but only to invite them to support the principle; nobody's character or good faith is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She’s as bad at maths as she is at structured literacy. Kāinga Ora has delivered more new-build homes in the last 23 months under our Government than the entire three years under the last Labour Government. Those are the facts.
civility.explanation: Opens with a direct attack on the questioner's numeracy and literacy — the person, not the argument. The delivery comparison that follows is civil; the first sentence is not.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m grateful to the advice from my colleague Minister Stanford, who advises that some children require repeated instruction in order to grasp concepts.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed squarely at the questioner, likening her to a child needing repeated instruction. Nothing in it engages the funding question asked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If that member is so wrong-headed to think that every single construction job in New Zealand is dependent on public infrastructure, then perhaps she needs to get a little bit more reading done, because, as is actually the case, the construction sector relies heavily on private sector development—things like housing development, which tends to be funded also by the private sector, Member Andersen, and things like the Auckland Port development, which is being funded by that organisation.
civility.explanation: 'So wrong-headed' and 'needs to get a little bit more reading done' land on the member rather than her argument, though the second half does engage the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In relation to political parties’ positions, I think, as I’ve acknowledged, the intent of all parties at the time following the tragedy that was the Canterbury earthquakes was right, but lived experience has indicated in the intervening period that it has been appropriate first to pause the enforcement of the current rules, as we’ve legislated, but also to take another look, which is what we’re pleased now to have done.
civility.explanation: Invited by a supplementary to declare that one party alone was right and the rest wrong on the 2016 bill, he credits every party's intent and locates the fault in the rules' workability instead. A real opportunity to be uncivil, declined.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While this bill is a step in the right direction, it is no thanks to the current Government, even though the Minister responsible—Minister Potaka—has, in the past, continuously tried to take credit for it.
civility.explanation: Imputes credit-taking to a named Minister — a charge about his conduct rather than about the bill or the decisions made on it. Short of an insult, but no longer directed at the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We interrogated this abject ridiculousness at the committee of the whole House stage, and the Minister could not provide us with any evidence whatsoever for those fundamentally baseless assertions, nor was the Minister willing to engage in the many amendments that we put forward as members of the Opposition to try and actually work with—if we were to take in good faith—the rationale from the Minister to protect high-protected areas: to do what it says on the tin.
civility.explanation: Harsh language — 'abject ridiculousness', 'fundamentally baseless' — but aimed at the justification offered, which is fair game. The aside 'if we were to take in good faith' edges toward questioning the Minister's sincerity rather than his reasoning, which is what costs it.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, I heard one comment from a parliamentarian this morning: “MPs’ homes should be safe places. No members of Parliament should have their people protesting outside their house.” Then I heard another member of Parliament saying, “It is appropriate to protest outside MPs’ houses.” The first was from the leader of the Labour Party, the second was from the justice spokesman of the Labour Party, but both of them voted against the bill. It appears that at least Duncan Webb is more consistent than his leader.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific attributed quotations from that morning and a vote position for both MPs on the bill before the Justice Committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media and Hansard records of statements made on 7 October 2025 by the Leader of the Opposition (Chris Hipkins) and Labour's justice spokesperson (Duncan Webb) about protests outside MPs' homes, plus the division record for the first reading of the Government's residential-demonstration bill. True if both quotations are substantially accurate and both MPs voted against the bill; false if either quotation is misattributed or either voted otherwise.

veracity.statement: The Government knows that Kiwi families and businesses are feeling the pressure of high power bills. That’s why our energy package tackles the root causes: limited fuel supply, a shortage of back-up generation in dry years, and years of policy uncertainty. The issues add a risk premium of between $240 and $400 annually on Kiwis’ household power bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantified risk premium attributable to fuel supply, back-up generation and policy uncertainty, in dollars per household per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Frontier Economics report and MBIE analysis underpinning the Government's October 2025 energy package. True if that analysis estimates a security-of-supply risk premium of roughly $240–$400 per household per year; false if no such estimate exists or the published range is materially different.

veracity.statement: The report specifically cited the ban on offshore exploration, the 100 percent renewable target, and Lake Onslow as to why we are short on investment in fuel and firming, and that has left us dangerously short of reliable back-up generation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what a named commissioned report found about the causes of underinvestment in firming generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Frontier Economics report on the New Zealand electricity market. True if the report identifies the 2018 offshore oil and gas exploration ban, the 100 percent renewable electricity target and the Lake Onslow project as causes of underinvestment in fuel and firming; false if it does not name those three, or attributes the shortfall elsewhere.

veracity.statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current unemployment rate, described as just over 5 percent, sits below the 15-year average.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the most recent quarter published before 7 October 2025, compared with the mean of that series over the 15 years to that date. True if the current rate is below the 15-year mean; false if it is equal to or above it.

veracity.statement: Because getting stuck on the benefit at such a young age can have lifelong impacts. Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific lifetime-duration figure, drawn from evidence, for people who enter the benefit system before 25.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD's actuarial valuation of the benefit system (the benefit system valuation reports). True if it estimates an average of about 18 further years on benefit over the lifetime for people entering the system before age 25; false if the published figure is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two full-time minimum-wage incomes exceed the parental income threshold by about $33,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two full-time (40 hours per week, 52 weeks) adult minimum wage incomes at the New Zealand adult minimum wage in force on 7 October 2025, compared with the $65,529 parental income threshold. True if the combined income exceeds the threshold by approximately $33,000; false if the excess is materially different.

veracity.statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
veracity.explanation: Asserts an official expected count of young people who will lose jobseeker support in the coming year under the announced change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet paper and regulatory impact statement for the Parental Assistance Test. True if official forecasting puts the number of 18- and 19-year-olds losing jobseeker support in the first year at about 4,300; false if the published forecast is materially different.

veracity.statement: She’s as bad at maths as she is at structured literacy. Kāinga Ora has delivered more new-build homes in the last 23 months under our Government than the entire three years under the last Labour Government. Those are the facts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora new-build delivery over 23 months under the current Government exceeds delivery over the previous Government's full three-year term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora's published new-build completions. True if completions from December 2023 to October 2025 exceed completions across the 2020–2023 parliamentary term; false if they do not.

veracity.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a construction sector job loss of 20,000 and a cut of almost $1 billion to Kāinga Ora's building spend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS and filled-jobs series) between late 2023 and September 2025, and Budget documents for changes to Kāinga Ora's building capital allowance. True if construction employment fell by approximately 20,000 over that period and the Kāinga Ora building spend reduction is close to $1 billion; false if either figure is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: Was Kāinga Ora wrong when they advised that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 Kiwi jobs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of specific agency advice on the jobs-per-dollar multiplier for building spend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora advice to the Minister (briefings or OIA-released papers) on employment supported by building expenditure. True if that advice estimates approximately 5,200 jobs supported per $1 billion of building spend; false if the estimate is materially different or no such advice exists.

veracity.statement: Last week, the Government announced what we considered to be a risk-based, balanced system for earthquake-prone buildings that keeps life safety at its heart while saving $8.2 billion. The current system has the best of intentions but has placed a heavy financial burden on property owners, leaving 5,800 buildings currently still awaiting either remediation or demolition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a total national saving figure for the announced changes and a count of buildings currently awaiting remediation or demolition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's regulatory impact statement and announcement material for the October 2025 earthquake-prone building system changes, and the national earthquake-prone building register. True if the estimated saving is about $8.2 billion and about 5,800 registered buildings are awaiting remediation or demolition; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific percentage declines in Hauraki Gulf fish stocks, seabirds and marine mammals, attributed to named pressures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf reports. True if they record declines of approximately 57 percent in key fish stocks, 67 percent in seabirds and 97 percent in whales and dolphins; false if the reported declines are materially different or not stated on those measures.

veracity.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a near-$1 billion spend on Mycoplasma bovis eradication and a much smaller commitment to the Caulerpa incursion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI's reported cost of the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme, and government funding allocated to the exotic Caulerpa response. True if M. bovis spending approaches $1 billion and Caulerpa funding is very substantially smaller; false if the M. bovis figure is materially below that or the Caulerpa allocation is comparable.

veracity.statement: We did not need New Zealand First’s support to pass this legislation. We could have passed it in its original format with members of the Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a parliamentary majority existed for the bill in its pre-amendment form without New Zealand First's support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Party seat counts in the 54th Parliament and the recorded positions of National, Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori on the unamended Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill (the Environment Committee reported it back unanimously). True if a 61-vote majority for the unamended bill was available without New Zealand First's votes; false if it was not.

focus.statement: Well, I heard one comment from a parliamentarian this morning: “MPs’ homes should be safe places. No members of Parliament should have their people protesting outside their house.” Then I heard another member of Parliament saying, “It is appropriate to protest outside MPs’ houses.” The first was from the leader of the Labour Party, the second was from the justice spokesman of the Labour Party, but both of them voted against the bill. It appears that at least Duncan Webb is more consistent than his leader.
focus.explanation: A bill and a vote are named, so it is not pure tribalism, but the weight of the answer is the other party's internal inconsistency rather than the merits of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why we’ve got fast track—which that member and Labour oppose—and that’s why we’re opening up mining and oil and gas. Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
focus.explanation: Names specific measures — the fast-track regime, mining, oil and gas — so it engages policy rather than party character, though a share of the weight is carried by attributing outcomes to the Opposition's stance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve. But I, as a Māori, am not willing to enable the department or others to dictate to iwi and Māori what customary rights happen to be.
focus.explanation: Names a specific amendment made to the bill and the reason for it. Other parties are mentioned only to mark the disagreement on that provision, not as the subject of the point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But sadly, despite the Environment Committee unanimously recommending to this House that the bill be passed with no substantive change, at the eleventh hour, because of some active lobbying of the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, we saw this Government cave to that pressure, and they have chosen to water-down the protections in the original bill.
focus.explanation: Names the select committee's recommendation, the stage at which the change was made, and the specific effect on the bill's protections. Scrutiny of a named legislative decision, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: New Zealand is experiencing a renewable energy boom, which will bring prices down over time, but there is one barrier standing in our way: the energy system does not have enough back-up supply to keep the economy running when we can’t rely on hydro lakes and wind to generate electricity.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current build-out of renewable generation will lower electricity prices as it comes on stream — an outcome in the market, not a promise about the Minister's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE's quarterly sampled residential electricity price series (real terms, CPI-adjusted). True if the average real residential electricity price in calendar 2028 is below its 2025 level; false if it is equal to or higher than the 2025 level.

rigor.statement: The report specifically cited the ban on offshore exploration, the 100 percent renewable target, and Lake Onslow as to why we are short on investment in fuel and firming, and that has left us dangerously short of reliable back-up generation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference on the policy: cited findings about three named decisions are offered as evidence for a shortfall in back-up generation. The step from 'the report cites these' to 'that has left us dangerously short' leans on the report's authority without showing the magnitude, but the conclusion tracks the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why we’ve got fast track—which that member and Labour oppose—and that’s why we’re opening up mining and oil and gas. Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion that those sectors' opportunities exist in Australia but not here 'because the Opposition opposes those' does not follow, since the Opposition is not in government and cannot be the operative cause of what the Government has or has not opened up.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because getting stuck on the benefit at such a young age can have lifelong impacts. Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: a cited lifetime-duration estimate is offered as the reason young benefit receipt has lasting effects. The conclusion follows, though the evidence is correlational and the step to causation is left unstated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If that member is so wrong-headed to think that every single construction job in New Zealand is dependent on public infrastructure, then perhaps she needs to get a little bit more reading done, because, as is actually the case, the construction sector relies heavily on private sector development—things like housing development, which tends to be funded also by the private sector, Member Andersen, and things like the Auckland Port development, which is being funded by that organisation.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member claimed a $1 billion cut contributed to construction job losses, not that every construction job depends on public infrastructure. The rebuttal defeats a position nobody advanced, so the conclusion does not touch the claim at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy on the policy: two biosecurity incursions, unequal response. The inference is real but the analogy is asserted rather than established — no case is made that the two threats are comparable in tractability or expected damage, which is what the parity conclusion needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Crayfish and scallops have become functionally extinct.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that crayfish and scallop populations in the Hauraki Gulf have collapsed to the point of functional extinction (no longer playing their ecological role), as a present-tense fact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: University of Auckland / Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' reports and Fisheries NZ stock assessments for CRA2 and the SCA CS scallop fishery; true if those sources describe Gulf crayfish and scallops as functionally extinct or ecologically collapsed, false if either is assessed as at or near a sustainable biomass.

veracity.statement: There are around 2 million - odd people who live in the area around where the Hauraki Gulf marine protected areas are going to be established, in Auckland, Waikato, and the Bay of Plenty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the resident population of the three named regions adjacent to the new marine protected areas is roughly 2 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions at the date of the statement; true if the combined figure is of the order of 2 million, false if it is materially different (e.g. under 1.5 million or over 3 million).

veracity.statement: You actually can’t even kill Caulerpa or treat pests and other invasive species in a marine reserve. You’re not allowed to do anything. That doesn’t seem to make much sense when we’re thinking about how we increase protection and improve the abundance of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the marine reserve regime prohibits killing Caulerpa or controlling invasive species inside a reserve.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Marine Reserves Act 1971 and DOC's permitting practice for pest and incursion response inside marine reserves; true if there is no lawful route to control Caulerpa or other pests in a reserve, false if DOC can and does authorise such management.

veracity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific figures: protected area of the Hauraki Gulf currently at 6.7 percent, rising to over 18 percent under the bill. A Green MP in the same debate puts the protected share at about 6 percent, so the figures are contested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's regulatory impact statement and DOC's published figures for protected area as a share of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park before and after the bill; true if 6.7% and >18% match those published shares, false if the post-bill share is materially below 18% on the same definition.

veracity.statement: Today, eight of those beaches are currently closed due to waste-water overflows.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the speech, eight of the named Auckland beaches were closed because of waste-water overflow.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Safeswim / Auckland Council beach water quality status records for the named beaches on 7 October 2025; true if eight of them carried a no-swim or overflow warning that day, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: If I just go back a few months to 11 May, 64 beaches were either black or red flagged for waste contamination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 11 May 2025, 64 Auckland beaches carried a black or red Safeswim flag for waste contamination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Safeswim historical status data for 11 May 2025; true if the count of black/red-flagged sites was 64, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.explanation: Two specific assertions: 158 days of shellfish harvesting closure for Mahurangi oyster farmers in 2025 to date, and 4 million litres of sewage discharged into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/Auckland Council shellfish harvesting closure notices for the Mahurangi growing area in 2025, and Watercare's reported overflow volumes for the Warkworth/Mahurangi network; true if the closure days total about 158 and the discharge volume is about 4 million litres, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: So that has been done, and $15 million has already been put forward to deal with Caulerpa, which is that exotic invasive species which is causing a great concern right around the gulf and also up into Northland and down into the top of the Coromandel as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $15 million has been allocated by the Government to Caulerpa response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and MPI/Biosecurity NZ funding announcements for exotic Caulerpa response up to October 2025; true if cumulative allocations reach about $15 million, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Gulf is 99 percent exploited, that the bill protects 6 percent, and that commercial fishing is still permitted inside high protection areas — the 6 percent figure directly contradicts the 18 percent cited by another member in the same debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as passed and DOC's published figures for the share of the Hauraki Gulf under each protection category, plus the bill's provisions on ring-net and other commercial fishing inside high protection areas; true if protected area is about 6% and commercial fishing is permitted in HPAs, false if the protected share is materially higher on the same definition or no commercial fishing is permitted in HPAs.

veracity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill roughly triples the protected area of the Gulf and creates 800 square kilometres of high protection areas, and that this is the highest level of protection ever applied there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's schedules and DOC's published area figures; true if the high protection areas total about 800 km² and the total protected area is close to three times the pre-bill figure, false if either figure is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Conservation's own Cabinet paper states ring-net fishers could have fished elsewhere with minimal impact, and that ring-netting remains permitted in two high protection areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister of Conservation's proactively released Cabinet paper on the late amendments to the bill; true if it records that ring-net fishers could have fished in other parts with minimal impact and if the enacted bill allows ring-netting in two HPAs, false if the paper says otherwise or the number of HPAs differs.

veracity.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Government undertook to speed the bill's passage and that the bill nevertheless remained on the Order Paper for about two years before its third reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's introduction date and Order Paper history in the Parliament record, plus coalition or ministerial statements undertaking to progress it faster; true if roughly two years elapsed and such an undertaking exists, false if the delay was materially shorter or no such undertaking was made.

veracity.statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 fisheries plan consulted on options excluding bottom trawling from between 74 and 89 percent of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 Fisheries NZ consultation document on bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf; true if the consulted options span roughly 74–89 percent exclusion, false if the range is materially different.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the House, while the Minister is here, that, as far as I am aware, the Gazette notices to finalise that South-East Marine Protection areas has not yet been undertaken, and, and I hope that it is very soon.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Gazette notices required to give legal effect to the South-East Marine Protection areas had not been issued as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette record for the South-East Marine Protection Forum areas up to 7 October 2025; true if no gazettal had occurred by that date, false if the notices had been published.

veracity.statement: In November 2020, the High Court ruled that regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the associated minimum standards in the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were unlawful and invalid.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific High Court finding in November 2020 invalidating the named regulations and minimum standards on farrowing crates and mating stalls.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand High Court judgment of November 2020 on the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018; true if the court held regulations 26 and 27 and the associated Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 minimum standards unlawful and invalid, false if the ruling was narrower or reached a different conclusion.

veracity.statement: The new confinement period, totalling seven days, is a significant reduction from the current 33-day setting, and will be amongst the lowest in the world, with most countries we currently import pork from allowing their use for 33 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a comparative fact about international regulation: that most countries New Zealand imports pork from permit farrowing crate confinement for up to 33 days, making the proposed seven days among the world's lowest.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Farrowing crate rules in New Zealand's main pork-source jurisdictions (EU Directive 2008/120/EC and member state rules, plus Australia, Canada, US); true if most of those permit confinement of about 33 days or more and none permit materially less than seven, false if several major suppliers impose limits at or below seven days.

veracity.statement: There are fewer than 80 farms, with around 45 indoor piggeries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the size of the New Zealand commercial pig farming sector: under 80 farms in total, about 45 of them indoor piggeries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Pork and MPI figures for the number of commercial pig farms and indoor piggeries in 2025; true if the totals are close to under 80 and about 45, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: There are around 2 million - odd people who live in the area around where the Hauraki Gulf marine protected areas are going to be established, in Auckland, Waikato, and the Bay of Plenty.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a rough magnitude and names the three regions, but the figure is deliberately loose ('2 million - odd') and no boundary for 'the area around' is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the bill sets some time frames: 25 years will be the milestone where the first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity and improvement in the gulf will be carried out.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete statutory mechanism and timeframe — a comprehensive biodiversity assessment at 25 years — which a reader could look up in the bill and hold the department to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable percentages tied to a named area — a before-and-after figure someone could verify or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
specificity.explanation: Named location, named operator, a day count and a volume — a claim someone could take straight to the council or the operator and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So that has been done, and $15 million has already been put forward to deal with Caulerpa, which is that exotic invasive species which is causing a great concern right around the gulf and also up into Northland and down into the top of the Coromandel as well.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named response programme and the affected areas, though no timeframe or breakdown of what the money buys.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: During the committee of the whole House, Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments aimed at ensuring that there is a mandatory consultation process when giving permits, ensuring that the process requires consultation with mana whenua.
specificity.explanation: Names the stage, the instrument (tabled amendments) and the mechanism sought (mandatory consultation with mana whenua on permits), but gives no detail on the trigger, the threshold or who decides.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
specificity.explanation: Carries three checkable quantities — 99 percent exploited, 6 percent protected, commercial fishing permitted in high protection areas — rather than a general complaint about weak protection.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Gives an area in square kilometres and a multiple of the previous protection, both checkable against the bill, though 'highest ever level' is not operationalised.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: A named instrument with a precise numeric range that can be checked against the consultation document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In November 2020, the High Court ruled that regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the associated minimum standards in the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were unlawful and invalid.
specificity.explanation: Names the court, the month and year, the exact regulations and the code — enough for anyone to pull the judgment and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Firstly, regulation 25, which sets space requirements for grower pigs: this bill increases the k-value used to calculate minimum lying space from 0.03 to 0.034, a 13.3 percent increase.
specificity.explanation: Names the regulation, the parameter, the old and new values and the resulting percentage change — fully concrete and checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You actually can’t even kill Caulerpa or treat pests and other invasive species in a marine reserve. You’re not allowed to do anything. That doesn’t seem to make much sense when we’re thinking about how we increase protection and improve the abundance of the Hauraki Gulf.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if a protection tool forbids active intervention, it is a poor fit where restoration requires intervention. The conclusion follows from the stated premise, though 'you're not allowed to do anything' overstates it and no authority is cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think we stretch these services to the point of breaking and then we blame the organisations when things break.
rigor.explanation: A real causal inference offered in reply to the Watercare criticism — under-resourcing causes the failures, so blame is misdirected — but nothing is offered to establish the under-resourcing premise or to rule out the operator's own performance. A reasonable point with a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the exemption was unnecessary — is drawn from the Government's own impact assessment rather than asserted, so the inference tracks the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer was no, we can’t use either of those different tools, and that is, in part, because the Marine Reserves Act 1971 is very much about protection and being very, very focused on that protection only, and these reports had identified that there needed to be more than protection.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — bespoke legislation was required — is drawn from a stated mismatch between what the existing statutes do and what the reports said was needed, with the regulatory impact statement cited as the source. The inference follows from the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealand Pork, MPI, and NZVA advised that confinement for no more than three days before and four days after farrowing, combined with the provision of manipulable and deformable materials during farrowing, meets the needs of the sow while also minimising piglet mortality.
rigor.explanation: The justification for the seven-day limit rests on an appeal to the advice of the industry body, the regulator and the veterinary association rather than on the evidence itself. The authorities are relevant ones, but the underlying science is not shown, and one of the three is the regulated industry.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill provides a 10-year transition period. This aligns with international norms for changes of this scale and gives farmers time to plan, finance, and implement infrastructure changes.
rigor.explanation: The length of the transition is justified by an appeal to unnamed 'international norms' — no comparator jurisdiction, no capital cost or payback figure is offered to connect ten years specifically to what farmers need to finance and rebuild.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a policy failure with a named entity, a named waterway and named outcomes. Scrutiny of an infrastructure provider, not party point-scoring.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
focus.explanation: Directed at the operation of the permitting and enforcement regime the bill creates and who it will bear on — a specific policy consequence, not a characterisation of another party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to reflect that there’s this absolutely magic feeling when bills pass through this Chamber. It’s been a rare occurrence under this Government, unfortunately.
focus.explanation: A general swipe at the Government's legislative record with no measure, figure or outcome named. Nobody is insulted personally, but there is no policy content to hold on to either.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment and a specific outcome for a specific bill. Holding the Government to a stated undertaking on the measure before the House is scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So we have a long way to go if we want to ensure our gulf is cleaned up. We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation — 'unacceptable and totally objectionable' — aimed entirely at an organisation's practices and infrastructure failures. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed to anyone. Hard criticism of a record is the standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker
