divination.statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that enforcement of the new protections will fall on individual customary and recreational gatherers rather than on commercial fishing operators.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DOC and Fisheries NZ enforcement records for the new high protection and seafloor protection areas after commencement; true if prosecutions and infringement notices are predominantly against individual customary/recreational gatherers, false if commercial operators account for a comparable or greater share of enforcement action.

divination.statement: We will see the health of the ocean improve, and I’m looking forward to having visits in future years where we can actually point to real examples of where we are seeing fishery stocks grow back again in abundance.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the protections created by this bill will produce measurable recovery in ocean health and fishery stocks in the Hauraki Gulf.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DOC/Fisheries NZ monitoring and the Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' report following the bill's first statutory review period; true if biomass or biodiversity indicators inside the new protected areas show significant increases relative to baseline, false if indicators are flat or declining.

civility.statement: Now that we’ve heard nearly 10 minutes of spin, let’s put some facts on the record today about why this bill is such a shocker and a terrible indictment on this House, on this Government’s lack of commitment to animal welfare.
civility.explanation: Characterising the Minister's just-delivered speech as 'spin' imputes bad faith to him personally rather than engaging what he said. Short of a direct insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s called the Minister of animal welfare, but, in fact, this legislation proves he should rightly be called the “Minister of animal cruelty”, because it is undeniable: the evidence from animal welfare experts across the world is that keeping pigs like this is inhumane, fundamentally.
civility.explanation: Renaming the Minister as the 'Minister of animal cruelty' attaches the epithet to the person, not the legislation. A clear personal attack, even though it is tethered to a substantive claim about the evidence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I put it to the House and the Minister that this is not an accident; it is a cynical use of the parliamentary process to stop citizens who are concerned about legislation not being followed.
civility.explanation: Explicitly imputes bad faith — 'not an accident', 'cynical' — to the Minister's choice of legislative vehicle. A real civility failure, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the offer that I’m going to make to the Minister—which I’m not going to make through some botched hit job through the media, like the Prime Minister did with the energy reform hit job, and the more successful hit job that Erica Stanford did—is that we do want to work with the Government on an actual cross-party tertiary strategy that will actually endure a change of Government, because when the election happens next year and, God willing, I end up as the tertiary education Minister, I don’t want to have to rip up what’s already been done before.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and characterises their conduct as 'hit jobs', imputing bad faith to them personally. The constructive offer that follows does not undo the aside.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But those members want to focus on gender. Those members want to focus on those people’s ethnicity. I think by just focusing on gender and ethnicity, we are not going to deliver what polytechs should be delivering. Because that is just empty virtue signalling, and we don’t believe in that.
civility.explanation: 'Empty virtue signalling' imputes insincerity to the members opposite rather than engaging their position. Bad-faith imputation, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now that we’ve heard nearly 10 minutes of spin, let’s put some facts on the record today about why this bill is such a shocker and a terrible indictment on this House, on this Government’s lack of commitment to animal welfare.
focus.explanation: Names the bill and a specific policy area (animal welfare commitment), but the weight of the sentence is on the Government's character rather than on any mechanism or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, if anyone was in any doubt as to the essential animal cruelty of this Government, this bill proves the point.
focus.explanation: The bill is referenced, but the claim being advanced is about the Government's essential character rather than any provision, cost, timeframe or outcome. Mostly party framing with a thin policy anchor.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. There was a judicial review following that, which found it was a breach of the Animal Welfare Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that regulations issued in 2018 permitted farrowing crates and that a subsequent judicial review held this to breach the Animal Welfare Act 1999.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 as gazetted, and the High Court judgment in the judicial review brought against them; true if the regulations permitted farrowing crates and the Court held the relevant provisions inconsistent with the Animal Welfare Act 1999, false if no such finding was made.

veracity.statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the bill lifts minimum space allowances by 13.3 percent and that this figure is identical to what NZ Pork proposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The space requirements in the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill compared with the current code, and NZ Pork's public submission/consultation response; true if the increase is 13.3% and matches NZ Pork's proposed figure, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: Yet the SPCA have written to the Ministry for Primary Industries, asking for consultation; they’ve written to the Minister, asking for consultation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the SPCA made written requests to both MPI and the Minister to be consulted on this legislation and was not included.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SPCA correspondence with MPI and the Minister of Agriculture (obtainable under the OIA or from SPCA's public statements) over 2024–2025; true if written requests for consultation on the pig welfare regulations exist, false if no such correspondence was sent.

veracity.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately half of New Zealand pig farmers already farrow without crates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Pork industry statistics or MPI/NAWAC data on the proportion of NZ commercial sows farrowed outside crates; true if around 50% of farmers (or sows) use free farrowing, false if materially below that.

veracity.statement: Guess who liked the idea of that! The pork industry. Guess who advised against that! The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, the very advisers to the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NAWAC, the Minister's own statutory advisory body, advised against the 13 percent space increase and the ten-year timeline, while the pork industry supported it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NAWAC's advice to the Minister on the pig code of welfare and the draft regulations (published or released under the OIA); true if NAWAC recommended against the proposed space allowance/timeline, false if NAWAC supported or was neutral on it.

veracity.statement: It is happening all over the world, in the likes of Sweden, in the likes of Norway, right here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that free farrowing is already established practice in Sweden and Norway as well as in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Swedish and Norwegian animal welfare legislation on sow confinement at farrowing; true if both countries prohibit or effectively prohibit farrowing crates, false if either permits routine crate use as New Zealand does.

veracity.statement: I stand to speak on the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and I just want to point out that, actually, we’ve lost a large number of our pork producers over the last three or four decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a substantial decline in the number of New Zealand pork producers over roughly the last 30–40 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ agricultural production statistics / NZ Pork records on the number of commercial pig farms in New Zealand in the 1980s–1990s versus 2025; true if the count has fallen substantially, false if broadly stable.

veracity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 60 percent of pork products consumed in New Zealand are imported, principally from Canada, the US and Europe.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ import statistics and NZ Pork's published figures on the imported share of pork consumed in New Zealand; true if imports are around 60% and sourced mainly from those countries, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Just briefly to go back through history, the Animal Welfare Act was passed in 1999 by a visionary Government, a National Government actually, that saw the importance of animal welfare moving forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Animal Welfare Act 1999 was enacted under a National-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record and Hansard for the Animal Welfare Act 1999; true if it received Royal assent in 1999 under the National-led Government, false if enacted under another administration or in another year.

veracity.statement: The opportunity to tell the story to consumers that we indeed do have the highest standards of animal welfare for pork—and pork and chicken are 75 percent of the protein in the world—we can’t do that any longer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pork and chicken together account for 75 percent of the world's protein. The interposed claim is a quantitative one about global production shares.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FAOSTAT global production data; true if pig meat plus poultry meat account for about 75% of the relevant protein measure (global meat production or protein supply), false if the share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: In fact, these new requirements in the bill will be among the highest animal welfare standards in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the pig welfare requirements in this bill rank among the highest in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparison of the bill's farrowing confinement limits and minimum space allowances against EU Directive 2008/120/EC and the Swedish, Norwegian and Swiss regimes; true if New Zealand's requirements are at least as strict as the leading jurisdictions, false if they permit longer confinement or less space than those regimes.

veracity.statement: The committee received 210 written submissions, a relatively modest number in comparison to when Te Pūkenga was set up—I believe, from memory, there were about 2,000 submissions back then.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a submission count of 210 for this bill and roughly 2,000 for the legislation establishing Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on this bill and the committee record for the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill 2019; true if the counts are 210 and approximately 2,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 11 percent of those who submitted on the bill expressed support for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education's departmental report analysing submissions on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if roughly 11% of submitters are recorded as supporting the bill, false if the proportion is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Minister repeatedly says that Te Pūkenga was not financially viable, despite it returning a $16.7 million surplus last year, as it was intended to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga recorded a surplus of $16.7 million in its most recent reported financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual report for the 2024 financial year; true if the reported surplus is approximately $16.7 million, false if it recorded a deficit or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: We’ve already lost 19,000 construction workers, and last year, 3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships and there were 9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year under this National Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures: a loss of 19,000 construction workers, 3,700 fewer building apprenticeship enrolments last year, and 9,000 fewer apprenticeship completions year on year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ employment data for the construction sector and Tertiary Education Commission apprenticeship enrolment and completion statistics for 2024 versus 2023; true if the three figures match within rounding, false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: In fact, the Treasury analysis of this reform said that the newly established ITPs could expect financials that were the same, if not worse, than before Te Pūkenga was established.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's advice on the vocational education reforms concluded the new ITPs would face financial positions no better, and possibly worse, than the pre-Te Pūkenga status quo.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published advice and the regulatory impact statement on the vocational education and training reforms; true if Treasury recorded that view, false if its advice did not make that assessment.

veracity.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific outcome statistics for Australia's Free TAFE programme: a 37 percent lower likelihood of benefit receipt, and income increases for over half of participants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian Government (Department of Employment and Workplace Relations / Jobs and Skills Australia) evaluation of the Free TAFE programme; true if it reports a ~37% reduction in benefit receipt and income gains for over 50% of participants, false if the published figures differ materially.

specificity.statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (minimum space requirements) with an exact figure and an identified source for it. Directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This transition will not occur overnight; instead it will be managed over a defined period, providing certainty, enabling farmers to secure resources and support the need for compliance.
specificity.explanation: Speaks of a 'defined period' without defining it, and offers no figures, dates or mechanisms — a string of generic benefits in a debate where the length of the transition is the entire contested question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
specificity.explanation: A precise proportion with named source countries; checkable against trade data, though the category 'pork products' is left loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They will be statutory standard-setting bodies with majority of industry governance: six of the eight on the board will be from industry, ensuring that vocational education and training remains responsive to both new and emerging industry developments, as well as current industry needs.
specificity.explanation: A named institutional mechanism with an exact composition ratio that can be checked against the bill's text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill.
specificity.explanation: A single precise, checkable proportion tied to a named source of evidence (the submissions), stated without hedging.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Consultants have indicated that $190 million may be needed to restart the 16 polytechnics, and yet there’s only a minimum of $177 million in Government funding set aside to support this.
specificity.explanation: Two exact dollar figures, a named count of institutions, and the gap between requirement and provision made explicit. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would like to highlight two changes which ACT managed to get in this legislation: one is in new section 318, inserted by clause 22, which is about “Matters to be considered when appointing members of polytechnic’s council”.
specificity.explanation: Cites the precise provision by section and clause number and names its subject matter — anyone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Animal Law Association, who won a court case, and given that the Minister’s allowing this to run till February—we’ve got between December and February for another court case.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that fresh litigation over pig welfare regulation will be brought in the window between the December 2025 phase-out date and the February 2026 report-back.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand court filing records and public statements by the NZ Animal Law Association or SPCA; true if judicial review or other proceedings concerning farrowing crates or the pig code are filed between 2025-12-01 and 2026-02-28, false if no proceedings are commenced in that window.

rigor.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from evidence: existing adoption by half the sector is real support for feasibility. But the conclusion overreaches — that half have converted does not establish the remaining half can do so without a transition, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, of course, if you are changing regulations—and I know the other side of the House will say, “Well, Parliament is sovereign, and we can use Parliament’s resources to do this.”—what happens is that there is no recourse to the courts for judicial review for those regulations, for that secondary legislation.
rigor.explanation: A sound constitutional inference: primary legislation is not amenable to judicial review in the way secondary legislation is, so enacting regulatory content by statute does remove that avenue. The anticipated counter-argument is stated and answered rather than strawmanned.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have visited all 10 of the institutes of technology and polytechnics that will be stood up, and I’ve met with not only the senior management teams but also community leaders from their local community. Without exception, they have all been pleased and relieved that they are getting their polytechnics back in their regions.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote from a self-selected sample: meetings the Minister arranged with management and local leaders are offered as evidence of universal support ('without exception'), a conclusion the sample cannot bear, and one contradicted by the submission record cited in the same debate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
rigor.explanation: The evidence is offered and the conclusion tracks its direction, but the inference treats an observed association among Free TAFE participants as a causal effect of the programme, with no account taken of who selects into it. A real argument about a real policy, with a selection-effect gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But those members want to focus on gender. Those members want to focus on those people’s ethnicity. I think by just focusing on gender and ethnicity, we are not going to deliver what polytechs should be delivering. Because that is just empty virtue signalling, and we don’t believe in that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the provision at issue required councils to include Māori and to consider a range of factors, not to appoint on gender and ethnicity alone. The conclusion is drawn against an 'only these factors' position nobody advanced. This is a Rigor failure rather than a Focus one because it misrepresents the measure itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts about Te Pūkenga's formation: that it merged 16 polytechnics, that it merged nine workplace training providers (ITOs), and that it only began operating in earnest at the start of 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga establishment records and Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020 documentation: true if 16 ITPs and 9 ITOs were merged and the merged entity's operational start is fairly dated to early 2023; false if the counts differ materially or the entity was operating substantively well before 2023.

veracity.statement: I wonder if that is just because of their general dark approach on Dunedin, whereby the hospital where they promised to build a bigger and better one than what Labour promised; they just put it on hold for over a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government promised a bigger and better new Dunedin hospital than Labour had promised, and then paused the project for more than a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign commitments on the new Dunedin hospital and Health NZ / Ministry of Health project timeline records: true if the project was formally paused or under review for more than twelve months after the 2023 election; false if the gap was materially shorter or no pause occurred.

veracity.statement: When you see that only 11 percent of submitters on this bill were in full favour, there are big questions that need to be asked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure for the proportion of select committee submitters who fully supported the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, and its summary of submissions: true if approximately 11% of submitters are recorded as fully supporting the bill; false if the reported proportion is materially different.

veracity.statement: The member for Northland said, in an RNZ article, that the Government has no intention whatsoever to close NorthTec, and he promises that.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to another member: that Grant McCallum told RNZ the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec and gave that as a promise. The checkable question is whether he said it, not whether NorthTec closes.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ article referred to: true if it quotes the MP for Northland saying the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec; false if no such statement appears or the quote is materially different.

veracity.statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific counts of reductions across the vocational education sector in the preceding year: roughly 900 FTE staff, 500 programmes and 30 delivery sites.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga / Tertiary Education Commission reporting and Tertiary Education Union tallies of staff FTE reductions, programme closures and site closures for 2024: true if the three figures are approximately correct; false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Te Pūkenga merger cost $300 million in wasted money.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga annual reports and Tertiary Education Commission funding records: true if cumulative deficits plus establishment costs attributable to the merger total approximately $300 million; false if the verifiable total is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Well, I’m assuming most of the members know that the head office for Te Pūkenga actually is in the Waikato, in Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga's head office is located in Hamilton, in the Waikato — offered against the repeated characterisation of the merger as centralisation in Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's registered office and head office address in its annual report and Companies Office / Education Counts records: true if Hamilton, false if Wellington or elsewhere.

veracity.statement: As Chris Penk has previously stated in the House, it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly 50 percent trans-Tasman gap in the cost of building a stand-alone house.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative build-cost analyses for stand-alone dwellings (e.g. MBIE / NZIER / Productivity Commission work and Australian equivalents such as ABS building activity data): true if the New Zealand cost is approximately 50% higher on a like-for-like basis; false if the measured gap is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: You know, we’ve seen 20,000 jobs in building and construction gone since the day of the election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net loss of 20,000 jobs in the construction sector since the October 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs (monthly employment indicators) or HLFS employment for the construction industry, October 2023 compared with the most recent quarter before the statement: true if the net decline is approximately 20,000; false if materially smaller.

specificity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
specificity.explanation: Carries two counts, a named institution and a date — someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We met with an engineering organisation today: 20 percent difference between the salaries they earn in New Zealand and the salaries they earn in Australia; same company.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and a controlled comparison (same employer, two countries), though the organisation is unnamed so it is not fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because the locals know what they want, they’re going to stand it up. It will work. It will be much better than a Te Pūkenga.
specificity.explanation: No figures, no funding, no timeframe, no mechanism — an assurance that it "will work" with nothing attached that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete counts across three named categories with a stated period — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the biggest changes, I think, is that these small houses got bigger. They’re now 65 to 70 square metres and I think that’s fantastic.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete change the select committee made and gives the floor area in square metres — checkable directly against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You know, we’ve seen 20,000 jobs in building and construction gone since the day of the election.
specificity.explanation: A single figure with a named sector and a defined start point — checkable against official statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the Green Party will probably say, “Well, just tax the living daylights out of everybody.” That’s a guaranteed way of making sure we’ll actually all end up poorer.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: attributes a caricatured tax position to the Greens and then refutes the caricature. The conclusion ("guaranteed" universal impoverishment) is asserted with nothing offered to connect higher taxation to it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
rigor.explanation: A genuine internal-consistency argument: the stated purpose (local control) is tested against a specific structural provision of the bill she has just read out. The conclusion tracks the premise; it leans slightly on an unstated assumption that federation membership precludes local control.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because the locals know what they want, they’re going to stand it up. It will work. It will be much better than a Te Pūkenga.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: local preference is offered as the sole ground for concluding that the new polytechnic will work and will outperform the merged entity. Nothing connects wanting an institution to its being viable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But we didn’t really hear from homeowners, because they are not resourced to give those kinds of submissions in the select committee process, and so we will not know how this has a long-term impact on not only consumers and household owners who are affected by this but also for their insurance and for their banks.
rigor.explanation: A sound inference from a stated premise: an unrepresented group in the submission process means an unexamined class of consequences. The conclusion slightly overreaches — "will not know" treats select committee submissions as the only possible source of that evidence — but the reasoning tracks.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So in doing this, we need to make sure that we look after not just the core but also the areas around, the more far-flung areas.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the design of the regional polytechnic model and who it serves; no party framing at all. Vague on mechanism, but Focus asks what it is about, not how detailed it is.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
focus.explanation: Names a specific institution and a specific mechanism in the bill and holds the Government to its own stated rationale. This is scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wonder if that is just because of their general dark approach on Dunedin, whereby the hospital where they promised to build a bigger and better one than what Labour promised; they just put it on hold for over a year.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (the hospital timeline) but the weight of the sentence is party framing — a "general dark approach on Dunedin" attributed to the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A Government who has sat blindly on the side of seeing absolutely massive cuts in jobs in that town, watching a whole town become an absolute ghost town—that is on that Government.
focus.explanation: Names a specific town and a specific consequence of the policy — that is accountability, not party-bashing — but the framing ("sat blindly", "ghost town") carries much of the weight rather than the policy detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The risks here were raised with the committee over and over again—things like the way that hazards and stormwater might be dealt with on properties where people are building these properties without what you might expect in New Zealand for the kind of compliance checks.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill — the specific compliance risks created by the consent exemption. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It seems to be flip-flopping that’s based on vanity, and it’s vindictive and it’s full of lazy terms.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith motive — vanity and vindictiveness — rather than engaging the reasoning behind the changes. Short of a direct personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They sit there, and they sit really quiet currently about it because they know that what they are doing here, with this piece of legislation, is actually shameful for the sector—absolutely shameful.
civility.explanation: Imputes knowing bad faith — that Government members are silent because they privately know they are doing wrong. That is an attack on motive rather than on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This has been a personal vendetta, and today, here we are, another step in the process of achieving the Minister’s goal of overturning—the flip-flopping.
civility.explanation: A clear personal attack on the Minister: the reform is attributed to a private grudge rather than to any policy reasoning.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We think that there will be 13,000 more dwellings because of this legislation, and that is a good thing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the consent exemption for small stand-alone dwellings will produce roughly 13,000 additional dwellings — an outcome in the world, not a commitment to any action by the speaker.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE building consent and territorial authority records for consent-exempt small stand-alone dwellings after commencement, compared against the regulatory impact statement's baseline: true if approximately 13,000 or more additional such dwellings are recorded over the assessed horizon; false if the count falls materially short.

focus.statement: That’s really important, and I’d say that this Government has kind of done the opposite, really, by cancelling a bunch of State homes that would have been built over the last few years that would have helped address the housing shortage but also would have kept builders and construction companies employed during this time.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government decision (cancelled State home builds) and a specific consequence (supply and construction employment). This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing, so it scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s very good to see this Government doing something that isn’t flip-flopping.
focus.explanation: A remark about the Government's general habit of changing position rather than about any measure, cost, mechanism or outcome. No policy is named, so there is nothing here but party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where I come from, there’s a single Kāinga Ora house in Lyttelton, for instance—one house, and they’re selling that, and the woman who’s lived there for 42 years has been unceremoniously told that, in her 70s, she has to leave.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (Kāinga Ora asset sales) and a specific outcome in a named place. Holding the Government to account for the consequence of a named programme is on-policy scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst the contributions from the other side tonight haven’t been very substantive and we haven’t gleaned much more information from that tonight, we now found ourselves at the end of this process.
focus.explanation: A judgement on the other side's debating performance rather than on any measure, cost or outcome. Strip out the characterisation of opponents and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It would be good if we had a longer-term process leading up to this, because, if you look at the regulatory impact statement, it does say that it was developed in haste because it was part of the coalition agreement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for this bill itself records that it was prepared in haste because the policy came from the coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill; true if it contains a limitations/quality-assurance passage attributing constrained analysis to the timeframe set by the coalition agreement, false if it contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: This is also important in the context of councils’ consenting systems because, at the moment, council consents are at the lowest they have been over the last seven years, and I think there’s a lot of different reasons for that, but this takes some of that out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current level of building consents issued by councils is the lowest in seven years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued series (annual number of new dwellings consented) as at October 2025; true if the latest twelve-month total is below every corresponding total for the preceding seven years, false if any year in that window was lower.

veracity.statement: As I said in my first reading speaking, I’m really looking forward to how this is going to help the over 50 percent of migrants in my community now that we’ve got the parent visa up and running.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 50 percent of the people in her electorate are migrants, and that the parent visa category is currently operating.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census electorate profile for Takanini (birthplace: born overseas); true if the overseas-born share exceeds 50 percent, false if it is 50 percent or less. Immigration NZ visa pages settle whether the parent visa category was open to applications as at October 2025.

veracity.statement: It’s the worst February for home consents since 2012.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of new dwellings consented in February 2025 was lower than in any February since 2012.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly building consents issued (new dwellings, actual not seasonally adjusted) for each February from 2012 to 2025; true if February 2025 is the lowest of those years bar 2012 and earlier, false if any February from 2013 to 2024 was lower.

divination.statement: Our building code is, actually, wholly insufficient, and we will be facing another issue of something similar to the leaky buildings over the next 10 or 20 years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a further systemic building-failure crisis in New Zealand, comparable in kind to the leaky buildings crisis, arising within 10 to 20 years of 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE, Government inquiry or court/insurance records by 2045; true if a systemic construction-defect failure affecting tens of thousands of post-2005 dwellings is officially recognised (e.g. an inquiry or a national remediation scheme comparable to the Weathertight Homes Resolution Service), false if no such systemic failure is identified by that date.

divination.statement: It is interesting that the commentary to the bill notes that the Resource Management Act component of allowing these small, stand-alone dwellings to not have to go through a consenting process is going to be done through a proposed National Environment Standards for Granny Flats that is expected to take effect by the end of 2025.
divination.explanation: Relays the bill commentary's expectation that a National Environmental Standard for granny flats will be in force by the end of 2025, removing the Resource Management Act consent requirement for these dwellings.
divination.subject: other
divination.subject_name: the select committee commentary on the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette and legislation.govt.nz; true if a National Environmental Standard (regulations made under the Resource Management Act) covering granny flats / small stand-alone dwellings came into force on or before 31 December 2025, false if it had not commenced by that date.

rigor.statement: This sort of thing is going to be happening all over the place, but there isn’t that same support that we had for the leaky homes.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single constituent's damaged house to a nationwide pattern — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing offered to connect the one case to a population-level trend. The policy point about the absence of a remediation scheme is real, but the inference to 'all over the place' is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve built small buildings, I’ve tried to put them in backyards, dealt with the massive amount of issues that come up with councils that genuinely don’t want this to happen.
rigor.explanation: The case for the change rests on personal anecdote generalised to councils as a class, and the premise imputes intent ('genuinely don’t want this to happen') that is asserted rather than shown. Appeal to anecdote plus an unsupported motive premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And what’s more, that building certainly would not be a building which will fall under this regime regardless, because this regime is quite clearly about simple stand-alone single-story—no mezzanines—buildings complying with the Building Act and also delivered by licensed building professionals and other licensed practitioners—electricians, gas fitters and so on.
rigor.explanation: A valid rebuttal: he identifies the scope conditions of the regime and shows the counter-example offered (a consented 20-year-old house) falls outside them, so it cannot bear on this bill. The conclusion tracks the stated premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The shortcomings or the limitations of planning is that it enables something, but it doesn’t necessarily make that thing a reality.
rigor.explanation: A sound distinction between enabling regulation and delivered outcomes, which is exactly what supports her conclusion that further steps beyond this bill are needed. No fallacy; the gap is only that no evidence is offered for the size of the enable-to-deliver shortfall.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, councils, like any institution, are governed by the incentives around there, and there are some liability provisions in this, and it’s very good that those issues are thought through and that it is acknowledged that councils are creatures of statute and have to follow the statute.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that councils cannot be asked to act on the 'spirit' of the legislation — follows from two stated premises: councils respond to liability incentives, and as creatures of statute they must apply the letter of the law. The inference is valid on its own terms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that’s a good thing for us to focus on here because so much of the records that we’ve seen kept over time, and historically, around things like construction and building projects, have been kept in formats that are very hard to access, very hard to compare, and very hard to contrast, and because this bill has moved at pace, it does need to be closely monitored in its implementation.
rigor.explanation: Offers two premises — historical records are hard to access and compare, and the bill has moved quickly — to support requiring digital record-keeping so implementation can be monitored. The inference holds, though the link between record format and the specific monitoring need is asserted rather than demonstrated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: temporal sequence between the funding decisions and the consent decline is offered as the whole case for causation, with nothing to separate the policy effect from interest rates, developer margins or the wider construction downturn she herself describes.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s pretty simple: the dwelling must be simple in design, it can be up to 70 square metres, it must meet the building code, the building work must be done by authorised professionals, and councils have to be notified before and after construction.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the operative requirements of the regime with a figure (70 square metres) and named mechanisms (building code compliance, authorised professionals, council notification before and after). Someone could check each element against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Councils can use things that already exist in the Building Act. Section 72 allows councils to grant consent for building. Section 67 allows councils to take a liberalised view of a project and allow something to happen.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and two specific sections as the mechanism, so the claim is locatable and checkable, but the described effect of each section is loose ('take a liberalised view') with no procedure or threshold given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s time we started saying yes to easing planning restrictions and unshackling ourselves from the bureaucracy of local planning laws.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no restriction named, no mechanism, no figure and no timeframe — 'easing planning restrictions' and 'unshackling ourselves from bureaucracy' commit to nothing checkable, though the general policy area is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By simplifying the consenting process for small stand-alone dwellings, we are cutting red tape, supporting innovation, and enabling faster delivery of quality homes.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic benefits — cutting red tape, supporting innovation, faster delivery — with no figure, no timeframe and no mechanism beyond the bill's title subject. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
specificity.explanation: An exact count (33,595), an exact period (year to February 2025), a percentage change (7.4 percent) and a release date. Fully checkable against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And what’s more, that building certainly would not be a building which will fall under this regime regardless, because this regime is quite clearly about simple stand-alone single-story—no mezzanines—buildings complying with the Building Act and also delivered by licensed building professionals and other licensed practitioners—electricians, gas fitters and so on.
civility.explanation: Directly contests another member's central argument in a genuinely contested debate and stays entirely on the substance of the regime's scope; no imputation of bad faith or comment on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s the Greens—it’s the sanctimonious “tofu wouldn’t melt in your mouth” Greens—who are the ones who are driving the division and acrimony within our body politic, aided and abetted by Labour.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of two other parties. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the claim is about what the Greens and Labour are 'really like'. Civility is untouched because no individual is insulted, which is exactly the gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My encouragement to all parties across the House is to just think twice about the approach that is taken around intimidation and, frankly, to support this legislation that we have before the House to ensure that no New Zealander has to suffer people intimidating them in their private home—in their castle—and to do the right thing by that.
focus.explanation: Returns to the measure actually before the House and asks the House to support it, naming the problem the legislation addresses. Some party framing carries over from earlier in the speech, but this sentence is directed at the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
focus.explanation: Names two specific projects and a spend figure against a delivery outcome. This is scrutiny of a previous government's record on named policies, not content-free party-bashing, so it scores high even though the target is opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In a week where we've been talking about a 4:1 ratio of job seekers, that applies no more than the National front bench.
focus.explanation: Turns a live labour-market statistic into a joke about the other party's internal leadership politics. No policy, mechanism or outcome is engaged — this is about the other team's internal state.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There was an opportunity to do something to relieve New Zealand businesses and households of the burden of a broken energy system, and they fumbled it.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the government's energy reform package and what it was meant to deliver for households and businesses. Party framing in 'they fumbled it', but the subject is the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We will permit common low risk activities by default.
focus.explanation: Directly about the mechanism of the proposed consenting regime. Vague on detail — Specificity would mark it down — but Focus asks what it is about, and it is about the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Believe it or not, Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering has been removed at a time when talking about infrastructure, when those people opposite are talking about wanting to drive growth, they have cut the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme and a specific change to it, and tests it against the government's own stated infrastructure objective. Textbook scrutiny of a named policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealanders could ask the same thing right now, because Christopher Luxon promised a laser focus on bringing down the cost of living.
focus.explanation: Holds a named commitment on a named policy area up against the present outcome. Accountability for a stated promise is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Party members and the ACT Party members who are heckling across the other side, I challenge them to step up.
focus.explanation: There is a bill before the House, but this sentence engages none of it — it is directed at the conduct of the parties opposite in the chamber. No policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Chlöe Swarbrick and the Greens have been behind a lot of this, and the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and imputes bad faith to her personally — 'hypocrisy … outrageous' is directed at the person, not at a policy. Short of open abuse, but past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are not afraid of scrutiny, we welcome truth, but what we reject completely is the colonial gaze that turns Māori excellence into suspicion and Māori success into scandal.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism of the media and of an institutional attitude, in a genuinely contested exchange where he had ample opportunity to turn on individuals and did not. No person is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the only person in Auckland that doesn’t want that to go ahead is Helen Clark, but that is going to provide real economic opportunity for this country.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named individual for mockery, casting her as a lone obstruction rather than engaging her stated reasons. Light-hearted in tone, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is from the Government's own pollster, Curia, and I think this speaks very much to how weak and out of touch Christopher Luxon is showing New Zealanders he is.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Prime Minister's personal competence and character — 'weak', 'out of touch' — rather than on a decision or a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s not environmental protection; it’s performance art.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed entirely at a consent condition, not at any person. Derisive about the policy and civil toward everyone in the room — which is what a 0.9 looks like under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When people are trying to find some sort of vision, some sort of hope in New Zealand, they’re being driven overseas, because the only green shoots going on here is for those members’ mates in those circles that they operate in.
civility.explanation: Imputes cronyism — that the benefits are flowing to members' 'mates' — which is an allegation of bad faith against the members opposite rather than a criticism of a policy. No individual is named, which keeps it off the floor of the scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What an insult to our proud legacy, to the country that was the first to give women the vote in the world—the cowardice and ignorance of that passing shot by a member who did nothing to use the privilege afforded by being an MP in this Parliament and who threw passing shots and ran out the door, believing there would be no right of reply.
civility.explanation: Sustained attack on a departed member's character — cowardice, ignorance, having 'did nothing' with the role and run away. This targets the person's worth and conduct, not the substance of what they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You look at a quote from Benjamin Doyle saying that “No person should have to avoid going to the supermarket or the letterbox because they’ve been advised that doing so would expose them to violence.”, and yet, at the same time, you’ve got Ricardo Menéndez March writing letters in support of people who vandalise MPs’ offices and, at the same time, you’ve got the leader of the Greens in press conferences with a peace-loving actor who hands out the private addresses of MPs for people to go and hassle them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific factual matters: that Doyle said the quoted words, that Menéndez March wrote letters supporting people who vandalised MPs' offices, and that the Green co-leader appeared at a press conference with a person who distributed MPs' home addresses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Benjamin Doyle's statement; media reporting and any released copy of a letter of support written by Ricardo Menéndez March in relation to prosecutions for vandalising MPs' offices; footage or reporting of the Green Party leader's press conference and evidence that the person appearing distributed MPs' private addresses. True if all three are substantiated; false if the letter or the address-distribution cannot be evidenced.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that we’ve seen Duncan Webb saying, “Well, no, actually, we’re going to stick to our guns. We think people should protest outside MPs’ houses.” and Mr Hipkins has said that they shouldn’t, but they both voted against the bill that we’ve got in the House that deals with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Webb and Hipkins took opposite public positions on protest outside MPs' homes, and that both nonetheless voted against the government's bill on the subject.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the bill dealing with intimidation at MPs' homes, showing how Webb and Hipkins voted; plus the public record of each member's quoted statements. True if both voted against and the quoted positions match; false if either voted otherwise or the positions are misreported.

veracity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of 14 inquiries into Māori organisations and his party within 18 months, and that none of them upheld any allegation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published terms of reference and final reports of the inquiries named later in the speech (Public Service Commission, Electoral Commission, Te Puni Kōkiri, Stats NZ, SFO, Police) between roughly April 2024 and October 2025. True if the tally reaches 14 and no report upholds an allegation; false if the count is materially different or any report records an adverse finding — the Te Whatu Ora finding that Health NZ did not sufficiently protect public data is directly relevant.

veracity.statement: When faced with the Treaty principles bill, over 100,000 people hikoi-ed and over 300,000 submissions were made—over 90 percent in opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a hīkoi turnout above 100,000, more than 300,000 select committee submissions on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill, and an opposition share above 90 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police/organiser turnout estimates for the November 2024 hīkoi, and the Justice Committee's report on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill recording the submission count and the proportion opposed. True if the submission total exceeds 300,000 with over 90% opposed and turnout estimates exceed 100,000; false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Over a billion people saw the haka led by Hana in Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than one billion people viewed the November 2024 haka led by Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke in the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregate reported view counts for the haka footage across TikTok, X, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook as reported by platform analytics or contemporaneous media tallies. True if credible aggregate views exceed one billion; false if the best-documented totals are materially below that.

veracity.statement: That COVID hangover was caused by the previous Labour Government spending $66 billion of taxpayer money and raking up debt, over twice, to 44 percent of gross domestic product.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $66 billion COVID-era spend by the previous government and a more-than-doubling of debt to 44 percent of GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury records of the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund appropriations, and the Crown's net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP before and after (Budget Economic and Fiscal Updates). True if the fund totals approximately $66bn and debt roughly doubled to about 44% on the measure used; false if either figure is materially off or the debt measure has been switched between the two comparison points.

veracity.statement: That was the largest debt-fuelled spending binge in the developed world, according to the IMF.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, attributing it to the IMF, that New Zealand's COVID-era debt-funded fiscal expansion was the largest of any developed economy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IMF Fiscal Monitor database of discretionary COVID-19 fiscal measures as a share of GDP for advanced economies. True if New Zealand ranks first on above-the-line debt-funded measures; false if any advanced economy ranks higher.

veracity.statement: The gentailer’s share prices soared.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that gentailer share prices rose sharply on the day the government announced its energy reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZX closing prices for Meridian, Contact, Mercury and Genesis on the day of the energy reform announcement (early October 2025) against the previous close. True if they rose materially; false if flat or down.

veracity.statement: Simon Bridges, a former leader of the National Party, made it clear that the National Party had let the country down, that it had missed its opportunity and was not delivering what should be there.
veracity.explanation: Relays a criticism she attributes to Simon Bridges — that National had let the country down and missed its opportunity on energy reform. What is checkable is whether he said it and whether this is a fair rendering.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting or recording of Simon Bridges' public comments on the October 2025 energy reform announcement. True if he criticised the reforms in substantially these terms; false if he did not comment or said something materially different.

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that horticultural export revenue reached a record $8.5 billion in the year to 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI's Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries horticulture export revenue series. True if the 2025 figure is approximately $8.5bn and is the highest on record; false if materially different or not a record.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that apple export revenue never reached $1 billion in any year between 2017 and 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI apple and pear export revenue by year for 2018–2023. True if no year in that period reached $1bn; false if any did.

veracity.statement: In fact, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealander under his watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net fall of 20,000 construction jobs since the change of government in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs by industry (construction) comparing the quarter to September 2025 with the quarter to December 2023. True if the fall is approximately 20,000 or more; false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Every single day, 200 New Zealanders leave our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a departure rate of 200 New Zealanders per day. Ambiguous between gross departures of NZ citizens and net migration loss — the criterion should test both readings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the most recent year to September 2025: annual departures of New Zealand citizens divided by 365, and annual net migration loss of NZ citizens divided by 365. True if either reading is approximately 200/day; false if both are materially below.

veracity.statement: Australia is up 0.6 percent, the United Kingdom is up 0.3 percent, the United States is up 0.8 percent, Japan is up 0.5 percent, and China is up 1.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific quarterly GDP growth rates for five comparator economies over the same quarter in which he says New Zealand's GDP fell 0.9 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official quarterly real GDP growth for the June 2025 quarter from the ABS, ONS, BEA, Japan's Cabinet Office and China's NBS. True if each figure matches within rounding; false if any is materially different or drawn from a different quarter than the New Zealand figure he compares them to.

veracity.statement: In December 2024, the board sold Auckland Council’s shares in Auckland International Airport Limited at $8.08 per share.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the date and the per-share price at which the Auckland Future Fund board sold the council's Auckland International Airport shareholding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council and Auckland Future Fund disclosures, NZX announcements of the December 2024 block sale, and contemporaneous reporting of the sale price. True if the sale occurred in December 2024 at approximately $8.08 per share; false if the date or price is materially different.

veracity.statement: People are paying more for public transport in our city than they ever have in the last two decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland public transport fares are at a twenty-year high for passengers. Ambiguous between nominal and real fares, and between fare levels and total household spend — the criterion should test the real-terms reading, which is what the claim implies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport published fare schedules and average fare per boarding from 2005 to 2025, deflated by CPI, together with the level of fare subsidy over the same period. True if real average fares in 2025 exceed every prior year in the twenty-year window; false if any earlier year was higher in real terms.

divination.statement: After a period of consistent clarity about building, focusing on growth, focusing on investment, and giving confidence to the broader community, in our second and third terms the economy was growing well, and we managed to reverse the flow across the Tasman, and that’s going to happen again this time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that net migration flow between New Zealand and Australia will reverse again under the current government, as he claims it did in National's second and third terms after 2008.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ net migration series for New Zealand–Australia movements; true if annual net migration to Australia turns net positive to New Zealand (or at minimum reverses from net loss to net gain) at some point before the resolve-by date, false if New Zealand remains in net annual loss to Australia throughout.

divination.statement: There are at least four job seekers sitting on that front bench queuing up for that job, and Christopher Luxon’s days are numbered.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Christopher Luxon will be displaced as National Party leader, with a challenge coming from his own front bench.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The National Party leadership record. True if Christopher Luxon ceases to be leader of the National Party before the resolve-by date; false if he remains leader throughout.

divination.statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an increase of roughly 1,000 jobs in agriculture and horticulture in the Hawke's Bay region.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / employment by industry and region for Hawke's Bay, agriculture and horticulture, measured against the October 2025 baseline. True if employment in those industries rises by about 1,000 or more; false if it is flat or falls.

specificity.statement: The latest Electoral Commission figures show that, since April 2023, almost 31,000 voters have switched to the Māori roll, and more than 25,000 first-time voters have gone for the Māori electoral option.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, a named source and a start date. Anyone could go to the Electoral Commission's roll statistics and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s going to mean an estimated $4.5 billion does not need to be spent on strengthening buildings right across the Auckland division.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named reform and a named region. Missing the timeframe and how the estimate was derived, but there is something concrete here to check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In a few months, this Government—and it's set out in the Government's quarter four plan—will introduce a new resource management system with two focused laws: a natural environment Act which sets clear environmental rules suited to each region, so we stop arguing over trivia and focus on the real environmental risks that we need to manage.
specificity.explanation: Names the two replacement Acts, cites the quarterly plan and gives a rough timeframe, but no rules, thresholds or dates are supplied — the 'what' is named, the 'how much' and 'by when' are not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve slashed the red tape, we’ve got rid of the bureaucracy, and we’ve been out in the world hustling for trade deals so we have better markets to send our good products to, and, wow, is that making a difference.
specificity.explanation: No regulation named, no trade deal named, no figure and no timeframe. A claim of achievement with nothing in it anyone could check — and the surrounding text supplies no detail for these particular claims.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
specificity.explanation: A dated source, a dollar figure and an employment figure attached to a named scheme. Precise enough to look up and dispute.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the 2024-25 financial year, the fund generated $38.4 million in distribution income compared to just $10.2 million in dividends that would have come from retaining the airport shares.
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, a named financial year and an explicit counterfactual comparison. Fully checkable against the fund's accounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is esteemed to return 7.24 percent per annum over the long term, with 5.2 percent returned to council as an annual cash distribution, and the rest protecting the real value of the fund.
specificity.explanation: Precise return and distribution percentages with an explanation of what the residual does. No source named, which is the only thing holding it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This only further highlights that Māori will always be guilty by whakapapa, and that we will always be tried, convicted, and executed before the truth is revealed, whilst the wealthy get to hide behind name suppression and privilege.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from real premises — the cleared inquiries and the absence of follow-up coverage — but the conclusion is universal ('always') where the evidence is a set of recent cases, and the comparison to name suppression for 'the wealthy' is asserted rather than shown. Hasty generalisation, though the underlying pattern is offered as evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These aren’t isolated tales; this is the Resource Management Act.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from four anecdotes to a characterisation of an entire statute, and pre-empts the obvious objection by simply asserting the cases are not isolated. Hasty generalisation from anecdote — but it is a genuine inference about the policy, not a jibe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders cannot go to the regions and look for a job, because there aren’t any jobs there.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy suggestion, supported by the list of regional closures she has just given. But the conclusion — that there are no jobs in the regions — is far stronger than a list of closures can establish; closures at named sites do not show an absence of vacancies.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The lesson of Kerikeri, reinforced by the rapid success of Matawii, is clear: water security is the foundation of economic growth in Northland.
rigor.explanation: Evidence was actually offered — the Kerikeri GDP and jobs figures, land values, the Matawii-enabled joint venture — and the conclusion tracks it. The gap is that two irrigation cases are generalised into water being 'the foundation' of regional growth, with no counterfactual for what would have happened anyway.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer is worse, because this Government is making it happen.
rigor.explanation: Moves from a single observed instance — three children outside a New Brighton food bank — to the assertion that the government is causing it, with nothing offered to connect any decision to that outcome. Post hoc reasoning resting on an anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Apparently, we are to believe it is a really long bow to draw to suggest there is a connection. Well, I think not.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that a party is connected to an attack on a Minister's home from the fact of association alone, with nothing offered to link the two beyond proximity in time. Guilt by association, and the rebuttal is an assertion rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By comparison, had the sales occurred in late August 2025, when the share price had dropped to $7.60, Auckland would have received $78 million less. That timing protected significant value for ratepayers.
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic follows, but the conclusion does not: comparing the actual sale to one single later date at which the price happened to be lower shows the sale beat that date, not that the timing was skilful or that value was 'protected'. The comparison point is chosen after the fact, so the inference from it to a judgement about the decision is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are going through a difficult recovery. As I’ve said, it’s two speed at the moment. In our provincial industries, in the South Island, and our rural communities, they are experiencing growth but certainly in our cities it’s been very difficult.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a two-speed economy: growth in provincial, South Island and rural areas alongside contraction or weakness in the main cities during 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ regional GDP and regional economic activity indicators for 2025: true if provincial/South Island and rural regions recorded growth over the period while the main urban centres (Auckland, Wellington) were flat or contracting; false if the regional pattern is not split that way.

veracity.statement: Why should New Zealanders believe him that we are in a recovery when earlier this year he said that New Zealand was in a recovery, right at the very time the New Zealand economy was shrinking by almost 1 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the economy contracted by almost 1 percent in a quarter earlier in 2025, at a time when the Prime Minister was publicly describing New Zealand as being in recovery.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series for 2025: true if a quarter in the first half of 2025 recorded a contraction of close to 1 percent, and Luxon publicly described the economy as in recovery during that period; false if no such contraction occurred or the statements do not overlap in time.

veracity.statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government increased government spending by 84 percent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Chris Hipkins and the previous Labour Government
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure series, 2017/18 financial year compared with 2022/23: true if the nominal increase is approximately 84 percent, false if materially different on that measure.

veracity.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown debt tripled under the previous Government and that the Crown now pays about $10 billion a year in interest.
veracity.subject: speaker
