veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Crown accounts: net core Crown debt in 2017 compared with 2023 (true if roughly tripled), and the finance costs line in the latest Crown financial statements (true if approximately $10 billion a year).

veracity.statement: Yeah, it’s difficult, unemployment has ticked up a bit, but it’s the same as what it has been over a 30-year average, it’s significantly below what it has been over the last 15 years, and—unlike that member—we’re just not happy to actually be the party of people who don’t work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current unemployment rate is equal to the 30-year average and significantly below the average of the last 15 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the most recent 2025 quarter, compared with the mean rate over 1995–2025 and over 2010–2025: true if the current rate is at or below both averages, false if it exceeds either.

veracity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in NZIER survey data 4 percent of businesses name labour as their principal constraint while 63 percent name insufficient sales or demand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZIER Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion for the most recent 2025 quarter: true if approximately 4 percent name labour/staff as the main limiting factor and approximately 63 percent name sales or demand; false if the shares differ materially.

veracity.statement: You put the country into the biggest recession in 35 years, you created the longest COVID hangover of any in the Western world, you actually made sure that you tripled the debt, for goodness’ sake, and we now have a $10 billion interest bill.
veracity.explanation: Two distinct checkable claims: that the recent downturn was the deepest in 35 years, and that New Zealand's post-COVID recovery was the slowest of any Western country.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Chris Hipkins and the previous Labour Government
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ GDP series since 1990 (true if the 2023–24 contraction is the largest peak-to-trough fall in that period) and OECD comparative data on time taken to regain pre-COVID GDP per capita (true if New Zealand is the slowest among advanced economies).

veracity.statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 50 basis point cut announced that day, the eighth since August 2024, taking the OCR from 5.5 percent to 2.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Committee records for 8 October 2025 and the published OCR history since August 2024: true if the cut was 50bp to 2.5 percent and it was the eighth reduction in that run from 5.5 percent.

veracity.statement: Assuming today's reduction is passed on in full, a family with a 25-year $500,000 mortgage would have minimum repayments of $400 less a fortnight than they were in the middle of last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific saving — about $400 a fortnight — on a 25-year $500,000 mortgage between mid-2024 and after the October 2025 cut.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Recompute minimum repayments on a 25-year $500,000 mortgage using advertised floating rates in mid-2024 and after a fully passed-on 50bp cut in October 2025: true if the fortnightly difference is approximately $400, false if materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds receiving jobseeker support on health condition or disability grounds will be affected by the change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD advice and the regulatory impact statement for the parental assistance test: true if the number of affected 18–19-year-olds on jobseeker support (health condition and disability) exceeds 2,000; false if the official estimate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Our policy is designed for 18- and 19-year-olds that are on jobseeker benefit. When you go on a jobseeker benefit, you’re deemed able and capable of working.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that everyone granted jobseeker support has been assessed as able and capable of working — which bears directly on whether the sick and disabled recipients raised in the question exist within that category.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD jobseeker support eligibility criteria and category definitions: true if all jobseeker support recipients, including the health condition and disability category, are assessed as currently able to work; false if that category covers people medically assessed as unable to work at present.

veracity.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two labour-market movements since late 2023: 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey and filled jobs series: change in the number of unemployed 15–24-year-olds and in total filled jobs between the December 2023 quarter and the most recent 2025 quarter; true if the movements are approximately +10,000 and −36,000.

veracity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly 50 percent, 60,000-person increase in jobseeker support recipients over the previous Government's term, at a time when unemployment was 3.2–3.5 percent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets: jobseeker support recipient numbers in late 2017 compared with late 2023; true if the increase is approximately 50 percent and about 60,000 people.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents have fallen by $5 a week following the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords, against a counterfactual rise of $180 a week.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond data: true if median weekly rent fell by approximately $5 over the period since the interest deductibility change; false if rents rose or were flat on those measures.

veracity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the April–June 2025 emergency department six-hour target result was 73.9 percent, up from 71.2 percent a year earlier, on rising attendances.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand published quarterly health target results for April–June 2025 and the same quarter of 2024: true if the ED six-hour figures are 73.9 percent and 71.2 percent respectively and attendances rose.

veracity.statement: Well, 82 percent of children are now fully immunised by age two, up from 76.5 percent last year, representing the largest annual gain across all health targets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts childhood immunisation at 24 months reached 82 percent, up from 76.5 percent, and that this was the largest annual gain of any health target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand quarterly health target results for April–June 2025: true if the immunisation figure is 82 percent against 76.5 percent a year earlier and no other target improved by more percentage points over the year.

veracity.statement: The Opposition member wants talk about the wait-lists; I would just remind her that the number of people waiting more than four months for a first specialist assessment (FSA), under her watch, increased by over 6,000 percent while they were in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rise of more than 6,000 percent in the number of people waiting over four months for a first specialist assessment during the previous Government's term.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand first specialist assessment wait-list series, 2017 compared with 2023: true if the count of people waiting over four months rose by more than 6,000 percent; false if the increase is materially smaller on the published series.

veracity.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
veracity.explanation: Asserts there are 13,000 privately owned land parcels that block public access to the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: LINZ land parcel records for titles adjoining the coastal marine area: true if approximately 13,000 privately owned parcels abut the foreshore in a way that obstructs landward public access; false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the teaching workforce grew 2.5 percent in 2024, adding 864 teachers, the largest annual increase since records began in 2009.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts teacher workforce statistics, 2023 compared with 2024: true if the increase is approximately 2.5 percent and 864 teachers and no larger annual increase appears in the series from 2009.

veracity.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the teacher offer is below inflation and that Crown entity board members are receiving increases of up to 80 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The current NZEI/PPTA collective offer's annual percentage against Stats NZ CPI for the same period, and Public Service Commission / Cabinet Fees Framework decisions on Crown entity board fees: true if the offer is below CPI and any board fee increase reaches about 80 percent.

veracity.statement: We are determined to reverse the trend we inherited, which saw people under the age of 25 on jobseeker spend an average of 18 more years on benefit. This has been 49 percent longer than in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under-25 jobseeker recipients are now projected to spend an average of 18 further years on benefit, 49 percent longer than the 2017 projection.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit system valuation reports: average future years on a main benefit for jobseeker recipients aged under 25, latest valuation compared with 2017; true if approximately 18 years and about 49 percent longer than 2017.

veracity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures from the ERO attendance survey: 82 percent of students from poorer families and 84 percent from wealthier families regard school attendance as important to their future.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Review Office report 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?': true if the reported figures are approximately 82 and 84 percent for the two groups, and if the earlier survey showed a gap of about 10 points.

veracity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a review of 22 relevant studies found piglet mortality risk 14 percent higher where sows are not confined after farrowing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The literature review underpinning the MPI advice on the proposed pig welfare code: true if a synthesis of about 22 studies reports approximately 14 percent higher piglet mortality in non-confinement systems; false if the review's size or effect estimate differs materially.

veracity.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose farrowing crates and that every New Zealand animal welfare organisation, including NAWAC, opposes them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published polling of New Zealanders on farrowing crates (e.g. Horizon/SAFE surveys) and NAWAC's published advice to the Minister: true if a poll shows approximately 73 percent opposition and NAWAC's position is opposition to the practice; false if NAWAC accepted limited post-farrowing crating or the polling figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $61.8 billion budgeted for public infrastructure over four years, against $50.6 billion invested by the previous Government between 2019 and 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 capital allocations and the National Infrastructure Plan for the forward figure, and Treasury actual capital expenditure for 2019–2023: true if the two figures are approximately $61.8 billion and $50.6 billion on comparable definitions.

veracity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 761 private sector construction employers closed in the last year and that construction firms are being liquidated at a rate of two a day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Centrix / Companies Office liquidation statistics for the construction sector over the year to mid-2025 and Stats NZ business demography data on construction employers ceasing: true if approximately 761 employers ceased and liquidations average about two per day.

veracity.statement: It is a fact that I will repeat again: we have built more social homes in the past 23 months than the last Government did in its last three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts more social homes were built in the Government's first 23 months than in the previous Government's final three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD public housing supply reporting: number of new public/social homes delivered December 2023–October 2025 compared with October 2020–October 2023; true if the first figure is larger on a like-for-like 'newly built' definition.

veracity.statement: It’s quite interesting to see, today, the Minister of Finance saying, “I didn’t take any credit for it”, despite, in the first question before that, saying the Government takes credit for it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance both claimed credit for the OCR reduction and denied claiming credit, in the same question time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for 8 October 2025: true if Willis claimed credit for the OCR reduction in an earlier answer and disclaimed having done so in a later one; false if she attributed the decision to the independent Reserve Bank throughout and made no credit claim.

specificity.statement: How much smaller is the New Zealand economy today than it was when he became Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Asks for one precise, checkable quantity — the change in GDP over a defined period — rather than a general complaint about the economy. A precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
specificity.explanation: Two named percentages attached to a named source and a defined survey question — someone could pull the survey and check both figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact size of the change, the count of prior changes, the start point and the end point — every element is a number someone can verify.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is helping. We have introduced discipline to Government spending and we remain focused on responsible economic management that supports recovery, delivers the public services New Zealanders expect, and drives reforms for growth.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — discipline, responsible management, reforms for growth — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy change, the affected age band, a count of those affected and the particular sub-group — precise enough that the department could confirm or deny the number.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
specificity.explanation: Gives the unemployment rate range, the percentage rise and the headcount rise — all directly checkable against benefit statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances.
specificity.explanation: A defined target, a measured result to one decimal place, the comparison period and the direction of change.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are several cases that have been heard that will have to be re-heard in light of this legislation if it passes.
specificity.explanation: Asked directly how many customary marine titles would be exposed to re-hearing, the answer supplies 'several' — no count, no list, nothing that could be checked against the court record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
specificity.explanation: A percentage, a headcount, a year and a stated record baseline — all recoverable from published workforce data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re surging $413 million into improving classrooms and schools across the country. The investment package includes $58 million for maintenance work for all schools, which is a 50 percent uplift in their school maintenance grant; $255 million for improvements for small, rural, and isolated schools; $100 million over five years to fund urgent and essential infrastructure work.
specificity.explanation: The total, each component, what each is for, and the period over which one is spread — a fully itemised and checkable account.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m advised that around 4,300 fewer 18- and 19-year-olds will be eligible for the jobseeker support as a result of the parental assistance test, which has two parts: the parental income test and the parental support gap test.
specificity.explanation: Answers the question asked with a number and names the two mechanisms producing it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this side of the House, we believe that all parents want the best for their children and to ensure that their 18- and 19-year-olds are set up for a great life, which means they’re in employment, education, or training.
specificity.explanation: Offered in response to a precise question about the interaction with Working for Families, it commits to nothing checkable — a statement of belief about what parents want, with no mechanism, threshold or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete actions — fee increases, the Apprenticeship Boost cut, youth unemployment — but attaches no figures or dates to any of them, and closes on a general cost-of-living claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
specificity.explanation: Names the evidence base, its size and the effect magnitude — enough for someone to go and locate the review.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
specificity.explanation: A precise count of firms that have closed and a stated rate of liquidations, both tied to a defined period.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
civility.explanation: Turns a mocking nickname — 'the 66 billion dollar man' — on a named member rather than criticising the policy. Short of a direct insult, but it is sneering at the person, not the record.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, unlike the member, I get out of Wellington most weeks and I actually get out and see the real economy and I see real businesses.
civility.explanation: The contrast 'unlike the member' imputes to a named opponent that he is confined to Wellington and out of touch with reality — a jab at the person rather than at his argument about business survey data.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she accept responsibility for the anger that teachers, principals, and support staff are feeling, or will she continue to stick her head in the sand?
civility.explanation: 'Stick her head in the sand' imputes wilful evasion to the Minister personally rather than pressing the substance of the pay dispute. Pointed enough to land on the person, though well short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister explain what giant leap in comprehension it takes for people to realise that the first responsibility for a family member lies with the family and not the taxpayer?
civility.explanation: The 'giant leap in comprehension' framing casts those who disagree as slow to understand an obvious point — condescension aimed at the people opposite rather than at their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While education may not have done well for Duncan Webb, this Government thinks it’s important.
civility.explanation: A direct jibe at a named member's intelligence and education, made in response to his point of order. It engages nothing in the argument and exists only to belittle the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister is so out of touch that I bet you—and I’m willing to take a wager from anyone here in Parliament—that he hasn’t got a clue at all, because, in his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
civility.explanation: A sustained attack on the Prime Minister personally — that he 'hasn't got a clue' and is out of touch by virtue of his wealth. The target is the man's understanding and circumstances, not any decision he has made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: does he remember, with respect to the policies that he inherited, that the then former Prime Minister had had a huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up one night, and got rid of all those policies—how much more quickly could we have recovered if he had done that much earlier in his career?
focus.explanation: A set-up question whose content is a jibe about the opposition leader's 'policy bonfire' rather than any measure, cost or mechanism. There is a gesture at policies inherited, but no named policy and nothing to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I agree with the member that there must be tremendous regret from the Labour Government that had an absolute majority in the last three years and did very little with it, delivered nothing, increasing debt, spending, and borrowing.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other party's term in general terms — 'did very little', 'delivered nothing'. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here that could be checked or argued with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The jeering from the other side of the House during the last speaker’s speech is exactly why that side of the House and the Government is so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders, because you can jeer and laugh at the teenagers who need jobs, you can jeer and laugh at the fact that we are doing nothing for climate change in this House because of that Government, and you can jeer and laugh at the fact that this economy is tanking because of their inaction, but they won’t think that’s funny, because they are so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Wholly about how the other side behaved in the chamber and what that shows about them. Policy areas are gestured at in passing, but no measure, figure or outcome is named — the subject throughout is the opposing party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government isn’t on the side of ordinary New Zealanders; they’re on the side of tobacco companies, of property speculators, of the oil and gas industry.
focus.explanation: Characterises whose side the other party is really on. The three industries gesture at policy areas, but no measure, decision or figure is named, so there is nothing to engage with beyond the framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you have high inflation because spending went up 84 percent, you end up with 12 to 13 interest rate rises. That then, because of high interest rates and high inflation, means that, actually, businesses get squeezed because the economy’s in a recession, and, as a result, people, unfortunately, lose their jobs.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal chain about a real policy — spending to inflation to rate rises to recession to job losses — and each link is at least arguable. But the conclusion required (that today's job losses are the previous Government's doing) needs the chain to run past two years of his own Government's decisions, and nothing is offered to bridge that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No. The economy is where it is now because harmful and painful inflation in 2021, in 2022, in 2023—fuelled by reckless Government spending—had to be brought down over time with high interest rates.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal account: inflation required disinflationary interest rates, which suppressed activity. The weak link is treating government spending as the driver of that inflation without offering anything to separate it from global pandemic-era price shocks.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, anybody in a boat can access the foreshore and seabed, from any particular angle.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. The question concerned privately owned land blocking access from the landward side; that boats can reach the coast from the sea does not bear on whether people can get there over land.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I explained in the primary question, farrowing crates reduce piglet mortality by 14 percent.
rigor.explanation: The question put a list of specific harms to the sow; the answer rests entirely on a piglet mortality figure, which does not address the premise it is offered against. The figure is also inverted from the one he gave earlier (14 percent higher risk without confinement is not a 14 percent reduction).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have visited pig farms, where I have been there after piglets have been farrowed, and I saw absolutely no sign of any of that.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote against a behavioural claim from welfare science — and the anecdote is drawn from after farrowing, while the claim concerns nesting behaviour in the 24 hours before it, so it could not have observed what it purports to rebut.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me explain: the statement of commitments does not indicate a drop in planned spending, it records, instead, at a particular point in time, where contracts have been signed that would involve the Crown spending money but the money hasn’t yet been paid or even owed.
rigor.explanation: A valid technical correction: it identifies what the cited accounting measure actually records and shows why the inference drawn from it (a fall in planned spending) does not follow from a fall in that figure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
rigor.explanation: The comparison does not carry the weight put on it: a four-year forward budget allocation is set against four years of completed investment, in nominal dollars and without adjusting for construction cost inflation. Budgeted is not invested, so the 'huge step up' does not follow from the two numbers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are not enough jobs in this country for the beneficiaries that this Government is intent on punching down upon. It does not matter how hard you seek to punish people when there are not enough jobs for them to move into.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks its premise: if vacancies are outnumbered by job seekers, sanctions cannot move all of them into work. It leans on the earlier four-seekers-per-job figure without re-establishing it, and it does not engage the counter-argument that sanctions reallocate rather than create jobs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: departures to Australia are attributed to this Government's spending decisions with nothing offered to rule out the long-standing wage gap and historical migration cycle, and the closing clause asserts intent rather than showing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: According to the National Party MPs, they do not work hard.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The interjection being answered was that the Prime Minister worked hard; it is recast as a claim that people working two and three jobs do not, which nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Yes, it is the case that, as the economy recovers, we expect that more jobs will be created in the construction sector.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that construction sector employment will rise as the economy recovers.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / employment in the construction sector: true if construction employment at the end of 2026 exceeds the September 2025 quarter level, false if it is the same or lower.

divination.statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that departures of New Zealanders, particularly to Australia, will fall as the economy recovers.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, annual NZ-citizen departures: true if the annual total falls below the year-ended-September-2025 figure, false if it is the same or higher.

divination.statement: It’s now growing again in quarter 3; the growth in quarter 4 will step up.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that quarterly GDP growth in the December 2025 quarter will be stronger than in the September 2025 quarter.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases: true if December 2025 quarter growth exceeds September 2025 quarter growth, false if it is lower or negative.

veracity.statement: As a member of the Governance and Administration Committee that examined this bill, I can report that we've unanimously recommended that it be passed without amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the select committee's recommendation was unanimous and carried no amendments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Governance and Administration Committee's report on the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill: true if the committee recommended the bill be passed without amendment and recorded no minority or differing view; false if amendments were recommended or a party dissented.

veracity.statement: That is why, in addition to all the other things that Auckland Council already has on its list—there’s a $4 billion shortfall between the infrastructure it knows it needs to fund and the amount of money it can get from ratepayers—it also is going to have to turn its mind to another million people coming, according to the Auckland plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific $4 billion gap between Auckland's identified infrastructure need and its rates-funded capacity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's Long-term Plan 2024-34 / infrastructure strategy: true if the identified gap between required infrastructure investment and available rates-funded revenue is approximately $4 billion; false if the documented shortfall is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the food scraps collection programme has cost at least half a billion dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council budget and Auditor-General reporting on the food scraps collection service: true if total capital plus operating cost of the programme is $500 million or more; false if materially less.

veracity.statement: Well, this Government has committed to the City Rail Link projects and put down around $200 million for the first stage of grade separation in some of those really important parts of the network out in South Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific government funding commitment of around $200 million for the first stage of Auckland rail grade separation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/NZTA funding announcements and Budget documents for Auckland rail level-crossing removal: true if approximately $200 million has been allocated to a first stage of grade separation in South Auckland; false if no such allocation exists or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: I would note that of all the big metropolitan councils in the country, their rates increase over the last two years is the smallest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Auckland Council's two-year rates increase is the lowest among the large metropolitan councils.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Adopted rates increases for 2024/25 and 2025/26 across Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Hamilton, Tauranga and Dunedin city councils: true if Auckland's combined two-year residential rates increase is the lowest of that group; false if any of them is lower.

veracity.statement: So, in the first place, they said they were going to sell; they then decided they weren’t going to sell; they then managed to be the only council in the country that that managed to torpedo their entire long-term plan; they then became the only council in the country which ended up an observer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Wellington City Council was uniquely the only council to collapse its long-term plan and the only one to receive a Crown observer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council long-term plan 2024-34 records and the Minister of Local Government's appointment notices: true if WCC was the only council in that period to abandon/re-do its adopted long-term plan and the only one to have a Crown observer appointed; false if any other council did either.

veracity.statement: How can we talk about securing the future for generations to come when Māori, the fastest-growing population in Tāmaki Makaurau, over 250,000 strong, are not explicitly included in the governance of this fund?
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that Auckland's Māori population exceeds 250,000, and that it is the region's fastest-growing population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census usual resident counts and inter-censal growth rates by ethnicity for the Auckland region: true if the Māori population exceeds 250,000 and grew faster than other major ethnic groups; false if the count is materially below 250,000 or another group grew faster.

veracity.statement: To answer the question from that member, the official cash rate (OCR) has dropped from 5.5 percent to less than half of that, to 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the OCR has fallen from a peak of 5.5 percent to 2.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR series: true if the OCR peaked at 5.5% and stood at 2.5% on 8 October 2025; false if either figure is different.

veracity.statement: What that means is, when you refix the average mortgage, anywhere in New Zealand, you are saving $400 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that refixing an average New Zealand mortgage now saves $400 per fortnight.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ average new residential mortgage size and average one-year fixed rate at the 5.5% peak versus October 2025: true if the fortnightly repayment saving on refixing an average-sized mortgage is around $400; false if materially less (or if it only holds for a mortgage far above average size).

veracity.statement: It's a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, but how revealing that we had a National Party MP just stand up and tell us that he was half-hearted about Auckland—a third of New Zealand's population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a National MP had just told the House he was half-hearted about Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Tim Costley's speech earlier in this debate: true if he said he was half-hearted about Auckland; false if the remark was directed at a smaller area (e.g. Te Atatū) rather than Auckland as a whole.

veracity.statement: The previous system would have, if it had been continued, cost an additional $1 million to administer that fund, so it is useful to have that system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $1 million additional administration cost for the arrangement the fund replaced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council business case / select committee evidence on the Auckland Future Fund's administration costs: true if continuing the previous arrangement was estimated to cost about $1 million more to administer; false if no such estimate exists or it is materially different.

veracity.statement: It is, in fact, one of the world’s most diverse cities, and more than 30 percent of its population is, in fact, Asian.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 30 percent of Auckland's population identifies as Asian.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census ethnicity data for the Auckland region: true if the Asian ethnic group is more than 30% of the usual resident population; false if below 30%.

veracity.statement: If she thinks this is such a great policy and such a great bill to put in place protections around safeguarding public assets in an elected organisation like Auckland Council, why didn't the National Party do that when they flogged off a 50 percent share of the energy gentailers in 2013, 2014, and promptly frittered away the billions of dollars that came into the Government coffers as a result of that privatisation exercise that the National Party did?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National sold a 50 percent share of the energy gentailers in 2013-14.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Mixed Ownership Model legislation and the share sale records for Mighty River Power, Meridian and Genesis: true if 50 percent of the gentailers was sold; false if the sales were capped at 49 percent with the Crown retaining a majority.

veracity.statement: As I said before, they frittered away billions and billions of dollars of public value without actually reinvesting that in things that would seriously improve the productivity of New Zealand's economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the asset sale proceeds were spent without being reinvested in productive capital.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury records of the Future Investment Fund: true if the gentailer sale proceeds were not allocated to identifiable capital investment; false if the proceeds were placed in the Future Investment Fund and allocated to named capital projects (schools, hospitals, KiwiRail, irrigation).

specificity.statement: It requires public consultation through a long-term plan process and a resolution to be passed by at least 75 percent of council members.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (long-term plan consultation) and the exact threshold (75 percent of members) governing distributions; someone could check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been far too many bills going through a curtailed process and it will not only have bad effects in the community but it will waste time in the next Parliament when we could be working constructively.
specificity.explanation: A substantive complaint about legislative process, but no bill is named, no count given and no consequence quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Auckland Council: last year, 6.8 percent on the residential rates; this year, 5.8.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, dated figures for a named council's residential rates increases; directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, make no mistake, there's more work that needs to be done to ensure that councils across the country—and certainly in our largest city—have the resources that they need to do well and to provide the basic essentials that people deserve, whether it's picking up the rubbish, whether it's clean drinking water, whether it's adequate public transport, and a thriving natural environment to protect us against extreme weather events.
specificity.explanation: Lists service areas but supplies no funding mechanism, no amount and no timeframe; 'more work needs to be done' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What that means is, when you refix the average mortgage, anywhere in New Zealand, you are saving $400 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: A concrete dollar figure attached to a named event (refixing a mortgage), precise enough to be checked or acted on, though the mortgage size it assumes is left out.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They’ve put in this clause, clause 11, which requires a supermajority of 75 percent—75 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and the exact threshold it imposes; fully checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Their expectation is that they will receive 7.24 percent in terms of returns, and they will invest 2 percent of that return back into the fund to grow the share of the fund and return 5.25 percent to the council where they can actually spend it or invest it on whatever the Auckland Council deems fit to use that fund for.
specificity.explanation: Precise expected return, reinvestment rate and distribution rate, with the mechanism for each; directly checkable against the fund's statement of investment policy.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, that's the way, in my view, that Minister Goldsmith should have been looking at any changes to voter enrolment.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested criticism of a named Minister's handling of enrolment law, aimed entirely at the process he chose rather than at him personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That must sound like Armageddon to the Green Party. I’m sure that Julie Anne Genter would be having an absolute meltdown if she was here right now, but, in fact, growth demands infrastructure, and it’s not always the infrastructure that we like.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and mocks her presumed emotional state ('an absolute meltdown'); a personal jibe rather than engagement with her position on infrastructure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was fascinating listening to Simon Court there. I think he probably spent the fund about a hundred times over!
civility.explanation: Pointed teasing directed at a colleague rather than at his argument, but light and short of sneering or an attack on competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They can’t see the woods for the Woods on that side!
civility.explanation: A pun turning a named member into the punchline; mockery of a person rather than of anything she argued, though brief and not abusive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, but how revealing that we had a National Party MP just stand up and tell us that he was half-hearted about Auckland—a third of New Zealand's population.
civility.explanation: 'How revealing' imputes an indifference to Aucklanders to a named colleague personally, on the strength of an aside, rather than engaging anything he argued about the fund.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also want to acknowledge the courage of Auckland Council in the face of the regressive forces which say, “No matter what assets you’ve got, whether they’re performing well or badly, you should never sell them. Assets should always remain stashed in a cupboard under the stairs or at the back of the garage because they’re assets.” That makes no sense.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing position on asset retention is restated in a deliberately absurd form (assets 'stashed in a cupboard under the stairs') and then refuted in that form. The refutation does not touch the actual argument for public ownership.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: a single kerbside food-scraps collection programme is offered as the cause of a council-wide infrastructure funding shortfall of billions. Even granting the cost figure, the conclusion is orders of magnitude larger than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: None of those homes can be delivered without the enabling infrastructure, such as a four-lane bypass around the little town of Kumeū, which, if that bypass goes in, will be able to grow and flourish just like other towns are when bypasses go in.
rigor.explanation: Argument from analogy with no connecting evidence: because some Kāpiti towns grew after Transmission Gully, Kumeū is said to be certain to grow after a bypass. It also asserts a strict necessity ('none of those homes can be delivered') without support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The current mechanisms, including letters of expectation, statements of intent, and council policies, are weak tools for protecting Māori interests. They do not ensure that Māori voices are heard where it matters at most, particularly at the decision-making table.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the bill: because the named instruments are expectations rather than binding requirements, they cannot guarantee representation. The step from 'non-binding' to 'will not deliver' is asserted rather than evidenced, but it follows reasonably.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The real value of the capital has to increase every single year.
rigor.explanation: Overstates what he has just quoted: clause 8(b) requires maintaining or increasing real capital value over time, so an annual increase does not follow from the text he read out. The conclusion is stronger than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That traffic volume is only going to increase.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that daily traffic volumes through Kumeū and Huapai will rise from their current level.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Transport Agency / Auckland Transport traffic count data for SH16 through Kumeū and Huapai: true if the average daily vehicle count is higher than the ~15,000 cited at the date of the statement; false if it is flat or lower.

divination.statement: It might make $40 million, $50 million a year, that’s going to be a significant benefit, but it’s not going to pay for all of those things—and certainly not all the things that Simon Court was talking about—in a short period of time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the annual income the fund will generate for distribution to the council.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Future Fund / Auckland Council annual reports: true if the fund's annual income available for distribution falls in the $40-50 million range; false if it is materially outside that band.

focus.statement: If this fund is to protect intergenerational wealth, then Māori must have a say in what gets sold, how funds are invested, and who benefits from the returns.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill's mechanism — asset disposal, investment decisions and distribution of returns — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If she thinks this is such a great policy and such a great bill to put in place protections around safeguarding public assets in an elected organisation like Auckland Council, why didn't the National Party do that when they flogged off a 50 percent share of the energy gentailers in 2013, 2014, and promptly frittered away the billions of dollars that came into the Government coffers as a result of that privatisation exercise that the National Party did?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (the 2013-14 gentailer share sales) and a specific contrast with the safeguards in this bill. Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure, not content-free party-bashing, though the framing is partisan.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is growing at a rate of about 50,000 people per year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Auckland's population is growing by roughly 50,000 people annually.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region: true if annual population growth in the years to 2025 is approximately 50,000; false if materially lower (e.g. under ~35,000) or higher.

veracity.statement: The sell-down of council’s final shareholding in the airport last year, as has been articulated, formed the basis for this $1.3 billion fund that now sits as the Auckland Future Fund.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council long-term plan documents and NZX disclosures on the 2024 Auckland Airport share sell-down: true if the sale was of the council's remaining stake and the fund was established at approximately $1.3 billion; false if the amount or the residual-stake description is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: As has also been mentioned, there have been other contributions—one being in June, by the Port of Auckland, when they announced the special dividend of $45 million to be paid as a capital contribution into the Auckland Future Fund. veracity.explanation: Asserts Ports of Auckland declared a $45 million special dividend in June paid as capital into the Auckland Future Fund, in addition to a $52 million ordinary dividend to the council.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ports of Auckland Ltd annual report / Auckland Council announcements for the year to June 2025: true if a special dividend of about $45 million was directed to the Auckland Future Fund alongside an ordinary dividend of about $52 million; false if the figures or destinations differ materially.

veracity.statement: Of course, that was only made possible by the likes of the fast-track legislation, another amazing bit of legislation that this Government has passed through the House for the economic growth of New Zealand and of Aucklanders—similarly, this key bill as well, which will also add to that economic growth.

veracity.statement: It has particularly been requested by women who have been stalked by people who obtained their home address through the Companies Office records.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions to the select committee on this bill, the bill's explanatory note and MBIE/Companies Office policy material: true if submissions or documented requests from stalking victims are on the record; false if no such submissions or requests exist.

divination.statement: In fact, Auckland could reach 2 million people by 2030, so that just gives you some indication of the challenges that lie ahead and the infrastructure need that is unrelenting.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Auckland's population reaches 2 million by 2030.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Auckland region resident population estimate as at 30 June 2030: true if at or above 2,000,000; false if below.

divination.statement: Let’s not forget the City Rail Link that’s opening next year, guys, and that being a council and that being a former National Government that kicked that off and that will be there to cut the ribbon.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the City Rail Link opens in 2026, the year following the statement.

divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / City Rail Link Ltd opening announcements: true if the CRL opens for public passenger service on or before 31 December 2026; false if opening slips into 2027 or later.

specificity.statement: This Government is working very closely with this council, as you can see. specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill, the select committee it sits with, a named agency reform programme and a 30-year transport plan; concrete enough for a listener to look each item up, though it gives no dollar figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s so good to have these safeguards in place so that this money will be used for the long-term benefit.
specificity.explanation: A substantive debate on the fund's design, but the statement names no safeguard, no mechanism, no figure and no timeframe — 'long-term benefit' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is the kind of Government we are; we are a Government that is focused not on the here and now but on the next 10, 20, 30 years.
specificity.explanation: A self-description with no policy, mechanism, figure or milestone attached; 'the next 10, 20, 30 years' is a rhetorical horizon rather than a checkable commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: An Order in Council is an order that’s issued by the Executive Council—that’s the Ministers of the Crown—to put something into effect, and it’s often used to bring legislation into effect. So, in effect, what it will take for this legislation to come into effect is a Cabinet decision. Unless that hasn’t happened, there’s a hard line there of a year from the date of Royal assent.
specificity.explanation: Defines the mechanism, identifies who exercises it, and gives the backstop period and the date it runs from — a listener could check the commencement clause against this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the member also explain why new section 360E was necessary when section 192 already provides address for service requirements. specificity.explanation: Names the new section, the existing section it is said to duplicate, and the precise comparison sought; anyone could take the two provisions and check the claim of duplication.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Really, it's about what mechanisms are in place in this interpretation to ensure that the alternative addresses that are given are still functional for legal and services purposes.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete issue — whether a substituted address remains usable for service and legal purposes — but names no test, no verification step and no provision that would supply one.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I could only possibly speak for 10 minutes if I had a plethora of notes in front of me, because that’s what some members obviously need to spend 10 minutes talking in the House—but not me.
civility.explanation: Not an argument about anything before the House but a sneer at other members' need for notes — mockery of colleagues' ability rather than of any policy position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I’m not going to denigrate the speaker—I’m sure she misspoke and was just trying to give the right amount of praise to Auckland—but, of course, we have a number of brilliant cities in this country: Christchurch, Dunedin, Timaru.
civility.explanation: A genuine opportunity to attack an opponent for an overstated claim; he corrects the substance, expressly declines to denigrate her, and attributes the slip to good intentions.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m assuming the member uses a smartphone and that, in fact, he could call up the Companies Act himself and have a look at it.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner rather than the question — the implication is that he has not bothered to do elementary preparation, which is a comment on him rather than on the clause.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Dr Duncan Webb seems to have an issue with members of this Chamber scrutinising legislation as it comes through the passage of Parliament.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named member — that he objects to scrutiny itself — rather than engaging whatever the interjection actually was.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Jan Tinetti pipes up. She might finally have something meaningful to contribute to this Chamber.
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on a named member's worth as a parliamentarian, with no reference to anything she said or to the clause under debate.

civility.statement: There's not much else taking up the brain space; I'll tell you that.
civility.explanation: A jibe at the intelligence of the member heckling him — an attack on personal capacity rather than on an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course, it allows for internal or external governance structures, including trusts or other entities. That’s important, because we don’t want to put this investment fund inside a square box with very hard, thick, bold outlines that they can’t be manoeuvred in and out of. We want to provide some flexibility, because we don’t know what the future’s going to bring in the next 30 years for Auckland.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: future institutional forms are unknown, therefore the governance provision should not be locked to one structure. The premise supports the conclusion, though the case for flexibility over a defined structure rests on assertion rather than any evidence about how such funds have fared.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The director may well go to all extents to provide an alternative address, but if there’s no requirement to actually change it and make sure that the public record reflects that fact, wouldn’t that therefore defeat the intention of the bill in the first place?
rigor.explanation: A sound inference drawn from the drafting: if the bill's purpose is to keep a residential address off the public record, a permissive 'may' leaves that purpose defeasible. The conclusion tracks the premise about the word used in the clause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, this bill has a different purpose. The purpose of this bill is to ensure that, in some cases, a director doesn’t have to put their own personal address in the Companies Office records; they can use an alternative address. Calling it an address for service would confuse it with the legal reason of having a place where papers can be served.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows cleanly from the distinction drawn: the two provisions serve different functions (locating a director versus serving documents), so reusing the existing term would conflate them. Premises and conclusion are properly connected, with no appeal or gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Then Mr Rutherford talked about the administrative burden for companies. There is no extra administrative burden for companies. They already have to keep track of the addresses of directors.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is supported by the stated premise — an existing duty to maintain director addresses means substituting one address for another adds no new obligation. It leaves a small gap (the alternative address must itself be maintained alongside the process for obtaining it), which she closes only later.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I'm going to suggest further that a director who goes to the efforts to have an alternative address—and there is a process there—will also be similarly motivated to ensure that the company's register is updated.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable point, but it answers a question about legal requirement with an assumption about motivation — the inference from 'a director will want to' to 'no obligation is needed' leaves the gap the questioner identified.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, it allows for internal or external governance structures, including trusts or other entities. That’s important, because we don’t want to put this investment fund inside a square box with very hard, thick, bold outlines that they can’t be manoeuvred in and out of. We want to provide some flexibility, because we don’t know what the future’s going to bring in the next 30 years for Auckland.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism in the bill — how the fund may be governed and why the provision is drafted permissively — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A director has an incentive to get that address changed to an alternative address. I don't think we need to legislate that the director needs to do that, and it gives the company the capacity to act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the clause: because directors are self-interested in changing the address, a permissive "may" suffices. The conclusion outruns the premise — an incentive on the director says nothing about a company that declines to act, which is the gap the question was about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These are not mere frivolous applications for the sake of it. A person has to be able to say that they think they are at risk of physical or mental harm. I sincerely doubt that all 650,000 directors on the register of directors are going to turn up tomorrow the minute the bill is through asking for one of these, and I think it's not reasonable to engage in that kind of scaremongering.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference from the statutory test: because the application requires a declaration of likely physical or mental harm, mass uptake by all registered directors is implausible. The conclusion tracks the premise; the only slack is that it addresses the extreme version of the objection rather than a merely high volume.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I was, of course, admitted to the New Zealand Institute of Chartered Accountants myself in 1992. There are plenty of us in the Labour caucus who have owned businesses, have business experience, and know our way around the Income Tax Act, amongst other things.
rigor.explanation: A rebuttal by counterexample: the claim that there are no chartered accountants on the Government benches is answered by naming one. The inference is sound; the second sentence broadens to "business experience", which is a looser claim than the one being rebutted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other thing that I think is a useful thing that has been put into this is that each application can apply to more than one company. It would be, again, a nonsensical situation if every company that each director was a director of had to be individually applied for.
rigor.explanation: A clean reductio: the alternative drafting would force multiple identical applications from one director, which supports the multi-company provision. Conclusion follows from what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My fear is that the way it is drafted now, reasonableness applies to (a) and not to (b). Therefore when the registrar is looking at what they have to do to ensure the alternative address is publicly available from the New Zealand register, they therefore have to take all steps. Because a plain interpretation of that section is that if Parliament had intended those steps to be reasonable, it would have said so. But by deliberately excluding it from (b) and including it in (a), the only interpretation available to a court of law in interpreting the section is that that is an absolute provision.
rigor.explanation: A standard expressio unius interpretive argument: the qualifier appears in one limb and not the other, so the second limb is unqualified. The inference is sound; "the only interpretation available to a court" overstates what the premises establish, since purposive reading could cure it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many Māori organisations’ trustees, Dr Russell, are listed as shareholders in their personal names, and not because they own the shares themselves but because they’re often holding them on behalf of iwi, hapū, and whānau. These trustees often aren’t directors, and yet they can face the serious risk and pressure and even the harassment from within their own communities, especially when decisions are contested.
rigor.explanation: Premises (trustees appear as personal-name shareholders; they are not directors; they face harassment) support the conclusion that the bill's director-only eligibility leaves a real gap. The harassment premise is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the main slack.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason I ask that is that this is about safety and security and the wellbeing of directors of companies, and these are not all the big corporate companies that we might be thinking of. You know, when you look at an electorate like mine on the Kāpiti Coast, but it’s representative of all of New Zealand, that the average company has one employee, maybe one director, they are working hard to get this country ahead, and not everyone necessarily has the means to pay for a fee.
rigor.explanation: An argument that the prescribed fee should be ruled out: most registered companies are very small, small operators may lack the means, therefore a fee would ration a safety protection by ability to pay. The conclusion follows; the step from "not everyone has the means" to a fee being a real barrier is asserted rather than sized.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To the question from Tom Rutherford about inconsistencies between the company's records and the register of companies records, if the member cared to go to section 215 in the Companies Act, he would see that a company is required to keep records available for inspection by a person who serves written notice of intention to inspect on the company.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what section 215 of the Companies Act 1993 requires: that a company keep records available for inspection by a person who serves written notice of intention to inspect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of s215 of the Companies Act 1993; true if it requires a company to make records available for inspection on written notice of intention to inspect, false if it imposes no such requirement or a materially different one.

veracity.statement: I was, of course, admitted to the New Zealand Institute of Chartered Accountants myself in 1992. There are plenty of us in the Labour caucus who have owned businesses, have business experience, and know our way around the Income Tax Act, amongst other things.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker was admitted to the New Zealand Institute of Chartered Accountants in 1992, and that the Labour caucus contains members with business ownership and tax experience.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZICA/Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand membership records and Deborah Russell's published biography; true if she was admitted as a chartered accountant in 1992, false if she was never admitted or admitted in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: It's actually comparatively easy these days. Most justices of the peace run public desks in libraries or in malls and so on. LynnMall on a Thursday night—the JPs are there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of justices of the peace staff public service desks in libraries, malls and similar venues.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal Federation of New Zealand Justices' Associations records on JP service desks and the number of accredited JPs; true if more than half of JPs staff public desks, false if service desks are staffed by a minority of the JP roll.

veracity.statement: The briefing materials indicate that there are over 650,000 directors currently on the Companies Register.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 650,000 directors are currently recorded on the New Zealand Companies Register.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office / MBIE published register statistics for 2025 on the number of directors on the New Zealand register; true if the count exceeds 650,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Currently chartered accountants cannot sign a statutory declaration, so they’re going to have to deal with the large volumes that my colleague Tom Rutherford has referred to if potentially up to 650,000 directors who could apply go to their accountant as part of the annual reporting process, etc., and have these statutory declarations signed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that chartered accountants are not currently among the persons before whom a statutory declaration may be made in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 9 of the Oaths and Declarations Act 1957 and its schedule of persons authorised to take statutory declarations; true if chartered accountants are absent from that list, false if they are included.

veracity.statement: The member just referred to statutory declarations and said that there will be a large number of these that will require a statutory declaration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in her immediately preceding answer the member in charge said a large number of statutory declarations would be required.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Deborah Russell's answer earlier in this committee stage; true if she stated a large number of declarations would be required, false if she said the opposite or gave no volume estimate.

veracity.statement: Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa recommended that all shareholders should be able to apply to keep their residential address private; not just those connected to a director.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa's submission on the bill — that address-protection eligibility should extend to all shareholders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written submission of Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa to the select committee on this bill, and the committee's report; true if it recommends extending eligibility to all shareholders, false if it made no such recommendation.

veracity.statement: The reason I ask that is that this is about safety and security and the wellbeing of directors of companies, and these are not all the big corporate companies that we might be thinking of. You know, when you look at an electorate like mine on the Kāpiti Coast, but it’s representative of all of New Zealand, that the average company has one employee, maybe one director, they are working hard to get this country ahead, and not everyone necessarily has the means to pay for a fee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the typical New Zealand company has about one employee and roughly one director, and that this is representative nationally rather than peculiar to his electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics on employee count per enterprise; true if the typical (modal/median) enterprise has around one or no employees, false if the typical enterprise has materially more.

civility.statement: To the question from Tom Rutherford about inconsistencies between the company's records and the register of companies records, if the member cared to go to section 215 in the Companies Act, he would see that a company is required to keep records available for inspection by a person who serves written notice of intention to inspect on the company.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly condescending — "if the member cared to go to section 215" implies the questioner did not bother to read the Act — but the substance of the answer is entirely about the provision, not the man.

civility.statement: These are not mere frivolous applications for the sake of it. A person has to be able to say that they think they are at risk of physical or mental harm. civility.explanation: "Scaremongering" imputes bad faith to the questioner — an accusation of deliberately manufacturing alarm rather than a rebuttal of what was argued. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.

civility.statement: About absolutely nothing. It’ll be just full of hot air—hot air.
civility.explanation: A direct jibe at a named member, characterising what he will say as worthless. It targets the member rather than any argument he has made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh, I look forward to you taking a call, Jan Tinetti, and contributing something to the committee.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at a named member, implying she has contributed nothing. Mockery of a person, not of a position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I appreciate the time to gather my thoughts after the shocking revelations from Dr Webb—rich coming from a lawyer, of course, which is one of the least trusted professions alongside politicians.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named member, discrediting him by his profession's reputation rather than engaging anything he said.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It's actually comparatively easy these days. Most justices of the peace run public desks in libraries or in malls and so on. LynnMall on a Thursday night—the JPs are there.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism and a real, checkable instance (JP service desks; LynnMall on a Thursday night), but offers no figures on coverage, cost or waiting time.
specificity.subject: speaker
