specificity.statement: Can the member, firstly, confirm how many directors currently have their residential address publicly available on the Companies Register and what volume of applications the Companies Office is expecting under new section 360D?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question: it names the provision, the administering agency and the two quantities sought. Someone could go and produce the numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How will new section 360D(6)’s inclusion of proposed company, prospective director, and prospective shareholder work in practice when the company does not yet exist?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact subsection, the three extended definitions and the concrete operational difficulty (no company in existence to hold the records). Precise enough to be answered directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My fear is that the way it is drafted now, reasonableness applies to (a) and not to (b). Therefore when the registrar is looking at what they have to do to ensure the alternative address is publicly available from the New Zealand register, they therefore have to take all steps. Because a plain interpretation of that section is that if Parliament had intended those steps to be reasonable, it would have said so. But by deliberately excluding it from (b) and including it in (a), the only interpretation available to a court of law in interpreting the section is that that is an absolute provision.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision, the two subsections, the precise textual defect and the drafting change that would fix it. Directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa recommended that all shareholders should be able to apply to keep their residential address private; not just those connected to a director.
specificity.explanation: Names the submitter and the exact change sought, and identifies the eligibility boundary at issue; no clause reference or drafting proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Really, my question is about who determines who resides and what “residing” actually means. How will “reside with” be defined in practice? And what proof will be needed to kind of furnish, to actually prove that this person, then, does reside with the director?
specificity.explanation: Pins down a particular undefined term in new section 360D(3)(b) and asks concretely who decides it and what evidence is required, though it stops short of proposing a test or threshold.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: About absolutely nothing. It’ll be just full of hot air—hot air.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the conduct of a member of another party during a debate on clause 5. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, Winston Peters would have, I'm sure, really appreciated had that requirement not been in there and then wouldn't have had to necessarily declare his address being a director of a company, for example, and being publicly available—let alone people knowingly sharing it widely, which is just terrible, the harm that incited and the support that's been given from political parties in this House.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — an illustration of why the harm threshold in 360D(3)(b) may be too tight — but half the weight of the sentence is an accusation about what other parties in the House supported.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m sure we’ll understand a lot more about the implementation of any tax policy that that side comes up with, because, clearly, without any chartered accountants on that side, they don’t know.
focus.explanation: A sarcastic characterisation of the other party's membership. Tax policy is gestured at but no measure, provision or figure is engaged; strip out the swipe at the other side and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My fear is that the way it is drafted now, reasonableness applies to (a) and not to (b). Therefore when the registrar is looking at what they have to do to ensure the alternative address is publicly available from the New Zealand register, they therefore have to take all steps. Because a plain interpretation of that section is that if Parliament had intended those steps to be reasonable, it would have said so. But by deliberately excluding it from (b) and including it in (a), the only interpretation available to a court of law in interpreting the section is that that is an absolute provision.
focus.explanation: Wholly on the measure before the House — the wording of new section 360D(2) and its legal effect. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Many Māori organisations’ trustees, Dr Russell, are listed as shareholders in their personal names, and not because they own the shares themselves but because they’re often holding them on behalf of iwi, hapū, and whānau. These trustees often aren’t directors, and yet they can face the serious risk and pressure and even the harassment from within their own communities, especially when decisions are contested.
focus.explanation: Engages the scope of new section 360D directly, identifying a specific class of people the mechanism does not reach. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So our officials and, particularly, the drafters from the Parliamentary Counsel Office said, actually, if we really want to capture the intent of this bill, if we want to capture the nuances, then this is the way to draft it. So we very gratefully accepted their drafting recommendations to try to capture the various different situations that might occur, and it’s all designed to put that in place.
rigor.explanation: Asked why the wording differs between parts, the answer rests on the drafters' say-so rather than on any reason for the wording. A legitimate appeal to expertise, but it is still an appeal to authority: no explanation of what nuance the different wording captures is offered, so the conclusion ('the drafting is right') is only as good as the deference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, when we’re looking at this clause, clause 6, which says that says that service of documents on directors in legal proceedings must be done by leaving them at the director’s alternative address as that address is shown in the register, that alternative address cannot be the company that they work for, which is the legal address of service. So there’s a contradiction in terms there.
rigor.explanation: The inference turns on reading section 387A as saying service 'must be done by' the alternative address, when the section lists it as one of several permissive methods. Once the premise is 'may be served by', no contradiction follows from clause 5's bar on using the registered office as an alternative address. A real argument about the text, but the conclusion does not follow from what the clauses say.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we go back to new section 360E, inserted by clause 5: the alternative address must not be the company’s registered office, but the company’s registered office can still be used for service. It doesn’t stop it being used for service; you just have an alternative address instead of the residential address.
rigor.explanation: Isolates the distinction the opposing argument conflates — a restriction on what may be nominated as an 'alternative address' is not a restriction on what may be used for service — and the conclusion that there is no contradiction follows directly from that distinction.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Surely, the second clause here actually supersedes the first clause, really, because, otherwise, we’re not really adding anything more under (ba). I think it’s maybe a bit of a drafting error here, and we have ended up adding a bit of complexity.
rigor.explanation: A genuine redundancy argument about the drafting, but it assumes the two subclauses do the same work. They do not — (ba) covers leaving a document at an address and (b) covers posting to it — so the 'otherwise we're not adding anything' premise is unestablished and the conclusion of a drafting error overreaches.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It made me reflect that we’re very lucky here. We have a small country and it’s quite possible for us to close that gap, and really that overseas convictions gap was really that one. We don’t have the same complexity as people who can move from state to state.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from a structural difference (a unitary state with no internal jurisdictional borders versus an Australian federation) to the conclusion that the information-sharing gap is easier to close here. The inference tracks the premise; the gap is that the analogy is drawn from a single conference impression rather than any evidence about how the transfer of conviction data actually works.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, if the service at an alternative address fails—it may be undelivered mail or undeliverable mail—will the service at that alternative address then actually be legally effective, or is there some sort of fall-back mechanism which the Companies Register could then actually work? I think a prime example of some of these alternative addresses is a building that has lots of different occupiers.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what new section 360E does and does not provide for. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The job of members of Parliament is not to stir up hate in the community, not to incite things to take place.
focus.explanation: Prompted by a Green interjection, this leaves the clause entirely and characterises what the other side does with its time. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; it is a claim about the other team's conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think we shouldn’t just brush off this question. I think that it’s actually a very, very important question and a very important point, and I think, at this late hour of the night—it’s 9.30 p.m. on a Wednesday—we risk not taking seriously a point of law that has been very carefully and diligently found by one of my colleagues.
focus.explanation: Anchored to a specific point of law raised about the drafting, but the weight of the sentences is on how the House is treating the point rather than on the substance of the alleged contradiction itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And to be heckled by members of the Green Party for saying that we're sitting here filibustering, when they sit there day after day after day abusing members of Parliament in title changes of bills, is really disappointing and it only reflects more on them than it does on us.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's general conduct and hypocrisy. Strip out the characterisation of the Greens and nothing about the clause, or any policy, remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We live in a mixed-terrain country with long gravel roads, windy roads—very mixed terrain. What if they are driving a Toyota Corolla and it’s supposed to be for four-wheel drives, hypothetically? What if people want to fly business class but there is only economy available? What would you do if you were a member of the Green Party, with that option?
focus.explanation: There is a live policy question underneath (which of two registered addresses a process server should attend), but these sentences drift into unrelated hypotheticals about vehicles and airline seats and close with a swipe at the Greens. Some policy tether, mostly padding and party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, if the service at an alternative address fails—it may be undelivered mail or undeliverable mail—will the service at that alternative address then actually be legally effective, or is there some sort of fall-back mechanism which the Companies Register could then actually work? I think a prime example of some of these alternative addresses is a building that has lots of different occupiers.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision and identifies a concrete failure mode (undeliverable mail, multi-occupier commercial buildings), but supplies no figures and proposes no specific mechanism to fix it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question remains: how will the clause 7 amendments to section 388A affect legal practitioners serving documents on directors? Will there be any hierarchy of service methods, or will alternative addresses, under these provisions, have equal status with residential addresses? How will legal practitioners know which address under section 388A to use for service?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the section it amends, and asks a precise, answerable question about the ordering of service methods. A precise question counts as fully as a precise answer; it stops short of 1.0 only because no concrete alternative rule is put forward.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The briefing materials associated with the legislation note that there are currently almost 3,200 registered John Smiths on the company's register—almost 3,200.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a named register and a precise figure repeated for emphasis — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that some of the other contributors to that horrendous abuse that took place in State care and in faith-based institutions was also a consequence of having untrained staff members, a lack of institutional safeguards, a lack of safe regulations, and also the location that some of these institutions were at—for example, Great Barrier Island or Aotea in the 1970s during the Whakapakari boot camp.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific institution, a specific location and a period, alongside concrete causal factors (untrained staff, absent safeguards) — well above a general statement about abuse, though no figures or provisions are cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of new section 28A, I just had a question about the interaction between the determination under section 28 and name suppression provisions. What consideration is there when a determination is made under the new section 28 and there’s a clear indication that there will be an application for review?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific new section, the existing section it interacts with, and the precise legal interaction at issue. Concrete enough that the Minister could answer it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How would I as, say, a legal practitioner, maybe a chartered accountant that was slandered recently by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb—how will legal practitioners know which address to use for service?
civility.explanation: A named member is accused, in passing and gratuitously, of slandering someone. The imputation of wrongdoing to an individual is not needed for the question about service and is the sort of aside the re-anchored scale treats as a real failure, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the member is making a mountain out of—it’s not even a molehill, it’s just a blip in his mind somewhere. I think filibustering is all very well but at least it should have some point.
civility.explanation: Moves off the argument and onto the member: the point exists only 'in his mind', and he is charged with time-wasting in bad faith. Mockery plus an imputation of bad faith, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is great. You’re embarrassing yourself wonderfully.
civility.explanation: A direct personal jibe at the member speaking — about her, not about anything she argued. Interjection, but it carries a clear personal claim.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The briefing materials associated with the legislation note that there are currently almost 3,200 registered John Smiths on the company's register—almost 3,200.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of directors sharing the name John Smith on the Companies Register, sourced to the bill's briefing materials.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The briefing/departmental materials accompanying the Companies (Directors’ Residential Address) Amendment-type member’s bill, and a Companies Office register search for directors named 'John Smith'. True if the figure of roughly 3,200 appears in those materials or a register query returns a comparable count; false if the register/briefing figure is materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude off).

veracity.statement: I understand that the Minister has indicated that he intends to introduce comprehensive reforms which include director identification numbers (DINs).
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible Minister has publicly signalled a forthcoming Companies Act reform package containing director identification numbers. A claim about what has already been said, not a forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and Cabinet/ministerial releases from the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs on Companies Act reform up to 8 October 2025. True if the Minister has publicly signalled a reform package including unique director identification numbers; false if no such indication exists or DINs are not part of the announced package.

veracity.statement: First thing: we had a royal commission for six years, and they were very clear in their recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission into Abuse in Care ran for a period of six years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The establishment date and final-report date of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (order in council establishing the inquiry; delivery of the final report). True if the elapsed period is approximately six years; false if materially shorter or longer.

veracity.statement: This part of the bill was relatively uncontroversial. We didn’t have many—hardly anyone, in fact, I believe—saying anything about this part of the bill that meant they were opposed to it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that submitters to the select committee raised almost no opposition to the Part 1 provisions specifically, as distinct from the more contested later parts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's report and the published submissions on this bill, filtered to the Part 1 (Children's Act / overseas convictions) provisions. True if few or no submissions opposed those provisions; false if a substantial number of submitters opposed them.

veracity.statement: We know that some of the other contributors to that horrendous abuse that took place in State care and in faith-based institutions was also a consequence of having untrained staff members, a lack of institutional safeguards, a lack of safe regulations, and also the location that some of these institutions were at—for example, Great Barrier Island or Aotea in the 1970s during the Whakapakari boot camp.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whakapakari programme was operating on Aotea/Great Barrier Island in the 1970s. The existence of the programme and its location are well documented; the decade attribution is what is at issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's findings on the Whakapakari programme on Aotea/Great Barrier Island, specifically its operating dates. True if the programme was running on the island during the 1970s; false if it began later (e.g. from around 1979-1980 onwards).

veracity.statement: I also want to acknowledge that last night, in Parliament, we celebrated 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, and, I guess, the significance that that holds in the space we stand in today and as we talk about abuse in State and faith-based care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the Waitangi Tribunal has reached 50 years and that a commemoration of that was held at Parliament on the evening of 7 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The date the Waitangi Tribunal was established (Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975) and the parliamentary event record for 7 October 2025. True if the Tribunal's 50th anniversary falls in 2025 and an event marking it was held at Parliament the previous evening; false if either the anniversary year or the event is wrong.

veracity.statement: The select committee rejected the suggestion out of concern for what was seen as unintended consequences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee considered and declined the proposal to replace "vulnerable adult" with "adult at risk", and that its stated reason was unintended consequences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the abuse-in-care omnibus bill; true if the report records the committee declining the "adult at risk" substitution and citing unintended consequences, false if the report records no such consideration or a different stated reason.

veracity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a child with foetal alcohol spectrum disorder cannot access Ongoing Resourcing Scheme funding in the New Zealand education system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education published ORS eligibility criteria and verification guidance; true if FASD is not of itself a qualifying basis for ORS and children with FASD alone are routinely declined, false if FASD is listed as a qualifying condition or routinely verified for ORS.

veracity.statement: Obviously, at the extreme end, we see that quite a lot in the adult prison system, where you have reports like the report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit (PERU) at Auckland Prison, where there were people in there who spent 900 consecutive days in, essentially, solitary confinement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit at Auckland Prison documented prisoners held for 900 consecutive days in conditions amounting to solitary confinement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Office of the Inspectorate (Corrections) report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit at Auckland Prison; true if it records at least one prisoner held roughly 900 consecutive days in conditions it characterises as equivalent to solitary confinement, false if the longest documented period is materially shorter or the report makes no such finding.

veracity.statement: And I’ve tried to visit Korowai Manaaki as well but have been denied three times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker made three requests to visit the Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence and each was declined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki correspondence and visit-request records for Korowai Manaaki, or a written parliamentary question answer on MP visit requests; true if three requests from this member were declined, false if fewer requests were made or they were not declined.

veracity.statement: They don’t sit for three days with no contact with a person.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that children and young people in secure care in a youth justice residence are not left without human contact for the three-day period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki secure care policy and the monitoring reports of the Office of the Children's Commissioner / Independent Children's Monitor and the Ombudsman on youth justice residences; true if secure care requires and delivers routine staff and social-worker contact throughout, false if monitoring reports document young people held in secure care for extended periods without such contact.

veracity.statement: The Privacy Commissioner in his submission on this bill found the restriction on the retention of images was generally appropriate, so we won’t be supporting that amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Privacy Commissioner's written submission on this bill found the 24-hour image retention restriction generally appropriate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's written submission to the select committee on this bill; true if it describes the image retention restriction as generally appropriate, false if it recommends tighter restrictions or does not address retention.

veracity.statement: Just in regard to the questions that have just been asked around harmful items: the harmful items are the same as the list in the Corrections Act, for starters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the harmful items list in this bill matches the equivalent list in the Corrections Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the harmful item list inserted by clause 17(2) of the bill against the unauthorised/harmful item provisions of the Corrections Act 2004 and its regulations; true if the enumerated items substantially correspond, false if the bill's list contains materially different categories.

veracity.statement: They can be used as shanks that can cause major damage, and even death, with just that item alone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that items such as vapes and tobacco products have been fashioned into weapons capable of causing major injury and death in New Zealand custodial or residential settings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Corrections and Oranga Tamariki incident and coronial records, and Inspectorate reports, on weapons improvised from vapes, lighters or tobacco items; true if such items are documented as causing serious injury and at least one death, false if no fatality and no major-injury incidents are recorded.

veracity.statement: Standard operating procedure is that physical intervention can only be used when verbal de-escalation techniques have failed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Oranga Tamariki's standard operating procedure permits physical intervention only after verbal de-escalation has been attempted and failed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki residence standard operating procedures and use-of-force policy documents; true if they require verbal de-escalation to be attempted and to have failed before physical intervention, false if physical intervention is permitted without that precondition.

veracity.statement: That was the recommendation, which was to include or add “disability,” to the definition of “vulnerable adult” which is currently in the Crimes Act, and it is well-established and it has a lot of case law around it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the royal commission recommended adding disability to the existing Crimes Act definition of "vulnerable adult", rather than replacing that term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) recommendations on the Crimes Act; true if a recommendation adds disability to the existing "vulnerable adult" definition, false if it recommends replacing the term or makes no such recommendation.

veracity.statement: A first question here would be what advice did the Minister seek regarding how the use of force is consistent with the royal commission's findings and recommendations that found that laws and regulations surrounding the use of force were often ignored when they were in place, and, in reality, legitimised the use of force, leading to severe harm, abuse, and trauma in far too many cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the royal commission found that use-of-force laws and regulations were often ignored where they existed and in practice legitimised force that led to severe harm, abuse and trauma.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) findings on use of force in State care; true if it finds that such rules were frequently disregarded and operated to legitimise harmful force, false if it makes no such finding.

veracity.statement: The Whanaketia report shows very clearly that they were not exaggerations; they were the horror that people lived through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whanaketia report documents conditions in State care matching the "dark and dank", locked-in, contact-deprived description the Minister called overexaggerated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) survivor accounts and findings on secure/isolation conditions in State care residences; true if it documents locked isolation in dark, poor conditions without contact, false if it contains no such findings.

rigor.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: trust in the State is low, submitters asked for a language change, therefore making the change would itself rebuild trust. The link between the terminology change and the trust outcome is asserted rather than evidenced, but the conclusion broadly tracks the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are many people who live their lives and who have disabilities who we wouldn’t consider vulnerable; they’re completely independent, they’re capable of making their own choices, and they’re capable of moving around and exercising their own discretion and power in whichever way they see fit.
rigor.explanation: A counterexample argument against the definitional link between disability and vulnerability: if many disabled people are independent and capable, the categories do not coincide. The inference is sound against a universal reading of the definition, but it does not engage the possibility that the definition is a protective threshold rather than a description, which leaves a gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
rigor.explanation: A worked arithmetic demonstration: the two counting conventions are applied to the same starting point and the 18-hour gap follows correctly from them. The conclusion — that the day-count is the shorter limit — is genuinely supported by what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Privacy Commissioner in his submission on this bill found the restriction on the retention of images was generally appropriate, so we won’t be supporting that amendment.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (reject the amendment) rests on an appeal to authority. The authority is a relevant expert regulator, which makes the appeal a reasonable one, but the Commissioner's endorsement of the existing restriction does not itself establish that a tighter restriction would be wrong — there is a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Reducing the period to three hours is not a practical time frame in which a court decision can be sought.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the amendment's operation: the statutory period exists to allow a court extension to be sought, and three hours is too short for that, so the amendment would not work as drafted. The conclusion follows, though the impracticality of three hours is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would say, without this provision to use force in the context of a search on entry, Oranga Tamariki would have no authority to touch the child or young person who is not cooperating—for example, even to just guide them to a scanner.
rigor.explanation: A reductio against the amendment: removing all force provisions would remove even minimal physical guidance. The inference follows if force is defined broadly enough to cover guiding someone by the arm, which is the premise doing the work and is not established here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t always mean that you’d necessarily agree with the suggestions made, but that does not equate with ignoring.
rigor.explanation: A valid distinction drawn against the implicit charge: disagreement with a submission is not the same as failing to consider it, so the inference from "the change was not made" to "submitters were not listened to" does not hold. Sound as far as it goes, though it does not show that consideration actually occurred.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from the structure of the statute: the term is used across the Crimes Act, so redefining it reaches beyond this provision. The conclusion follows, but the harm is left at "ramifications that may be unintended" — no consequence is actually identified, which weakens it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So while I completely understand the Minister's explanation of it not being an isolated sort of cell that this young person is in, there are certainly large restrictions that are made around young people in care and a huge amount of discretion, so just one general point.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that restrictions and discretion are large — is drawn from a single recalled anecdote about a missing pen at one residence. An argument from anecdote: it establishes that such restrictions can occur but not that they are large or widespread.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the wording in Part 2 and whether to amend it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are many people who live their lives and who have disabilities who we wouldn’t consider vulnerable; they’re completely independent, they’re capable of making their own choices, and they’re capable of moving around and exercising their own discretion and power in whichever way they see fit.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the definition of "vulnerable adult" in the bill and how disability is folded into it; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the amendment and its statutory reach; no reference to any party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What has happened in the amendment of the law, or will happen, is that we’ll move from a continuous period of 72 hours of detention, and we’ll be moving to a situation where there is clarity over the period that there hasn’t been before, including the actual period “commencing on the day on which the child or young person is first placed in secure care”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause's mechanism precisely — the move from a continuous 72-hour period to a period commencing on the day of first placement — and quotes the statutory wording. Checkable against clause 16, though it carries no figures beyond the 72 hours.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If I go down to the list, under paragraph (b), of things that have already been identified as likely to cause harm, we get to an example here of an “electronic communication device”.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific paragraph of the clause and a specific listed item, so the point can be checked against the bill text directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific funding scheme (ORS), a specific condition (FASD) and a specific consequence (ineligibility), so the claim can be checked and acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Obviously, at the extreme end, we see that quite a lot in the adult prison system, where you have reports like the report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit (PERU) at Auckland Prison, where there were people in there who spent 900 consecutive days in, essentially, solitary confinement.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific unit, a specific prison, a specific report and a specific figure (900 consecutive days).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
specificity.explanation: Exact times, days, and the resulting 18-hour difference; the whole mechanism is laid out so anyone could check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So under new section 384A(2) in clause 17(2), search can be any article.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact new section and clause and states precisely what the scope of the search power is, so the point can be verified against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So this picture of sitting in a cell, with the door locked, dark and dank, and not being able to leave their room, and have no contact with people for three days, is absolutely untrue and overexaggerated.
civility.explanation: A blunt rejection of another member's characterisation of secure care. It is aimed at the description, not at the member — no bad faith is imputed and nothing personal is said — but "absolutely untrue" edges toward the person who advanced it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: From what I’m hearing this morning, I can hear intention, but I don’t hear deep conviction in that way, and I’d like to understand that better.
civility.explanation: A judgement about the Minister's personal commitment rather than about the policy, which moves off the substance and toward the person. It is softened by being framed as the speaker's own impression and by the invitation to explain, so it stops well short of an insult or an imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this clause replaces the wording “must be carried out by a member of staff who is of the same sex as the child or young person being searched” with “must not be carried out in view of another child or young person in the residence”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and quotes both the removed and the replacement statutory wording verbatim; anyone could open the bill and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re keen to understand how those are stored, who has access to those images, and whether there has there been any communication with the Privacy Commissioner or people in those kinds of roles who specialise in privacy and storing sensitive information and data?
specificity.explanation: A precise question with named things to answer — storage method, access list, consultation with a named office. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s only to be used in shared spaces, and the dogs will be controlled by Police or Corrections handlers, not youth justice staff.
specificity.explanation: Names the limit (shared spaces only) and the mechanism (external Police or Corrections handlers rather than residence staff) — a checkable operational answer rather than a reassurance.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So anything that we can do to improve this, bring some more accountability into this space, speed up the process, and actually make sure that we’re doing the right thing to help people reflect on their history, heal in their present, and empower their future is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — accountability, speed, doing the right thing, healing — with no figure, timeframe or named mechanism attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the amendment, its mover, and quotes the exact words proposed for insertion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”. The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, quotes the existing statutory interval and the replacement wording, and identifies exactly what the amendment removes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This will require rehearing seven cases, including four where customary marine title has already been recognised.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable consequence of the retrospective schedule — a count of affected cases and how many have already resulted in recognised title.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re keen to understand how those are stored, who has access to those images, and whether there has there been any communication with the Privacy Commissioner or people in those kinds of roles who specialise in privacy and storing sensitive information and data?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the imaging-search provisions of the bill and their privacy consequences; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named definitional provision and a specific proposed amendment to it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is simply easing the way—even more so for this Government—to just ram through their policy and run ahead with what they see fit.
focus.explanation: There is a policy point inside it — that the bill lowers a barrier to the Government's programme — but no provision, figure or outcome is named, and the weight of the sentence is on how the Government behaves in general rather than on what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Some of us might recall—a couple of years ago, I believe—there was this kind of big drama about police taking lots of images of young Māori on the street and not storing those images securely, and the Privacy Commissioner found that there were tens of thousands of unauthorised, unsecure photos of young Māori children just floating around and being stored on these devices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Privacy Commissioner inquiry found tens of thousands of unauthorised, insecurely stored police photographs of young Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The joint Office of the Privacy Commissioner / Independent Police Conduct Authority inquiry report into NZ Police photographing of members of the public. True if it found unauthorised collection and insecure retention of images of young people on the scale of tens of thousands; false if the inquiry made no such finding or found a materially smaller number.

veracity.statement: This bill’s not changing the existing time limits for secure care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no provision of the bill alters the statutory maximum duration for placing a young person in secure care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as reported back, checked against the secure-care duration provisions of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. True if no clause amends the maximum periods for secure care placement; false if any clause lengthens, shortens or otherwise alters them.

veracity.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”. The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what section 33 of the Public Records Act 2005 currently requires and what clause 34 of the bill does to it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 33 of the Public Records Act 2005 and clause 34 of the bill as reported back. True if the current section states an audit interval of not less than five and not more than 10 years and the clause replaces it with direction by the Chief Archivist; false if either the current wording or the amendment differs.

veracity.statement: However, in 2023, the Court of Appeal interpreted the CMT test in a way that significantly reduced the need for continuity and exclusivity in the scope of what can constitute a substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 Court of Appeal decision on customary marine title lowered the continuity and exclusivity requirements by narrowing what counts as a substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's 2023 Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) judgment on section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, read with the Supreme Court's judgment on appeal from it. True if the Court of Appeal held that exclusive use and occupation could be established without continuous exclusivity and narrowed 'substantial interruption'; false if it maintained or tightened those requirements.

veracity.statement: The Minister has made it very clear, and this Government have made it very clear, about their willingness and their policy to exploit the minerals of Te Takutai Moana, and the Minister has just confirmed that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister, in the speech just given, and the Government in its stated policy, have confirmed an intention to exploit the minerals of the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's second reading speech in this debate, and the Government's published minerals and CMT policy statements. True if either states an intention to extract or permit extraction of minerals in the common marine and coastal area; false if the only reference is descriptive — that ownership of non-Crown minerals is one of the rights a customary marine title carries.

rigor.statement: But what I would like to say is it's not as uncommon as we think. You walk through an airport; you get scanned at an airport, if you want to catch a flight. You often can come to these restrictions when going to court. There are multiple places where you walk through a scanner and nothing to see here and not a problem.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy, and the analogy is weak: airport and court scanning applies to adults who choose to enter a public facility, whereas the concern raised was imaging searches of children in State custody and of whānau visiting them. The conclusion that the technology is unremarkable does not follow from the disanalogous cases offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like for people who are listening today to hear a little bit from the Minister about what kind of dogs are involved and whether there have been any instances where those dogs have got out of control, because it’s very hard to control a dog, actually. One the challenges that many of us who’ve had dogs face is they’re not, actually, entirely in our control.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote and personal experience: the premise is ordinary pet ownership, and it is generalised to trained detector dogs under Police or Corrections handlers, which is the case that would need to be shown. The concern may be sound but the support offered does not reach it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It looks to me as if it’s balanced towards risk rather than benefit, and in most areas of the law we’ve moved to balancing those two things in our words as well, saying we need to actually look at the benefit as well as the risk when we decide whether to prohibit such an object.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the drafting: the regulation-making criteria refer only to harm, so the test is one-sided. The supporting premise — that most areas of the law now require benefit to be weighed alongside risk — is asserted as general practice without an instance being named, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Following the Supreme Court’s December judgment, the High Court issued a decision that has made extensive findings of CMT, illustrating that the Supreme Court’s test has not altered the approach of the courts in practice. Parliament, clearly, did not intend CMT would be available at that scale, so to resolve Parliament’s intent, legislative clarification is still required.
rigor.explanation: Two gaps. A single High Court decision is generalised into a claim about the approach of the courts in practice, and the number of titles awarded is treated as evidence that the test is wrong rather than that the interests exist. The second step is close to circular: parliamentary intent is inferred from the outcome being disliked, and then invoked to justify changing the test that produced it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I respect the role of the courts as one decisionmaker under this regime and the challenge in interpreting the CMT test in the context of the wider Act, but for this regime to work as Parliament intended, a rigorous test for CMT needs to be maintained.
civility.explanation: On a genuinely contested bill that overturns judicial decisions, the disagreement is put entirely to the interpretation and the statutory test. No judge, court or opponent is impugned; the difficulty of the interpretive task is acknowledged.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I want to remind the House that that bill was carefully negotiated between the Māori Party and the National Party of the day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was the product of a negotiation between the Māori Party and National.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and political record for the passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 — Hansard, the National–Māori Party relationship/confidence-and-supply agreement of the time, and contemporaneous reporting. True if the Act was negotiated between the two parties and passed with Māori Party support; false if it was a National-only measure passed without Māori Party involvement.

veracity.statement: Mr Finlayson is very clear that what this Government is doing is wrong.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Finlayson, the Minister who took the 2011 Act through the House, has publicly stated that the current Government's amendment is wrong.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Christopher Finlayson (op-eds, interviews, select committee submissions) on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill. True if he has publicly opposed the amendment; false if he has supported it or has made no such statement.

veracity.statement: It is a 700-year-old sailing waka found on a beach at the top of the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the age and find-location of the Anaweka waka — roughly 700 years old, found at the top of the South Island.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published archaeological reporting on the Anaweka waka (radiocarbon dating and find site). True if the dating puts it around 700 years old (circa early 1400s) and it was recovered at the top of the South Island; false if the dating or location is materially different.

veracity.statement: Mr Christopher Finlayson, who wrote this bill, the former Attorney-General, put it plainly, “these amendments do not restore the original intent of Parliament, they undermine them”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Finlayson, the former Attorney-General responsible for the 2011 Act, made this specific statement about the amendment bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Finlayson's published statements or submissions on the amendment bill. True if he is on record with that wording or its clear substance; false if no such statement exists or he said the opposite.

veracity.statement: In fact, the Supreme Court agreed that the Court of Appeal got that wrong.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal had erred in its interpretation of the customary marine title test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in the Whakatōhea / Re Edwards appeal. True if the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal's interpretation of the s 58 test was wrong; false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach.

veracity.statement: The Justice Committee—and I acknowledge the chair, the Hon James Meager—received and considered submissions from 6,692 interested groups and individuals and heard oral evidence from 69 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts precise submission counts for the select committee stage: 6,692 written submissions and 69 oral submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, which records submission numbers. True if the figures match; false if materially different.

rigor.statement: Now we’re saying not only are we going to change the rules while everyone’s playing the game but we’re going to push you all back to the start line. Why does this sound familiar to our people in the House here? That’s what they did on pay equity—it’s the same thing.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: retrospective legislation extinguishing claims already in progress here is said to parallel the pay equity amendment. The parallel is asserted rather than demonstrated — the two mechanisms are not compared — but the inference from 'retrospective law change that resets existing claims' to 'this is the same pattern' does track the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Where Seymour failed to clumsily rewrite our founding agreement, this bill undoes a settled pathway for rapprochement, for settlement, and, therefore, it is fundamentally an anti-New Zealand bill.
rigor.explanation: An explicit 'therefore' carrying a very large leap: from 'undoes a settled pathway for settlement' to 'fundamentally anti-New Zealand'. The conclusion is a much stronger and differently-framed claim than the premise supports — a non sequitur resting on an unstated equation of the settlement pathway with the national interest.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My colleague the Hon Shane Jones has stated that recent court decisions have made the test for customary marine title too easy, and that rights creep—rights creep—could enable iwi to obstruct critical development projects such as ports.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the central premise is that a ministerial colleague has said so — an appeal to authority — and the harm is a speculative chain ('could enable') with nothing offered to connect a lowered title threshold to obstruction of ports. The statement engages the measure, but the inference is weak.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I listened to the ACT Party contribution on this bill, such as it was—the minute or so that it took—and I was aghast because the ACT Party’s promoting a bill that says that we shouldn’t take or impair property rights without proper compensation. I want to recognise that customary and marine title is, essentially, a property right. Yet, the ACT Party, for all of its pro-property rhetoric, doesn’t believe in protecting the property rights for Māori that are enshrined in customary title.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument with both premises stated: ACT promotes a bill protecting property rights against uncompensated impairment; customary marine title is a property right; therefore supporting this bill is inconsistent with that position. The inference follows; the weak link is that the middle premise — that customary title is relevantly a property right for the purposes of that principle — is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member doesn’t know what he’s talking about.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on another member's competence and knowledge rather than on the argument he advanced.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Anyone who thinks there can be a cohesion, or a lasting contentment, in our nation, for any of us, without upholding and making good on the dignity and the intent of that founding agreement— Te Tiriti o Waitangi—is a fool, frankly.
civility.explanation: Attaches a personal epithet to anyone holding the opposing view rather than engaging why that view is wrong. Not aimed at a named member, but the target is people rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister resurrects the darkest tradition of Crown betrayal, evokes the tradition of colonial theft, and should we be surprised, because that particular Minister believes colonisation was a good thing for iwi Māori, so surely doing more colonisations would be good in his estimations?
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Minister personally a belief in the goodness of colonisation and mocks him with it; the charge is about the man's character and motives, not about the bill's provisions.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But even to have this reading on the Order Paper this year, as we celebrate 50 years, Minister, this is cynical. It is cynical, and under your Government, you continue to kick Māori down.
civility.explanation: Addressed to the Minister personally and imputes bad faith — that the scheduling was a deliberate slight — rather than contesting the bill's substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no reason for it, no reason other than keeping their crony mates happy so that they can get the consent they want to exploit coastal areas, whether it be for sandmining, for fishing, for wind farming—for whatever it might be.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive — legislating to serve 'crony mates' — to the members opposite, going past the policy to the integrity of the people advancing it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When we’re talking about cynical—someone from the other side of the House spoke about cynicism—it’s cynicism to work people up into a frenzy when they’re not saying what the actual truth is.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate dishonesty and inflammatory intent to the members opposite rather than contesting what they said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That member can chirp all he wants—and I look forward to hearing what he has to say when it comes to his party’s call on this bill, because I can tell that member that when the ACT Party get up in this House and talk about Treaty settlement bills, we’re all going to sit here and go: “Two-faced.”.
focus.explanation: The weight of the statement is a charge of hypocrisy against ACT as a party. It gestures at 'his party's call on this bill' but names no policy, provision or outcome — the content is what the other side is like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But again, the backbench is reflective of their leadership, and that leadership is cynical. It is cynical, it is mean-spirited, and it continues the punch-down of our indigenous people in this country.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side — their backbench, their leadership, what they are like. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every opportunity that I have in this House, I will remind Government members of the bad choices that they have made for our country and for Māori alike: repealing Te Aka Whai Ora, taking us backwards on Māori wards, removing Te Tiriti from legislation.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny that names three specific measures — the Te Aka Whai Ora repeal, the Māori wards change, and the removal of Treaty clauses from legislation — rather than trading in general party character.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This wretched bill will be the first bill on the repeal list of things that we will do to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi when there is a change of Government in one year’s time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a change of Government at the general election roughly a year hence, and that this Act would head the incoming Government's repeal list.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The 2026 New Zealand general election result and the incoming Government's first legislative programme. True if the government changes at that election and repeal of this Act is the first repeal introduced; false if the current Government is returned, or if a new Government does not put this Act first on its repeal list.

specificity.statement: So what we are simply doing is making sure it’s very clear what the customary title test should be.
specificity.explanation: Describes the bill's effect without naming the clause amended, the limb of the test being changed, or what the restored threshold actually requires — a direction with almost no checkable content, in a debate where the provision is readily citable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The test for the customary marine title is primarily contained in clause 58(1) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act and has two limbs.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise statutory provision and its structure; anyone can go and check it against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is the Parliament of New Zealand that sets the laws of this land, and this inserts a statutory declaration that overturns the court’s reasoning and ensures the intent of this House is clear.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism — a statutory declaration of intent overriding the court's interpretation — but gives no clause, no wording, and no account of what the restored test requires.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re restoring what Parliament’s intent was when we were fixing up the brokenness of Māori, thanks to the 2004 bill that was passed under that Labour Government back then.
specificity.explanation: Offers no account of what the restored test is, which provision changes, or what the court decision actually held — a general statement of purpose where the mechanism was readily available to state.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: All told, Government contracts are worth more than $50 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the total annual value of New Zealand government contracts for goods and services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / New Zealand Government Procurement published estimates of total annual government third-party spend; true if the figure is above $50 billion a year, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: The IMF’s latest world economic outlook shows that in 2023, out of all the world’s advanced economies, New Zealand had the largest positive output gap.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that IMF data ranks New Zealand first among advanced economies on 2023 output gap.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF World Economic Outlook database, output gap (percent of potential GDP) for 2023 across the advanced economies group; true if New Zealand's value is the largest positive one, false if any other advanced economy exceeds it.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to report to the House that today’s Financial Statements of Government shows that debt, for the first time in five years, has not increased as a proportion of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the year's Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand show debt flat or falling as a share of GDP, and that this is the first such year in five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025 and the four preceding years; true if the stated debt measure as a percentage of GDP did not rise in the latest year and did rise in each of the previous four, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: It’s approximately $8 billion that we are paying to service the interest on our debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the annual cost of servicing Crown debt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Core Crown finance costs in the Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the most recent completed year; true if approximately $8 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m proud that, unlike the last Government, we’re actually funding Dunedin Hospital, that we’re rebuilding Nelson Hospital, that we’re building more classrooms every year than they ever managed, and that we built more social homes in the past 23 months than they did in three years.
veracity.explanation: Contains a comparative delivery claim: more social homes built in the Government's first 23 months than the previous Government built in three years, plus more classrooms per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD / Kāinga Ora public housing supply delivery figures for December 2023 – October 2025 versus any three-year window under the 2017–2023 Government, and Ministry of Education classroom delivery counts by year; true if the National-led totals exceed the comparators, false if not.

veracity.statement: In 2024, just this one event alone brought significant economic benefit to Auckland, resulting in 16,600 visitor nights to the region and injecting $3.4 million into the economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two measured economic impacts of the 2024 ASB Classic on Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The economic impact assessment for the 2024 ASB Classic (Tennis Auckland / Auckland Unlimited / MBIE major events reporting); true if it records approximately 16,600 visitor nights and $3.4 million of regional economic impact, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It is also the case, though—I would point out to members—that the number of unemployed New Zealanders at this point still remains lower than Grant Robertson was forecasting it would be at this point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that current unemployment is below the level forecast for this period in the previous Government's fiscal update.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023 unemployment forecast for the relevant quarter compared with the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey outturn for that quarter; true if the outturn is lower than the forecast, false if equal or higher.

veracity.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury has publicly acknowledged that its pre-election fiscal update growth assumptions were substantially too high.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury forecast performance / evaluation publications and select committee evidence relating to PREFU 2023; true if Treasury has stated its growth forecasts were materially overestimated, false if no such acknowledgement exists.

veracity.statement: But I would also point out that the assertion that rents have gone up under our Government is not correct. In fact, what we have seen is downward pressure on rents since being elected after a period of extreme rent rises under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents have not risen since late 2023 and that rent growth has been downward, following steep rises before that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond rental data and the Stats NZ rental price index from December 2023 onward; true if median/indexed rents are flat or falling over that period, false if they show a material increase.

veracity.statement: On Tuesday, with the backing of all the parties that were present that day in this fine Parliament, the tautoko and support of iwi around Tīkapa Maona, and thousands of New Zealanders, we passed this bill that will triple marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that every party present supported the bill's passage, and that it triples marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division/voting record for the final reading of the Hauraki Gulf marine protection bill in October 2025, and the bill's regulatory impact statement or DOC figures on protected area before and after; true if no party present voted against and protected area roughly triples, false if any party opposed or the increase is materially less than threefold.

veracity.statement: A 2023 NZ Institute of Economic Research report stated that the economic value of the Hauraki Gulf is $100 billion and produces over $5 billion of value each and every year, to this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what a named 2023 NZIER report found about the total and annual economic value of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 NZIER report on the Hauraki Gulf; true if it states an asset value of about $100 billion and annual value above $5 billion, false if the report contains materially different figures or no such finding.

veracity.statement: Does she consider the more than 2,500 hospitality closures and almost 300 liquidations in the past 12 months evidence that her Government is driving economic growth for the hospitality industry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts counts of hospitality business closures and liquidations over the preceding twelve months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Restaurant Association of New Zealand closure data and NZ Companies Office / Centrix liquidation statistics for the accommodation and food services sector over the twelve months to about September 2025; true if closures exceed 2,500 and liquidations approach 300, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a month-on-month net increase of 135 businesses in the accommodation and food services sector in August 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly business/enterprise counts for accommodation and food services, July to August 2025; true if the net change is about +135, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Hospitality job advertisements are up 3.8 percent in July compared to last July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a year-on-year increase in hospitality job advertisements for July.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Seek / Trade Me Jobs or MBIE jobs online series for hospitality, July 2025 against July 2024; true if the increase is about 3.8 percent, false if flat or negative.

veracity.statement: That's why I was pleased to see reports from the District Court's civil jurisdiction showing active cases down 20 percent in the year to July 2025 and the average age of active cases dropping by a remarkable 36 percent over the same period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two measured improvements in District Court civil caseload for the year to July 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice District Court civil jurisdiction statistics for the year to July 2025 against the year to July 2024; true if active cases fell about 20 percent and average case age about 36 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That’s why this Government set a target of 80 percent of people being seen in primary mental health services within one week. We are meeting that target, with 83.8 percent being seen within one week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the quarter four result for the primary mental health access target was 83.8 percent seen within one week, above the 80 percent target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health mental health target reporting for quarter four 2024/25; true if the national primary mental health result is about 83.8 percent within one week, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It is also a fact that Māori are disproportionately overrepresented as victims of crime in New Zealand, which is why this Government is focused on restoring real consequences for crime and reducing the number of victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are victimised by crime at rates disproportionate to their share of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey victimisation rates by ethnicity; true if the Māori victimisation rate materially exceeds the national rate, false if it is at or below it.

veracity.statement: When we came in, there were 185,000 New Zealanders suffering violent offences; we've reduced that down to 156,000 in the latest stats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall in the number of New Zealanders experiencing violent offending from 185,000 to 156,000 since the Government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey estimates of people experiencing violent interpersonal offences, 2023 cycle against the most recent cycle; true if the figures are about 185,000 falling to about 156,000, false if materially different or if the change is inside the survey's confidence interval.

specificity.statement: When considering tender applications, Government agencies will now be required to give a weighting of at least 10 percent to benefits to New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism with a numeric threshold — the weighting is checkable against the published rules.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a result, the number of rules is being reduced from 71 to 47—far, far simpler.
specificity.explanation: Exact before-and-after counts; anyone could check the rule set.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let me count the ways: tax relief for more than a million working New Zealanders; Investment Boost to encourage investment in our businesses so that they can grow; delivering fast-track infrastructure projects; investing in structured literacy in our schools; overhauling the Overseas Investment Act to welcome capital into this country.
specificity.explanation: Five named policies and one rough quantity, but no amounts, timeframes or delivery figures attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
specificity.explanation: Names a spending figure, a sector and a job-loss count — the claim can be checked and acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We announced a $5 million investment in a new centre court roof for Auckland’s Manuka Doctor Arena. This is the first infrastructure project from our $70 million major events and tourism package.
specificity.explanation: Named project, named venue, two dollar figures and its place in a named funding package.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces 19 new, expanded marine protection areas, and is the largest increase in marine protection in Aotearoa New Zealand in over a decade.
specificity.explanation: A precise count of protected areas plus a bounded comparative claim about scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is his message to the 32,000 Kiwis who signed the World Wide Fund for Nature’s petition urging his Government to remove the carve-out that allows commercial fishing in the Gulf’s high protection areas due to the risk that it sets a dangerous precedent where industry lobbyists could weaken future marine protections?
specificity.explanation: Names the petition, its sponsor, the signatory count and the exact provision at issue, though the harm asserted is a general precedent rather than a measured effect.
specificity.subject: speaker
