specificity.statement: Is it fair to subject 18- and 19-year-olds who are receiving jobseeker support (health condition or disability) to the new parental assistance test when they're suffering from severe ill mental health, recovering from a car accident, or undergoing cancer treatment as reported by 1News?
specificity.explanation: Names the benefit, the age band, the specific test being applied and concrete circumstances, with a source for the cases cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can hospitality in Auckland’s CBD thrive when the Heart of the City survey showed that 77 percent of business owners say that the Government does not listen to their needs?
specificity.explanation: Names the survey, the location and the exact proportion, so the figure can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 contained funding of $18.3 million over four years to fund two additional High Court judges and associated staff, as well as expand the number of community magistrates by three and appointing the Chief Community Magistrate.
specificity.explanation: Named budget, dollar figure, period, and exact headcounts for each appointment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he regret repeatedly cutting funding to the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, including cutting $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa work-ready programme at a time when Pacifica unemployment is 12.1 percent, more than double the national average?
specificity.explanation: Names the ministry, the programme, the dollar amount cut, and the unemployment rate it is set against.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That includes the Pacific Business Trust and Pacific Business Village, which placed hundreds of people in the last financial year; the partnership with Pacific Media Network, through the Moana Reo Media Fund, which, again, has placed hundreds of jobs; and Pacific Building Affordable Homes and Our Whare Our Fale, which are stimulating Pacific-led construction and employment, as just a few examples.
specificity.explanation: Five named programmes, but the outcomes are given only as 'hundreds' with no figures, targets or timeframes attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Southern district went from being one of the worst-performing districts, at 66.4 percent, to one of the best, at 91 percent of Southern residents accessing services within one week.
specificity.explanation: Named district, both endpoints of the change, and the exact service standard being measured.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This provision does not breach international trade agreements, because overseas companies have the same opportunity to demonstrate wider value to New Zealand, and similar provisions exist in many of our trading partners’ procurement rules.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the conclusion (no breach) is supported by the stated reason (the test is open to all bidders, so it is non-discriminatory), plus a precedent premise. The reason genuinely bears on the non-discrimination test, though precedent elsewhere does not by itself establish legality here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would also point out that those who are suddenly concerned about deficits might want to ask why they said that every time we made a spending reduction, whether it was pay equity, reducing the number of bureaucrats, reversing stupid programmes, that we shouldn’t be cutting spending—get consistent.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the alleged inconsistency of those raising the deficit does nothing to show the deficit figure is wrong or acceptable. It does engage real spending decisions, so it is an argument, but the conclusion does not follow from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Higher unemployment is a result of an economic downturn driven by high interest rates—high interest rates needed to bring down inflation, fuelled by reckless and undisciplined Government spending.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain (spending → inflation → higher OCR → downturn → unemployment), but every link is asserted rather than evidenced, and the sole attribution of inflation to domestic spending skips the alternative causes without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if that member’s version of economics is that every Government should take responsibility for every firm that ever fails, then I invite her to have a chat with Barbara Edmonds.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the question was about one firm's failure being connected to specific government settings, not about universal responsibility for every business failure. The rebuttal defeats a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, no. How could they possibly be left out when they are represented by Dana Kirkpatrick and Katie Nimon, two of the extraordinary members of Parliament in the National Party caucus?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: which MPs represent a region has no bearing on whether the region has lost the jobs and training roles the question cited. The conclusion rests on an assertion about the members' qualities, not on the outcome asked about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don't think that it is acceptable in a country like ours to leave a whole generation of New Zealanders to rot on welfare.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the alternative to tightening eligibility is characterised as abandoning a generation, which is not the position the question put. The conclusion rests on that substitution rather than on anything shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
rigor.explanation: Answers a twelve-month closure figure with a single month's net change. The conclusion that the sector is recovering does not follow from one month against a year of contraction — the timeframe is selected to fit the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I disagree. If you look at another quote from Hospitality New Zealand, you can see that they are incredibly supportive of the Government’s major tourism and events boost and they know the enormous difference that that will make.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: an industry body's endorsement of one funding package is offered against a survey of 77 percent of business owners. Approval from a peak body does not bear on what the surveyed owners reported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus appeal to emotion: a claim about systemic outcomes is recast as an accusation against individual staff, and the rebuttal is that those staff work hard. Whether the system produces racially disparate outcomes is untouched by how hard its employees work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if you're wanting to reduce the number of victims of crime, a very good place to start is with that very, very small section of New Zealand society that creates multiple victims over and over again.
rigor.explanation: A valid incapacitation argument in form — concentrate on repeat offenders to reduce victimisation — but the question asked for evidence and none is offered; the premise that a small group drives most offending is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Minister think that defunding the police and letting offenders go without prosecution has any chance of helping innocent Māori victims?
rigor.explanation: Loaded question built on a strawman: it attributes a position — defunding police, abandoning prosecutions — to opponents and then asks whether that position works. Nothing is offered to establish that anyone holds it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
civility.explanation: The substance is squarely on the capital spending decision, but the framing 'if she understands numbers' is a jab at the Minister's competence rather than at the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is her idea of an economic plan to deliver more unemployment, a shrinking economy, an inflation that is on the rise, and to blame everyone else except Nicola Willis?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the Minister deliberately deflects blame — rather than confining the criticism to the economic outcomes it lists.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
civility.explanation: The substantive point is about Treasury's forecasts, but the aside that the error 'may have been convenient for the Minister at the time' insinuates the then-Minister benefited from an inaccurate forecast — an imputation about the person, not the numbers.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Has she considered asking for help with her numeracy, considering that she considers negative growth to be a sign of recovery?
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence — suggesting she needs help with basic numeracy — rather than on the economic argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No. As my mother once said to me, if you can’t say anything nice, which I can’t right now, don’t say anything at all.
civility.explanation: A restrained put-down: it says there is nothing good to be said about the member, which edges toward the person, but stops short of an actual insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thank you for that patsy question from the member across.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at the member rather than a response to what was asked — and a sneer that misdescribes a critical question from an opposition MP as a soft one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the source of the phrase by category — 'a very easy phrase for an academic to use' — which goes at who said it rather than at the claim, though it stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister tell us exactly how many Māori accused did Moana Jackson ever defend at court?
civility.explanation: An attack on the standing of the person quoted rather than on what he said. It seeks to discredit the individual's record instead of engaging the claim about the justice system.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, it is not, but I think that those who commit arson and then blame the firefighter should not repeat the same mistake.
focus.explanation: A metaphor about the opposition's culpability. No policy, mechanism or figure is named — the content is a characterisation of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But isn’t it ironic that the very member who asked that question today also, along with her party, voted for it yesterday.
focus.explanation: Turns the answer onto the questioner's party and its consistency rather than onto the commercial fishing carve-out that was asked about. The vote is at least connected to the measure, which keeps it off the floor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did he allow eleventh-hour lobbying to influence changes that now enable commercial fishing in high protection areas, when reports show that it will further damage the health of the Gulf?
focus.explanation: Names a specific provision (commercial fishing in high protection areas), the process that produced it, and the claimed consequence. This is scrutiny of a measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I regret is the actions the previous Government took that put us in this position.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about a specific funding cut with a general attribution of blame to the previous Government. No policy, figure or mechanism is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I certainly can confirm that Corrections and the broader justice sector are very focused primarily on reducing the number of victims of crime, regardless of their ethnicity; unlike the previous Government, which had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison irrespective of what was going on in the community.
focus.explanation: Contrasts two named policy targets — victim reduction versus prison population reduction — which is real policy content, but the second half is framed as a characterisation of the previous Government's motives rather than of its measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence does he have that a higher prison population makes Māori safer?
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates the evidential basis of the Government's imprisonment policy. It names the mechanism and the claimed outcome rather than attacking the party.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This extra capacity will help relieve pressure across the justice system and improve timeliness, leading to a reduction in backlogs and the time that people do spend on remand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the additional judges and magistrates funded in Budget 2025 will reduce court backlogs and average time spent on remand.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court statistics on active case backlogs and average remand duration for the year to June 2027 compared with the year to June 2025; true if both fall, false if either is flat or rises.

veracity.statement: May I remind everyone in this House and out there that in 1975, just 5 percent of all Māori schoolchildren could speak and even understand their own mother tongue; 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 1975 only 5% of Māori schoolchildren could speak or understand te reo Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZCER's 1970s national survey of Māori language use among Māori schoolchildren (and Benton's reports on it); true if the proportion of Māori schoolchildren who were speakers/understanders around 1975 was approximately 5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Two years later, the Māori language petition, signed by over 30,000 New Zealanders, was carried to the very steps of this Parliament; ordinary people, extraordinary in their vision, stood up to say that the language of our tīpuna and of this whenua will not die.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 1972 Māori language petition carried more than 30,000 signatures and was delivered to Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and Ngā Tamatoa / Te Reo Māori Society records of the 1972 Māori language petition; true if the recorded signature count exceeds 30,000 and it was presented at Parliament in 1972, false if the count was materially lower or the date differs.

veracity.statement: Ruātoki stepped up first. They became the first bilingual school in the entire country in 1978.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Rūātoki School was New Zealand's first bilingual school and that this happened in 1978.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Te Ara / school records on when Rūātoki School was designated New Zealand's first bilingual school; true if it was the first and the year was 1978, false if another school was first or the year differs (several sources give 1977).

veracity.statement: In 1982, the first kōhanga reo, Pukeatua, was opened in Wainuiomata.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Pukeatua in Wainuiomata was the first kōhanga reo and opened in 1982.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Kōhanga Reo National Trust and Te Ara records of the first kōhanga reo; true if Pukeatua Kōhanga Reo, Wainuiomata, was the first and opened in 1982, false if another was first or the year differs.

veracity.statement: The committee received 62 submissions, and several of them dealt with constitutional matters, as you would expect for a bill of this nature.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Parliament Bill Committee received 62 submissions on the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House and the submissions listed on the Parliament website; true if the submission count is 62, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And there have been instances where the petitions that have been put on the Parliament website—which gives it the appearance of being approved in some way by this House—have had racist overtones or misogynistic overtones or something of that nature.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that petitions with racist or misogynistic content have in fact been hosted on the Parliament website.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Petitions Committee's submission to the Standing Orders Committee on discriminatory petitions, and the archive of e-petitions hosted at petitions.parliament.nz; true if one or more hosted petitions are identified as racist or misogynistic in content, false if no such instance exists on the record.

veracity.statement: We've only got to look at the incidents over the last week or so, particularly around our party leader’s home, and say that that is not something which we can take for granted and is something which we need to treasure and to look after.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that security incidents occurred at the New Zealand First leader's home in the week or so before 9 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police statements and contemporaneous news reporting for late September / early October 2025; true if one or more security incidents at Winston Peters' residence are documented in that period, false if no such incident is reported.

veracity.statement: I don't think they actually realised that they are published every quarter anyway, and, by crikey, I think we all know that the finance team are assiduous in pursuing every single receipt that we've got or haven't got.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that members' expenses are published on a quarterly basis.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Service members' expenses disclosure releases; true if publication is quarterly, false if the disclosure cycle is at a different interval.

civility.statement: One only has to turn to the Hansard to see in plain black and white how this Government and past Governments have perceived our people.
civility.explanation: A pointed and genuinely contested criticism of the conduct of governments over time; no individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would suggest that whenever we look at matters which strike to the constitution of our country, that is the approach that we should take, and, sadly, it hasn’t necessarily been the approach of this Government to date.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's legislative approach without attacking any individual or imputing bad faith to a person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Proposed new clause 190A requires officers to report to the chief executive within three working days when certain coercive powers are used, summarising the circumstances and reasons for their exercise. It applies to the use of powers to detain or handcuff persons and to the use of reasonable force.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the reporting timeframe, the recipient and the exact powers triggering it — fully checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The security, you guys are doing a great job, and I think we really did get some good wins in there for democracy.
specificity.explanation: Offered as a substantive assessment of the bill's committee stage but names no clause, change or outcome — 'good wins for democracy' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, those petitions could still occur on a paper form by doing the rounds in the kind of old-fashioned way. But that doesn't give it the appearance of this Parliament approving, as in any way legitimate, petitions which are outright offensive.
rigor.explanation: A sound argument: the objection is to implied parliamentary endorsement, and since the paper route remains open the remedy removes the endorsement without removing the petition right. Small gap in that hosting also confers reach, not only endorsement.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This will not prevent paper petitions of that nature from going out in the community; I don’t think, therefore, that anyone could argue that this is about restricting people’s ability to canvass petitions in their communities.
rigor.explanation: The premise supports a weaker conclusion than the one drawn: that paper petitions remain possible shows the restriction is partial, not that no one could argue a restriction exists. Overstated inference from a true premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that's potentially a really exciting proposition, because it means that we, as political parties, can't just charge off and say, “Hey, we're going to promise the world.” Our voters should know what the world is going to cost.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a named institution — a parliamentary budget office costs policies, so parties are constrained. But the conclusion overreaches: independent costing informs voters, it does not prevent parties from promising anything.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our committee services at the moment are under huge pressure, and again, this is one of the issues of ramming through legislation too fast. We end up having to select just a few submissions in some cases, or we have to break into subcommittees where actually all of us on a committee would like to hear more of the submissions.
rigor.explanation: A causal argument with a stated mechanism and observable consequences (submission triage, subcommittee splitting). The link from legislative pace to those consequences is asserted rather than evidenced, but the inference is coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would suggest that whenever we look at matters which strike to the constitution of our country, that is the approach that we should take, and, sadly, it hasn’t necessarily been the approach of this Government to date.
focus.explanation: A genuine process point about how constitutional legislation should be made, but the criticism of the Government is general — no specific bill or process failure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The special select committee received 62 submissions from some notable New Zealanders who had given some of the constitutional, weighty matters great thought and great consideration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of written submissions received by the Parliament Bill Committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House and Parliament's published submissions list; true if 62 submissions were received, false if the recorded number is materially different.

veracity.statement: This is the very reason why Hone Harawira actually left Te Pāti Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the foreshore and seabed / Marine and Coastal Area settlement was the cause of Hone Harawira's departure from the Māori Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and Harawira's own statements around his 2011 departure from the Māori Party; true if the takutai moana/foreshore-and-seabed deal is recorded as the cause, false if the record attributes it to other causes such as the party's confidence-and-supply relationship with National.

veracity.statement: Certainly to the Speaker directly, but there’s a useful case in Police v Beggs, which was a 1999 case where the courts were very clear that the Speaker must also have regard to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 1999 case named Police v Beggs held that the Speaker's exercise of powers over the parliamentary precinct is subject to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The reported judgment in Police v Beggs; true if it is a 1999 New Zealand decision holding that the Speaker must have regard to NZBORA in exercising precinct powers, false if the year, the holding, or the case name is materially different.

veracity.statement: I think, with 25 percent of our population identifying as having some sort of disability, there’s certainly a need for Parliament to consider whether it’s time for us to have that kind of review in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a quarter of the New Zealand population identifies as having some form of disability.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Disability Survey (most recent release) and census disability data; true if the disabled share of the population is approximately 25%, false if it is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The current rules deprive local broadcasters of, they think, around $6 million annually in advertising revenue, and, of course, as we all know the pressure that the broader media sector is under, every dollar helps and every dollar counts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that broadcasters estimate the existing restrictions cost them about $6 million a year in forgone advertising revenue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and departmental advice on the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill, and broadcaster submissions; true if the industry estimate of forgone annual revenue is approximately $6 million, false if the documented estimate differs materially.

veracity.statement: On 7 November 2024, TVNZ announced a further 50 jobs to be cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that TVNZ announced a further 50 job cuts on 7 November 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TVNZ's November 2024 restructure announcement and contemporaneous reporting; true if roughly 50 further roles were announced for cutting on or about that date, false if the number or the date is materially different.

veracity.statement: The other thing I’ve got here—I like lists; this is a list of dates, and on this list there are 49 dates during which Cabinet met and the Minister, in response to a question about what he took to that Cabinet meeting to help, what he took to those Cabinet meetings for immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector, the answer, for all of these 49 dates, is nothing—nothing taken; nothing offered; no immediate action.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across 49 Cabinet meeting dates the Minister's own answers record that he took nothing to Cabinet on support for the broadcasting and media sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister for Media and Communications' answers to written parliamentary questions listing papers taken to Cabinet on media matters over the period covered; true if the answers record no media-support paper across all 49 dates, false if any such paper is recorded.

veracity.statement: If we look at the last five years of advertising revenue that has been spent on our local media, in 2019 the total industry revenue spent was $2.76 billion of advertising across our media. In 2024, it had increased by 30 percent, to $3.59 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts total New Zealand advertising expenditure of $2.76 billion in 2019 rising to $3.59 billion in 2024, an increase of 30 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Commercial Communications Council / ASA annual advertising expenditure figures for 2019 and 2024; true if the totals match to within rounding, false if either figure or the stated 30 percent change is materially different.

veracity.statement: Twenty percent of New Zealanders subscribe to some form of faith, and I’d assume that many of those include Sundays being protected and days of rest and days of worship as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that one fifth of New Zealanders hold a religious affiliation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census religious affiliation data; true if approximately 20% of respondents reported a religion, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Broadcasting Standards Authority was involved, and there was huge outrage in 1999 about this little wee dog and others saying the word “bugger”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Toyota 'bugger' advertisement drew Broadcasting Standards Authority involvement and public complaint in 1999.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BSA decisions and complaint records for the Toyota Hilux 'bugger' advertisement; true if complaints were made and determined by the BSA in 1999, false if the year is wrong or the BSA had no involvement.

rigor.statement: It is a very transparent process, what is being proposed—very similar to how Officers of Parliament operate as well—and so it would mean that all parties would be represented on a select committee to decide and to consider budget applications from the Office of the Clerk and from the Parliamentary Service, and would be scrutinised by, basically, all parties in Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Answers the transparency objection by naming the mechanism that delivers transparency — all-party representation on the deciding committee and all-party scrutiny of the applications. The conclusion tracks what is offered; the only gap is that no comparison is drawn with the current process he says it improves on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of security, I encourage MPs to actually go and speak to some of our security officers around Parliament, and especially some of the ones that have been around for a little while, and they'll happily tell you why these changes are necessary.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority and to unstated anecdote: the necessity of the new powers is asserted by deferring to what security officers would say rather than by giving the reason. Nothing is offered that the listener could weigh.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I did look to see if there had been complaints made or anything that was very obvious in the media space in this area, and I really couldn’t find anything, which says to me that the rules are set in a reasonable way.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: an informal search of media coverage is treated as showing the rules are reasonable. Complaints about tribunal security powers would not be expected to surface in the media even if they existed, so the absence carries little weight.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what I like about these powers is they haven't gone too far. They're very much in line with the powers that have been given in courts and they're carefully considered.
rigor.explanation: Argument by precedent: the powers are proportionate because they mirror existing court security powers. The inference holds only if courts and the parliamentary precinct are relevantly alike, which is asserted rather than shown, and 'carefully considered' adds nothing to the case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In January 2025—that’s the beginning of this year—NZME proposes a reduction of 40 further roles, and the job losses go on and on and on and the cuts from central government for funding to the sector come through in that Budget, and what else do we see but just this week: The Hui and Te Karere, two very, very important programmes here in New Zealand—vital programmes here in New Zealand—are now faced with the prospect of no longer existing because this Minister, who promised immediate action, has delivered only a 73-word bill.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a chronology of commercial job cuts and programme decisions is presented as caused by the Minister having passed a short bill. No mechanism is offered connecting the absence of other legislation to NZME's or TVNZ's decisions, and several of the listed events pre-date the bill entirely.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you have a business with a limited number of customers and you’re not making enough money and you’re trading six days a week, the solution is not just to open on Sundays, because you just have the same number of customers, but you have to be open more and you have to work harder.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy, and it captures a real point: if total advertising demand is fixed, extending the permitted hours redistributes rather than creates revenue. The premise that the pool is fixed is assumed rather than shown, and the analogy ignores that the restriction currently sends that spend to competing platforms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To be fair, when we hear about the potential income that could be generated from allowing advertising on Sundays and public holidays, it’s just approximately $6 million. That’s not going to fundamentally fix the shortfalls that we have.
rigor.explanation: Perfect-solution fallacy. That $6 million does not close the sector's funding gap does not establish that it is not worth having; the argument would need to show a cost to taking it, which is asserted elsewhere but not connected here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I also point out that another really good way for linear television broadcasters to increase their revenue is to produce products that people actually want to watch, and so if people watch it and then the advertisers get revenue, maybe that's another way to fill the gap.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion assumes what is in dispute — that the audience decline is caused by programme quality rather than by structural migration to streaming platforms, which is the premise the rest of the debate rests on. Nothing is offered to support the causal step, so the advice follows only if you already accept it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we relax advertising standards at this point, it will be seen as a further dumbing down of our media space that we still do have control over.
rigor.explanation: An unsupported consequence claim shading into slippery slope: nothing is offered connecting the removal of a restriction on five days to a general decline in media standards, and 'will be seen as' substitutes an assumed public reaction for an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is pretty much in the dark ages when we are having one set of rules for broadcast television, which I've heard referred to as linear television, and in exactly the same programmes provided by exactly the same entity, if you stream them, you're not subject to those rules. That's just irrational.
rigor.explanation: A clean consistency argument: identical content from an identical provider is regulated differently depending only on the delivery pipe, and no reason for that distinction is available. The conclusion of irrationality follows directly from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the reality of this one is, as with most of the New Zealand calendar, which was imported from England, it is the Christian tradition that we always commemorate. I don't see any broadcasting advertising being taken away for Eid or taken away for Ramadan or those kinds of things.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument that does its work: if the restriction protects religious observance in principle, its confinement to Christian days is unexplained. The step from that inconsistency to repeal rather than extension is left implicit, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sure that, along with myself and Mr Costley, other veterans have far better things to be doing on Anzac Day than watching television.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from her own and one colleague's Anzac Day practice to what veterans as a group do, and uses that to dismiss the objection about advertising on that morning. Argument from anecdote, and it does not reach the people the objection was actually about.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'll summarise the changes that we made in increasing reporting and increasing monitoring, because there were concerns that were raised around whether there was enough reporting and monitoring of what those officers will be doing: if they use their new powers, that must be reported to the CEO within three days, and the CEO must report those at least annually.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual safeguard, who reports to whom, and both timeframes (three days, at least annually). Someone could check the bill against this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s language, for example, in the drafting that says, “involves no physical contact” when they’re using electronic screening devices, or only the “external examination of the person’s clothes”.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative words of the search provisions rather than characterising them, so a listener can go to the clause and check whether the restraint she claims is actually there.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I would argue we could go further. I think that perhaps we should look at some other iterations of this later, things like perhaps a buddy system.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete idea — a buddy system — but supplies no eligibility, cost, mechanism or timing, and hedges it twice ('perhaps'). A direction with a label attached rather than a proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill repeals section 81 of the Broadcasting Act 1989, which restricts broadcast television and radio advertising on Sunday and Anzac Day mornings, and both television and radio advertising on Christmas Day, Good Friday, and Easter Sunday.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, the Act, the year and the exact days and media affected. Nothing is left to interpretation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On 7 November 2024, TVNZ announced a further 50 jobs to be cut.
specificity.explanation: Exact date, named organisation, exact number. Checkable and actionable as it stands.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a system that needs a good review. We need to review and provide a clear direction in terms of where we are heading, a better coordinated, collaborative—and also something that brings together innovation, the online as well as the linear.
specificity.explanation: A call for a review and for coordination, with no terms of reference, no funding figure, no mechanism and no timeframe. 'Better coordinated, collaborative' and 'brings together innovation' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we look at the last five years of advertising revenue that has been spent on our local media, in 2019 the total industry revenue spent was $2.76 billion of advertising across our media. In 2024, it had increased by 30 percent, to $3.59 billion.
specificity.explanation: Two dated totals, the percentage change between them, and a defined scope. Precise enough to be checked line by line.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wanted to reiterate some of the points made around Government cuts to broadcasting, some of which are a $10 million cut to Whakaata Māori, our national Māori broadcasting channel; a forecast $18 million worth of cuts to Radio New Zealand, which is quite depressing given that they are also our kind of emergency national radio station, who have to communicate those really important messages to everybody; and the fact that TVNZ’s call for an extra $30 million worth of revenue has been ignored.
specificity.explanation: Three named broadcasters with three dollar figures attached, set against the $6 million the bill is said to raise. Each figure can be taken to the Budget documents and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When the Helen Clark Labour Government passed the foreshore and seabed, that shouldn't have happened. The reaction of the National Party in addressing that, that shouldn't have happened. And I can tell you that this amendment shouldn't happen either.
civility.explanation: Condemns the actions of his own former party's government, the National Party, and the bill before the House in the same breath. Fierce about the legislation and the decisions; no person is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I know there’s the obvious joke, and I’m not going to make it, about Minister Goldsmith being a clown, because I don’t think that would be fair, because, actually, Minister Goldsmith has been a mime: he’s moved around a whole lot and he’s waved his arms around, but he hasn’t said anything.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named individual, and the disclaimer delivers the insult it declines to make. The substitute image is no kinder — it ridicules the Minister personally rather than criticising a decision or a record.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As Reuben Davidson so clearly phrased it, there's lots of movement from the Minister for Media and Communications, but no real noise, no decisions, no statements, no effective actions. He's miming the position of Minister of broadcasting, and frankly he seems to be somewhat stuck.
civility.explanation: The first sentence is legitimate criticism of a record. The second turns to derision of the person — 'miming the position' and 'somewhat stuck' mock the Minister rather than the decision, which is where it drops below the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to touch on the fact that the bill makes the Parliamentary Library a standard business unit in the Parliamentary Service, and just acknowledge the role that the parliamentary librarians play in supporting us as MPs, particularly with our constituency work—the ability to engage and contact and get feedback that helps us answer constituents’ queries on a daily basis, for those of us who are hard-working constituent MPs like my colleagues on this side of the House.
focus.explanation: Names the specific change the bill makes to the Parliamentary Library and why it matters to constituency work, but closes on a team aside implying that the hard-working constituent MPs are on his side of the House. A real policy point with party framing bolted on.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it is also a speech about broken promises, because this is from a Government that came in saying they were going to get things back on track, and from a Minister a year ago—over a year ago—who said he was going to take immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector.
focus.explanation: Names a specific ministerial commitment — immediate action for the media sector, dated to a particular announcement — and measures the bill against it. This is scrutiny of a named undertaking, not party-bashing; the only party framing is the reference to the Government's general slogan.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sadly, this Government just continues to let New Zealanders down. They set big expectations, and I heard more ideas and contributions in this House today from my relation Jenny Marcroft. I think she could do a better job as the Minister and come up with better ideas in the absence of a Labour-led Government.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or named commitment appears. It is a general characterisation of the Government's record plus a comparison of who would fill the ministerial job better — the party-versus-party register rather than the policy one.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: If this bill passes, they will not be taking advantage of advertising and will not conduct any advertising or seek any advertising revenue with this repeal.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Radio Rhema will decline to sell advertising on the newly permitted days after the repeal takes effect. This is a prediction about a third party's future conduct, not a commitment by the speaker.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Radio Rhema's broadcast output and published rate card in the twelve months after the repeal comes into force; true if it carries no paid advertising on Sundays, Anzac Day mornings, Christmas Day, Good Friday or Easter Sunday, false if it carries any.

focus.statement: Was the Prime Minister or Cabinet Office made aware of any potential conflict of interest with the Minister for the Environment attempting to influence a consent process from which a National MP’s company could benefit, and does he consider this an appropriate action for his Minister to take?
focus.explanation: Names a specific Minister, a specific consent process and a specific Cabinet Manual-style conflict concern. This is scrutiny of a named action, not party-bashing, and scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Which thing is he most proud of: a shrinking economy, rising unemployment, more kids living in poverty, more homelessness, or record numbers of New Zealanders giving up and leaving the country?
focus.explanation: Names five specific outcomes — GDP, unemployment, child poverty, homelessness, net migration — so there is real policy content, though it is wrapped in a rhetorical 'what are you proud of' frame.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it works because you have an economic philosophy that you’re going to spend more, you’re going to borrow more, you’re going to tax more, and it doesn’t matter whether it’s Labour, the Greens, or Te Pāti Māori, that’s what that uni-party is going to do. They’re going to continue with the track and the mess that put us in this position.
focus.explanation: Asked a question about how tax cuts work, the answer is entirely a characterisation of three opposition parties as a single 'uni-party'. No measure, figure or mechanism is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did the Prime Minister give agricultural polluters a free ride instead of requiring them to do their fair share of emissions reductions, given that this means that households and businesses will have to shoulder more of the emissions reduction, increasing the cost of living for everyday New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the methane target decision and its consequence for who bears the rest of the emissions budget. A named policy and a named distributional effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, but I just say to the member, as part of a Labour-Greens Government who wanted to shut down New Zealand farms and send production overseas, why don’t you come on board and actually support that policy too? It’s going to be very interesting to see what the Labour Party says about that.
focus.explanation: Turns from the methane target to the questioner's former government's supposed intentions and to speculation about what Labour will say. No mechanism, figure or provision is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What good is capping fees when under-funded practices start charging for double consultations, leading to the pensioner who wrote to me saying, “I pay $91 for a 15-minute visit, and you’re only allowed to talk about one thing. If you want to talk about two things, you need to pay for another $91. I cannot afford to pay this.”?
focus.explanation: Names the policy (the 3 percent fee cap) and identifies a specific mechanism said to defeat it — double-consultation charging. This is exactly the scrutiny an opposition MP is there to do.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, as I said in my primary answer, 90 percent of adults without a community service card pay $70 or less to see their GP, and under her watch, the Labour Party let GP fees increase by 30 percent over their six years in office. As I say, you can’t trust Labour when it comes to GP fees.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy figure and a specific historical fee increase, but the answer closes on a general 'you can't trust Labour' framing rather than on the question about first-visit fees.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he continue to deny the link between his tightening of the emergency housing entry criteria and the unprecedented increase in homelessness, when even pregnant women are now being denied access?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy change — the emergency housing entry criteria — and a specific outcome. Legitimate accountability, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Of the Prime Minister, going from the questioner’s original draft of the primary question, would he have confidence if any Minister couldn’t spell “Ministers” properly?
civility.explanation: A supplementary whose only content is mocking the questioner's spelling — a jibe at another member personally rather than anything in the question's substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Isn’t it funny, the great gaslighter forgets about something called interest rates, which he doesn’t take responsibility for creating. How on earth do you increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation over 7.5 percent, have 12 interest rate rises, and then ask some questions about how the construction industry works? Get back and understand some economics.
civility.explanation: Labels the Leader of the Opposition 'the great gaslighter' — an attack on his honesty — and closes by telling him to go and learn some economics, an attack on his competence. The economic figures beside it are civil; the labels are not.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would encourage that member and her party to reflect on the retrograde decision they have made to not support the repeal of the oil and gas ban. In the feedback coming through in her sojourn round the boardrooms of Auckland, she will know that some of the feedback coming from the business community and the energy sector has been to plead with the Opposition to support the Government’s move on energy security. She should start listening to the voices of reason in the business community that want bipartisanship on energy policy, because the best thing we could do for this country’s energy security is firm up the gas supply to make sure we keep the lights on.
civility.explanation: 'Her sojourn round the boardrooms of Auckland' sneers at the member personally, and 'she should start listening to the voices of reason' is condescension rather than argument. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can he claim that his targets are based on anything other than corporate interests when world-leading climate scientists have described his weakening of methane targets as “a great way of shooting yourself in the foot” and “New Zealand is setting a dangerous precedent that other governments must not follow”?
civility.explanation: Imputes a corrupt motive to the Prime Minister — that the targets can only be explained by corporate interests — rather than contesting the target itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that member should know, because she has a very short memory. In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term. So if she wants to know how long it takes, she should ask herself that.
civility.explanation: 'She has a very short memory' is a jab at the member rather than at her argument — condescension short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But in my humble opinion, respectfully, I think it is potentially reckless and insensitive that the member would consider it appropriate for officialdom to ask women seeking emergency housing support, often in difficult circumstances, if they are hapū or not.
civility.explanation: Calls the questioner's conduct reckless and insensitive — a judgement on the member rather than on the housing question. The 'respectfully' framing does not change what is being said about him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, that they recognise that it was the US President and others from Muslim countries who brought this about and that anti-Americanism or any other sentiment is of no value when you’re concerned about peace, and particularly if you’re some arrogant twit that arrived here five minutes ago and doesn’t give a concern about this country’s initiative and its peace over the years.
civility.explanation: Calls another member 'some arrogant twit' who 'arrived here five minutes ago' — an attack on the person's character and standing, and on their right to hold a view, with nothing about the substance of the position.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, because we had a very poor inheritance from the previous Government, which was Government spending that went up 84 percent, a lot of it very wasteful. That drove up inflation over 7 percent. That drove up interest rates—there were 12 interest rate rises under the member’s previous Government—and that put the country into recession and raised unemployment. That’s what this Government is working incredibly hard to do. We’ve got spending under control. We’ve got inflation down. We’ve got interest rates down. Growth is coming; jobs are coming.
specificity.explanation: Carries three checkable magnitudes — an 84 percent spending increase, inflation over 7 percent, and 12 interest rate rises — rather than a general claim of poor inheritance.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So why did he cut $3 billion of public investment in infrastructure in his first year as Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: a named spending category, a dollar figure, and a defined period. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m actually very proud that we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas. That’s helping. But what we’re doing is actually getting spending under control. We’ve brought inflation down from a record high and pathetic 7.5 percent, from his economic management last time, to 2.7 percent. That’s lowered interest rates. Interest rates are down eight times under this Government; they were up 12 times under his.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, timeframe, two inflation readings and a count of rate decisions — concrete enough that each element can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week Treasury released the Government financial statements for 2024-25. These are actual numbers, not forecasts or projections. They’re the first year-end statements to fully reflect decisions made by the current Government, and they show progress in getting the country’s books back in order. As a share of GDP, core Crown expenses fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 in 2024-25. Our intention is to bring spending down even more as a proportion of the economy, and that intention is reflected in the Budget forecasts.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the fiscal years, and two exact percentages-of-GDP; anyone could look the figures up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The latest report shows an incredible improvement in the number of students who are reaching 20 weeks at school at expected levels of phonics, up from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3.
specificity.explanation: A named assessment, a defined cohort, two terms and two percentages — precisely the kind of claim someone can go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We mandated structured literacy; we introduced a new English curriculum backing structured literacy; we trained over 33,000 teachers in structured literacy; we provided cash to schools for more structured literacy resources; and we provided 349 structured literacy intervention teachers to over 1,240 schools to support students who need help.
specificity.explanation: Five named actions with counts attached — 33,000 teachers, 349 intervention teachers, 1,240 schools. Concrete and auditable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We, on this side of the House, are genuinely concerned by those who may be rough sleeping, and that’s why Minister Bishop and myself have taken direct action over the last six weeks to announce an additional 300 funded places for Housing First and additional support for transitional housing, and have also given some direction around both redirections and also the exercise of discretion by Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora—the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
specificity.explanation: A named programme, a number of places and a timeframe. Weaker at the end — 'additional support' and 'some direction around discretion' carry no quantity or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s important that we provide certainty to our farmers, processors, and exporters that is fair, pragmatic, and backed by science. This is why the Government has set the methane target at a range of 14 to 24 percent below 2017 levels by 2050.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target range, a baseline year and a target year. The opening sentence is generic, but the substance that follows is fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To back the new target, the Government is already investing more than $400 million with industry to speed up the development and roll-out of methane-cutting tools. Three methane-cutting tools are available now, with up to 11 rolling out by 2030—one of which will be available as early as next year.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, a count of tools available now, a count expected, and a date. 'Up to 11' is hedged, but the claim still carries checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the number of submitters and the proportion opposed — a precise, checkable question.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, because we had a very poor inheritance from the previous Government, which was Government spending that went up 84 percent, a lot of it very wasteful. That drove up inflation over 7 percent. That drove up interest rates—there were 12 interest rate rises under the member’s previous Government—and that put the country into recession and raised unemployment. That’s what this Government is working incredibly hard to do. We’ve got spending under control. We’ve got inflation down. We’ve got interest rates down. Growth is coming; jobs are coming.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core government spending rose 84 percent under the 2017-2023 government, that inflation exceeded 7 percent, and that there were 12 official cash rate rises under that government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series for 2017-18 to 2023-24 (true if the increase is ~84%, false if materially lower); Stats NZ CPI annual inflation peak 2021-2023 (true if above 7%); RBNZ OCR decision record October 2021 to October 2023 (true if 12 increases).

veracity.statement: So why did he cut $3 billion of public investment in infrastructure in his first year as Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that capital investment in infrastructure was reduced by close to $3 billion in the current Prime Minister's first year in office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 multi-year capital allowance and departmental capital appropriations compared with Budget 2023; true if net infrastructure capital investment fell by approximately $3 billion, false if the reduction is materially smaller or is an increase.

veracity.statement: I’m actually very proud that we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas. That’s helping. But what we’re doing is actually getting spending under control. We’ve brought inflation down from a record high and pathetic 7.5 percent, from his economic management last time, to 2.7 percent. That’s lowered interest rates. Interest rates are down eight times under this Government; they were up 12 times under his.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that inflation reached a record high of 7.5 percent under the previous government and is now 2.7 percent, and that the OCR has been cut eight times under this government against twelve rises under the last.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series (true if the peak print was 7.5% and the most recent print 2.7%; false if the peak was materially different, and 'record high' is false if any earlier NZ annual CPI print exceeds it); RBNZ OCR decision record (true if eight cuts since the 2023 election and twelve rises before it).

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “We’re determined to get the building and construction sector firing on all cylinders.”; if so, is 20,000 job losses in the construction sector the type of firing he was referring to?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the construction sector has shed approximately 20,000 jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs by industry for construction, peak to the September 2025 quarter; true if the fall is approximately 20,000, false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Last week Treasury released the Government financial statements for 2024-25. These are actual numbers, not forecasts or projections. They’re the first year-end statements to fully reflect decisions made by the current Government, and they show progress in getting the country’s books back in order. As a share of GDP, core Crown expenses fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 in 2024-25. Our intention is to bring spending down even more as a proportion of the economy, and that intention is reflected in the Budget forecasts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core Crown expenses as a share of GDP fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 percent in 2024-25 in the audited year-end financial statements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025, core Crown expenses as a percentage of GDP; true if the two figures match, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Our farmers are the world’s most productive, best, and most carbon-efficient farmers in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand farmers are the most carbon-efficient and most productive in the world. 'Best' is not operationalisable, but the carbon-efficiency and productivity claims are.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed life-cycle emissions comparisons of on-farm emissions intensity per kilogram of milk solids and meat across producing countries (e.g. AgResearch/Ledgard international comparisons, FAO GLEAM); true if New Zealand ranks first on emissions per unit of output, false if any comparable producer ranks lower.

veracity.statement: The latest report shows an incredible improvement in the number of students who are reaching 20 weeks at school at expected levels of phonics, up from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proportion of students at expected phonics levels at their 20-week check rose from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3 of 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education phonics check national results for 2025, 20-week cohort; true if the term 1 and term 3 figures are 36% and 58%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Today, 90 percent of adults without a community services card pay $70 or less to see their general practitioner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 90 percent of adults not holding a community services card face a GP consultation fee of $70 or less.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora annual GP fees review data for 2025 on standard adult casual and enrolled consultation fees by practice; true if 90% of the relevant patient population faces a fee at or below $70, false if the share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Our primary sector earns nearly $60 billion in export revenue each year for New Zealand. It provides more than one in 10 Kiwi jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts primary sector export revenue of close to $60 billion per year and that the sector accounts for more than one in ten New Zealand jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries, food and fibre export revenue for the year to June 2025 (true if near $60 billion); Stats NZ / MPI employment estimates for the food and fibre sector as a share of total employment (true if above 10%).

veracity.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 159,000 people made submissions on the Regulatory Standards Bill and that 99 percent of them opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the Regulatory Standards Bill and/or the Ministry for Regulation consultation summary, giving the total submissions received and the share opposed; true if the totals are approximately 159,000 and 99% opposed, false if either figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: I would encourage that member and her party to reflect on the retrograde decision they have made to not support the repeal of the oil and gas ban. In the feedback coming through in her sojourn round the boardrooms of Auckland, she will know that some of the feedback coming from the business community and the energy sector has been to plead with the Opposition to support the Government’s move on energy security. She should start listening to the voices of reason in the business community that want bipartisanship on energy policy, because the best thing we could do for this country’s energy security is firm up the gas supply to make sure we keep the lights on.
rigor.explanation: The case for the policy rests almost entirely on an appeal to authority — that the business community and energy sector want it — rather than on any mechanism linking gas supply to prices or security.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it’s very interesting. A number of New Zealanders started to leave in October 2020—I wonder what was going on then. Here is the graph. Here is the net departures, which started in 2020, and you can see this massive decline in the number of people leaving New Zealand during the months of 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023. Last time I looked, this Government wasn’t in charge then. Actually, the number of people leaving, on net, has flattened out. Do we have more work to do? Of course we do, but the facts are this: under that last Government’s epic mismanagement of the economy, people fled New Zealand. We are turning it around, and she should get on board with that.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered — a departures series beginning before this government took office — and the timing point does bear on responsibility. But the conclusion overreaches: showing a trend began earlier does not show the earlier government's 'mismanagement' caused it, and the description of a 'massive decline in the number of people leaving' during 2020-2023 cuts against the very point being made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I tell you, this Government is not going to shut down Kiwi farms and send that production to less carbon-efficient places, less productive places, and make global greenhouse gas emissions worse.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the question was whether weaker methane targets expose farmers to climate-driven weather risk and higher insurance costs. The answer substitutes a position nobody advanced — shutting farms down — and rebuts that instead.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he claim that his targets are based on anything other than corporate interests when world-leading climate scientists have described his weakening of methane targets as “a great way of shooting yourself in the foot” and “New Zealand is setting a dangerous precedent that other governments must not follow”?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on an appeal to authority: that climate scientists criticise the target is evidence the target is poor, not evidence about whose interests set it. The quoted criticism cannot support the conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, that member should know, because she has a very short memory. In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term. So if she wants to know how long it takes, she should ask herself that.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. The question was how much industrial action it takes before this government responds; the answer is that strikes also occurred under the questioner's government, which does not bear on the government's own response.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What good is capping fees when under-funded practices start charging for double consultations, leading to the pensioner who wrote to me saying, “I pay $91 for a 15-minute visit, and you’re only allowed to talk about one thing. If you want to talk about two things, you need to pay for another $91. I cannot afford to pay this.”?
rigor.explanation: The mechanism is a real one and, if it operates, the conclusion follows. But the only support offered for its prevalence is a single item of correspondence — an argument from anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in my humble opinion, respectfully, I think it is potentially reckless and insensitive that the member would consider it appropriate for officialdom to ask women seeking emergency housing support, often in difficult circumstances, if they are hapū or not.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member asked what the ministry records, not that officials interrogate women about pregnancy. The rebuttal is aimed at a position that was not put.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he continue to deny the link between his tightening of the emergency housing entry criteria and the unprecedented increase in homelessness, when even pregnant women are now being denied access?
rigor.explanation: The causal link between the criteria change and rising homelessness is asserted rather than shown, and the supporting evidence offered is a single reported case, which cannot establish the general link.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can’t solve climate change by shutting down the world’s best farmers and sending that production overseas.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on a strawman: it treats the alternative to this target as shutting farms down, when the contested options are different target ranges. Nothing offered connects a stronger methane target to closing farms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fact of the matter is that this bill was halfway through the House—it was a pre-emptive strike, if you like. If the Government had, in fact, not brought this bill, I don’t think it would still feel committed, because what we now have is a Government that’s stuck its oar in, if you like—or its paddle, I suppose—and is still committed to it, whereas, in fact, the concerns in the Court of Appeal were entirely ameliorated by the Supreme Court case. Now what we have is a further tightening, which is entirely not necessary.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the Supreme Court already resolved the Court of Appeal's error, the bill's stated justification is spent, so the further tightening is unnecessary. The chain holds, but it leans on a speculative counterfactual about what the Government would have done, and on the contested premise that the Supreme Court fully cured the problem.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
rigor.explanation: Offers evidence that tracks the conclusion — post-Supreme Court awards over large stretches of coast are cited as showing the test still departs from the intended threshold. The gap is that outcomes under a test do not by themselves establish the test is wrong, and only 'a couple of decisions' are relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: To back the new target, the Government is already investing more than $400 million with industry to speed up the development and roll-out of methane-cutting tools. Three methane-cutting tools are available now, with up to 11 rolling out by 2030—one of which will be available as early as next year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that as many as eleven methane-reducing tools will be rolling out to New Zealand farmers by 2030, with at least one additional tool becoming available during 2026. The roll-out depends on industry development and regulatory approval, not on the Government's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: ACVM/EPA approval registers and commercial availability of methane-inhibiting products and vaccines for New Zealand pastoral farming; true if at least one further tool beyond those already available reaches market during 2026 and the total approaching eleven is on track by 2030, false if no additional tool becomes available in 2026 or the total remains near three at 2030.

veracity.statement: That's why the legislation was passed with the support of the National Party and the Māori Party at the time, and was set to strike a balance there with what was described, at the time, as a high threshold.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2011 Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act was enacted with the support of both the National Party and the Māori Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill (2011); true if both National and the Māori Party voted in favour, false if either voted against or abstained.

veracity.statement: What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recognition orders made following the Supreme Court's interpretation have granted customary marine title over whole coastlines rather than discrete areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The customary marine title recognition orders made by the High Court under s 58 of the Act since the Court of Appeal's Edwards decision; true if the orders cover essentially continuous whole coastlines, false if they are confined to discrete specified areas within a coastline.

veracity.statement: On page 15 of that analysis, point 44: “If the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Crown, it could mean the additional time and resource on progressing amendments would not be required”, and the Supreme Court did rule in favour of the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in his own voice, that the Supreme Court's decision went in the Crown's favour — the factual premise on which his argument that the amendments are unnecessary rests.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The disposition of the Supreme Court's December 2024 judgment in the Whakatōhea (Edwards) customary marine title appeals; true if the Attorney-General's/Crown's appeal was allowed, false if it was dismissed or the Court of Appeal's approach was upheld.

veracity.statement: However, what smarts even more and rubs salt in the wound is the fact that there was consultation with commercial fishing interests, which have already got statutory protections.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that commercial fishing interests were consulted before the amendments were finalised, in contrast to Māori applicant groups who were not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The consultation record in the regulatory impact statement / supplementary analysis for the Amendment Bill and the Waitangi Tribunal's report on the takutai moana amendments; true if commercial fishing interests appear as consulted parties prior to finalisation while Māori applicant groups do not, false if neither or both were consulted.

rigor.statement: The common-sense reading of that, for most New Zealanders when they look at that—“exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption” was the threshold that Parliament set.
rigor.explanation: Settles a contested question of statutory interpretation by appealing to how "most New Zealanders" would read the words — an appeal to popularity/common sense standing in for an interpretive argument, in a context where three courts have reached different readings.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They clarified what the intention was from 2011, and through this amendment, the Minister is coming along with a sledgehammer and smashing that nail into the wall, destroying the actual intention of 2011, which was clarified by the Supreme Court finding.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the amendment destroys rather than restores Parliament's 2011 intention rests entirely on a nail-and-sledgehammer metaphor.
