Nothing in the analogy connects to the actual textual differences between the Supreme Court test and the bill's test; the imagery does the argumentative work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem there is that there is no indication of what weight this gives; it’s not set out, as these clauses would usually be drafted, for decision makers who then need to prove that their decisions have been made reasonably and in compliance with the law.
rigor.explanation: A well-formed inference: a direction to a decision maker to consider a category of evidence, without a weighting, leaves the decision unreviewable against the standard the same decision maker must meet. The conclusion follows from the premise about how such clauses are ordinarily drafted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don't expect Mr Andy Foster to get out every day and patrol the border of his house and dig something in the lawn out every six months to prove that he is physically using his lawn, do we?
rigor.explanation: A reductio drawing on a real disanalogy — freehold owners are not put to continuing proof of use. But the two regimes differ in kind (registered title versus a statutory test for recognising an unregistered right), and that gap is not addressed, so the analogy is asserted rather than earned.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There hadn’t been an Act of Parliament passed between 1854 and 2004 that actively extinguished the Māori right to the takutai moana, so it stands that it was still there in 2004.
rigor.explanation: Valid given its premise and the common-law rule it relies on: if customary rights survive until lawfully extinguished, and no statute in the period extinguished them, they subsisted. Whether the premise about the statute book is accurate is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
rigor.explanation: The core inference — a heavier evidential burden imposes costs that a constrained budget is not funding — holds up. But the trailing conclusion that the physical-use test is inconsistent with the tikanga limb is tacked on without support, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the member is quite within his rights to say that “That’s not the right threshold”, “It should be a different threshold”, “There should be no threshold”—that’s fine.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange where a dismissive reply was readily available; instead the opponent's position is stated fairly and conceded as legitimate before being disagreed with. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To an earlier point the Minister made about the problem of customary marine title interfering with other users’ rights—and acknowledging the well-made point of my colleague Hūhana Lyndon that it seems that, frequently, it is the rights of non-Māori that are preferenced time and again over the rights of iwi Māori: for a Minister that purports to believe in property rights, I wonder that he can’t recognise the first property rights of this country, customary marine title, with a greater confidence and certainty.
civility.explanation: "Purports to believe" imputes insincerity to the Minister personally rather than disputing his position — a suggestion of bad faith. Short of a direct insult, and the substantive point about property rights is real, but it lands on the person's honesty.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
civility.explanation: Framed as a question, but its content is an imputation of a discreditable personal motive to the Minister — that he legislated over the courts to stop paying claimants' legal costs. Imputing bad faith rather than contesting the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example, somebody wanting to put in a jetty on their property, or somebody wanting to renew a consent for a jetty that they’ve had for generations.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete categories of affected activity — new aquaculture, a new jetty, renewal of an existing jetty consent — which are checkable against the consenting regime. Still no figures or numbers of affected consents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Canadian case law that the Minister was talking about there were cases like Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia that was decided in 1973, which sets out a framework that is used all around the world in common law jurisdictions to determine both the extinguishment of title by radical title of the Crown and customary rights and interests that exist in land after that has occurred, and also Guerin v the Queen in 1984.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific authorities with dates and states what doctrinal work each does. Anyone could go and check the cases and the framework described.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Wairarapa? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Aotea Harbour?

focus.statement: If we’re going to give a genuine historical account of why we’ve got here, we should probably recognise that it’s really part of the Government’s approach to Māori and Māori interests, which is, basically, to roll back the progress that we’ve made over the past, I don’t know, 150 years or so.

focus.statement: It’s well and good that we have National Ministers turning up to celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, but, surely, if their research and their findings are valued enough, they should be reflected in the preamble of this bill.

focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As a result, applicants will be forced to have their cases reheard, burdening them further, financially and emotionally as well.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The status of the affected customary marine title applications (including the seven cases named in the preamble) after the Amendment Act commences; true if those applicants are required to have their applications reheard or redetermined under the new test, false if existing determinations stand and no rehearing is required.

veracity.statement: What occurs on 28 November 2023 is that Cabinet endorses the coalition agreement between the parties as the basis on which the coalition Government will operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet formally endorsed the National–NZ First coalition agreement as the basis of government on a specific date, 28 November 2023, before the court decisions the bill responds to.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet Office circular / Cabinet minute of 28 November 2023 endorsing the coalition agreements, published on dpmc.govt.nz; true if a Cabinet decision of that date endorses the coalition agreements as the basis on which the Government operates, false if no such decision exists on that date.

veracity.statement: Cabinet made policy decisions without a regulatory impact analysis actually being provided to them, and I would like to understand why that happened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet took the broad policy decisions on this bill before any regulatory impact analysis was supplied to it, with the supplementary analysis following afterwards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement / Supplementary Analysis Report published with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill and the dates of the associated Cabinet papers; true if the RIA post-dates the Cabinet policy decisions, false if a RIA was provided before them.

veracity.statement: I raise that as an issue in my kāinga, Whangārei-terenga-parāoa, where the claimants stood in hearings and are waiting for a judgment right now, knowing that very few parcels of land around Whangārei-terenga-parāoa remain within Māori hands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that a takutai moana application for Whangārei Harbour has been heard and is awaiting judgment as at October 2025, and that very little land abutting that harbour remains in Māori ownership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court takutai moana application list for Whangārei (Te Arawhiti / courtsofnz.govt.nz) for a heard-but-undecided application as at October 2025, and Māori Land Court / LINZ records of Māori freehold land titles abutting Whangārei Harbour; true if a judgment was pending and Māori-owned parcels are a small minority, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: The only thing I'd say in relation to that member's speech, of course, is that nothing in this legislation impacts on the ability of Māori or non-Māori to go and collect shellfish and have a connection with a piece of coastline that continues, and there's all sorts of arrangements in place in relation to customary fishing rights and shellfish-gathering rights and tītī gathering rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amendment bill leaves fishing, shellfish-gathering and tītī-gathering rights untouched, those being governed by separate arrangements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill against ss 26–28 and Part 3 of the 2011 Act and the Fisheries (Kaimoana Customary Fishing) Regulations 1998; true if no provision of the bill alters fishing/gathering entitlements, false if any clause does.

veracity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that s 106(3) of the 2011 Act reads as quoted, and that the amendment bill leaves that presumption against extinguishment intact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 on legislation.govt.nz, and the clause list of the Amendment Bill; true if the quoted wording matches and no clause amends s 106, false if the wording differs or s 106 is amended.

veracity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific appropriation of $15 million to meet the extra costs of rehearing the affected customary marine title cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Vote Treaty Negotiations appropriations and the Cabinet paper or Ministerial release accompanying the bill; true if $15m is allocated for rehearing costs, false if the figure or purpose differs.

veracity.statement: In response to that, all evidence has been and will continue to be relevant to the decision maker. The change is that cultural or spiritual evidence needs supporting evidence of physical use, but tikanga and oral evidence remain important.
veracity.explanation: Characterises new section 58(1A) as merely requiring cultural or spiritual evidence to be supported by evidence of physical use, with all evidence remaining relevant to the decision maker.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new s 58(1A)(a)–(b) in clause 8 as amended by Amendment Paper 380; true if the provision admits spiritual or cultural evidence where accompanied by physical-use evidence, false if it bars a decision maker from drawing the exclusivity inference from spiritual or cultural association at all.

veracity.statement: I'm not too sure if the Minister knows this—how toheroa spat works—but you might find the toheroa on the beach or closer to the waterline, but actually, the spat finds itself in the sand dunes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about toheroa biology: that while adult toheroa are found on the beach near the waterline, the spat is located in the sand dunes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed toheroa (Paphies ventricosa) biology — NIWA/MPI research on larval settlement and juvenile distribution; true if spat settle above the intertidal beach in dune sand, false if settlement occurs in the surf zone or intertidal beach face.

specificity.statement: What occurs on 28 November 2023 is that Cabinet endorses the coalition agreement between the parties as the basis on which the coalition Government will operate.
specificity.explanation: Names an exact date, the deciding body, and the instrument endorsed; someone could go and check the Cabinet record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the Act, the section, the subsection and the operative wording — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named purpose, though without a breakdown or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does new clause 6 mean that courts cannot award costs against the Government in marine and coastal area claims?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision and the exact legal consequence at issue; the answer is checkable against the clause and could only be yes or no.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the wording I'm proposing is that in this Act, “substantial interruption” means “an interruption to the applicant group's use and occupation of an area that was of such a nature, extent, and duration that it effectively severed the group's connection with the area and that was caused by factors within the group's control or by the group's voluntary abandonment of the area”.
specificity.explanation: Supplies drafted statutory wording for the definition in issue — a mechanism precise enough to be enacted or rejected as written.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because it’s looking like all arrows are pointing towards this being simply a provision within the coalition agreement that was enacted without proper due analysis.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from stated evidence — the RIS's short turnarounds, absent financial forecasting and missing pre-decision analysis support the conclusion that analysis was thin. The gap is that 'driven by the coalition agreement' is asserted rather than shown by the same evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is unfair on tangata whenua to have to show that somehow we’ve got a physical manifestation of connection to that space, when we may not own by Western law the whenua abutting that part of the takutai moana.
rigor.explanation: Premise (dispossession of adjoining land through public works) is offered in support of the conclusion (the physical-manifestation test is unfair), and it largely tracks. Minor gap: the clause requires physical activity or use of resources, not land ownership, so the link is asserted rather than fully closed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As he well knows, what the section refers to is that it prevails over section 7 of the legislation, which has the title “Treaty of Waitangi”; it’s not the Treaty of Waitangi itself. It is simply overriding section 7.
rigor.explanation: Draws a valid distinction between a statutory provision titled 'Treaty of Waitangi' and the Treaty itself, which is exactly the equivocation in the argument being answered. The conclusion follows from the text of the clause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet you’re saying here that this piece of legislation will override the Treaty of Waitangi. That’s exactly what this says.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the clause he quoted prevails over section 7 of the 2011 Act, a provision headed 'Treaty of Waitangi', not over the Treaty itself. The conclusion that the bill overrides the Treaty does not follow from the text offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s quite conceivable that there are customary rights which occur only once every few months or only once a year or conceivably once a generation, or even longer than that, but that doesn’t make them any less customary rights.
rigor.explanation: A valid point about the 'substantial interruption' test: frequency of exercise is offered as independent of the existence of a right, and the counter-examples (seasonal harvest, ceremonial navigation) support the conclusion that lawful third-party use need not interrupt anything.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So purporting to say that these rights had arisen in the agreement reached by the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011 and were then enshrined in that legislation is wrong and is an interpretation of the law which doesn't recognise that those rights were something that existed, that there were a bundle of property rights held by people in accordance with the legal system which was operative.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises she set out: the rights were litigated in 2003–05 precisely because they arose outside statute, therefore 2011 legislation could recognise but not create them. No fallacy; the inference tracks the offered history.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect one preamble in this bill to a general practice of directing judges from campaign documents in unrelated statutes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We took your words in good faith, and you bought no physical evidence. This whole House relies on testimony—oral testimonies—that we may question or test, but why would you deny something as powerful as the likes of the articulation of the relationship in a physical sense that an iwi produces on a regular basis in interaction, in telling their history with the land and the water?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the evidence clause, but resting on a weak analogy: the House accepting an unverified personal anecdote as courtesy is not the same standard as a court determining property rights, so the parallel does not carry the conclusion on its own.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the member’s genealogy extends maybe four or five times longer than my 180 years in this country, but that makes me no less of a New Zealander than he or any other New Zealander is.
civility.explanation: Answers a pointed personal challenge to his standing to bring the bill without any counter-attack on the member; concedes the other's longer whakapapa and argues from equal citizenship.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Given that there are a limited number of cases that fall in here, what is the massive policy objection to saying “Well, you got in under the law as it was”, which is how it works, we generally like to think that this is the concept of the rule of law; the Minister may not be familiar with it, but the idea is that you apply the law as it stands and you don’t pull the legal rug from under people and change legal history, but that seems to be exactly what’s going on here.
civility.explanation: The retrospectivity argument itself is on the substance, but the aside that the Minister 'may not be familiar with' the rule of law is condescension aimed at the person rather than the provision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They’ve done that recently and they won’t be doing it for a long time to come, I imagine, but you never know, they might, and that is the system that we have, and we’re accountable for that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that voters will not turn out the current Government at the next opportunity — an electoral outcome, not a commitment to any action of his own.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election declared by the Electoral Commission; true if the National-led coalition is returned to government, false if a change of government occurs.

focus.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — preambles plus interpretive directions to decision makers — but the weight of the sentence is party framing about what 'a National Government' would do.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why won’t you preserve the rights that exist now when the High Court has recognised them under the old test but will clearly meet your new test?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named decision against the bill's own new threshold, asking for a specific carve-out. Names the policy and the outcome sought — the opposition's job, entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Watch out, New Zealand, you’re getting the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Labour.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other parties as a bloc. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — nothing about the clause under debate survives if you remove the party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the amendment before the committee — customary marine title, resource consent powers and port operation. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to ask him first in respect of his change to the interim period, which at new clause 4 in new Schedule 1AA says, “Certain CMT [customary marine title] decisions made in interim period,”—so say, Ruapuke—“and related agreements and orders made, have no legal effect and never have had legal effect”; what does that mean for the cases where other decisions have been made in reliance upon them, and has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the Minister's own Amendment Paper and its downstream legal consequences. No reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So what I have done is I have drafted an Amendment Paper, Amendment Paper 388, explicitly modelled after new section 339—the same section around federation polytechnics—that will enable anchor polytechnics to be designated and removed from the designation of anchor polytechnics, using the exact same language and the exact same processes that the Minister has outlined for federations.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the bill before the committee, and offered constructively to a Minister from an opposing party. Contains no party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not financially viable. I haven’t seen any information, nor has anyone ever told me that this puts the sector in a more financially viable position than it was prior to Te Pūkenga, and I still encourage the Minister to share that information with the House.
focus.explanation: Engages the financial viability of the model the bill creates, benchmarked against a named predecessor (Te Pūkenga). A weak argument about the policy is still squarely about the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference about the policy (CMT plus consenting power over a port site would impede port operation), but the connecting step is never shown; it rests on an invitation to imagine and an appeal to what 'most New Zealanders could understand' rather than on any evidence about how consenting actually interacts with port operations.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So any arrangements that have been entered into would have been done in the knowledge that there was a risk that this legislation would pass and that the legislation would require those examples to be heard again under the new test, so I think everybody would have gone into it with eyes wide open.
rigor.explanation: The inference — announcement gave notice, therefore parties assumed the risk — is valid for arrangements entered after the announcement, but the conclusion is stated universally ('any arrangements'), which does not follow for anything entered before July 2024 or for evidence and consultations that predate it. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
rigor.explanation: A clean deductive step from stated premises: if applicants must prove no substantial interruption, and extinguishment counts as a substantial interruption, then applicants must prove non-extinguishment — which is inconsistent with a presumption of non-extinguishment. Whether the premises correctly read the clause is a separate question; the inference itself holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no evidence that has been brought to this House in this committee stage or at any stage of the select committee that confirms what the Minister keeps saying: that he’s restoring the intent. It is the invention of an imaginary intent.
rigor.explanation: An argument from absence of evidence: nothing has been produced, therefore the intent is invented. It has more force than usual because the burden of establishing original intent properly sits with the person claiming it, but 'no evidence tabled' still does not establish 'no such intent existed', so a real gap remains between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s no need for us to have that explicit in the legislation; it would be via an Order in Council.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (the Order in Council power suffices), but it is asserted rather than shown, and it does not engage the specific objection put to her — that the Order in Council power sits under the heading 'Establishment of polytechnics' and so may not reach institutions already established. The conclusion outruns what was supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not financially viable. I haven’t seen any information, nor has anyone ever told me that this puts the sector in a more financially viable position than it was prior to Te Pūkenga, and I still encourage the Minister to share that information with the House.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: nothing has been shown to him, therefore the model is not financially viable. His own not having seen the information does not establish the negative claim, though the demand that the Minister produce it is a fair one. A weak inference about a real policy question.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Amendment Paper—and I mentioned the use of occupation amendment, there's another Amendment Paper in my colleague Arena Williams’ name which refers directly to Part 1, clause 7, and it looks towards the removal of, under Part 1, clause 7 new 57B: replace every instance of “and occupation” with “stewardship”.
specificity.explanation: Names the part, the clause, the new section and the exact wording change proposed. Anyone could locate and act on this; it is a precise drafting proposition rather than a direction of travel. Falls short of 1.0 only because no consequence or threshold is quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to ask him first in respect of his change to the interim period, which at new clause 4 in new Schedule 1AA says, “Certain CMT [customary marine title] decisions made in interim period,”—so say, Ruapuke—“and related agreements and orders made, have no legal effect and never have had legal effect”; what does that mean for the cases where other decisions have been made in reliance upon them, and has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?
specificity.explanation: Cites the new clause, the schedule, the operative words quoted directly, and a named case (Ruapuke) as the test instance. The question is precise enough that the Minister could answer it with a document reference.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what I have done is I have drafted an Amendment Paper, Amendment Paper 388, explicitly modelled after new section 339—the same section around federation polytechnics—that will enable anchor polytechnics to be designated and removed from the designation of anchor polytechnics, using the exact same language and the exact same processes that the Minister has outlined for federations.
specificity.explanation: Names the Amendment Paper by number, the section it is modelled on, the precise gap it fills and the mechanism it borrows. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To ensure that a polytechnic is successful, it must be very engaged with their community, must be very integrated with their community, and must understand their community.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues offered in answer to a direct question about how Māori will be represented on ITP councils. No mechanism, no threshold, no appointment process — nothing a council or the Ministry could act on or that anyone could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if I turn to clause 4(2), in “Section 9 amended (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)”, which replaces section 9(2)(e) with section 314(d), the question for the Minister is: in her view, why has this wording been changed?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the clause, the section amended and the exact provisions substituted. A precise question of this kind carries as much checkable content as a precise answer would.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in relation to that question, when this policy to overturn the Court of Appeal decision was announced originally in July 2024, the Government signalled, of course, right at that point that we would seek to have the legislation take effect from that point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a date (July 2024) for the announcement of the policy to overturn the Court of Appeal decision, and that retrospective application from that date was signalled at the time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's July 2024 announcement of its response to the Court of Appeal's Whakatōhea/Edwards decision (Cabinet paper and Minister's press release). True if that announcement stated the intended amendments would take effect from the date of announcement; false if no such retrospective effect was signalled then, or if the announcement was made in a different month.

veracity.statement: Nobody’s bloody been successful in direct negotiations.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that the Crown engagement pathway has produced no successful outcome for any applicant group. Emphatic and unqualified, so a single concluded recognition agreement falsifies it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti records of applications resolved through the Crown engagement (direct negotiation) pathway under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. True if no applicant group has concluded a recognition agreement by that route as at October 2025; false if one or more have.

veracity.statement: I want to call back to what the officials told us in the supplementary analysis report, where Te Arawhiti said in their overall analysis—Te Arawhiti considered this reform was unlikely to address the primary concerns Māori have with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, as identified through the Waitangi Tribunal 266O inquiry, and any amendments proposed to address the coalition commitments only make it harder under the current law to prove customary marine title.
veracity.explanation: She is relaying an official agency assessment, not asserting the underlying policy judgement herself. What is checkable is whether the supplementary analysis report actually says this.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report / regulatory impact statement accompanying the Bill. True if Te Arawhiti's overall analysis states the reform was unlikely to address Māori concerns identified in the Waitangi Tribunal Wai 2660 inquiry and that the amendments make CMT harder to prove; false if the report contains no such assessment or reaches the opposite conclusion.

veracity.statement: I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour Government passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation in 2004 and that it took the coastal area for the Crown, roughly 21 years before this debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment record of the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 — the government that passed it, the year, and whether it vested the public foreshore and seabed in the Crown. True if passed under the fifth Labour Government in 2004 with Crown vesting; false on any of those three points.

veracity.statement: It certainly moves away from it in so far as it puts the burden of proof on iwi Māori and the onus on iwi Māori, rather than the onus being on the Crown to prove extinguishment, which was clearly articulated by the Minister at the time, Chris Finlayson, in that the onus had to be borne by the Crown to prove extinguishment; not that iwi Māori had to prove customary title.
veracity.explanation: The checkable element is the attribution to Chris Finlayson: that as the responsible Minister in 2011 he stated the Crown bore the onus of proving extinguishment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2011 passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill and Chris Finlayson's statements as Minister, read alongside section 106 of the Act. True if Finlayson stated the onus of proving extinguishment lay with the Crown rather than on applicants to prove customary title; false if he articulated the opposite or said nothing to that effect.

veracity.statement: The Minister has publicly stated and pledged to my local polytechnic, the Otago Polytechnic, and also to the Otago Daily Times, that if they meet the road to viability, which they’re on track to do, they will be able to exit the federation and exit their anchor polytechnic status.
veracity.explanation: Reports a commitment made by another member — that the Minister publicly pledged Otago Polytechnic could exit anchor/federation status on reaching viability.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting and Penny Simmonds' public statements about Otago Polytechnic. True if she publicly said Otago Polytechnic would be able to exit the federation and its anchor polytechnic status once financially viable; false if no such statement exists or she said the opposite.

veracity.statement: The member did refer to a lot of numbers, and I can assure the member that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million to the rehearing of cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has taken advice and allocated up to $15 million specifically for rehearing the affected CMT cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget or Cabinet documents and Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti appropriations for the Marine and Coastal Area amendments. True if an allocation of up to $15 million for the rehearing of customary marine title cases exists; false if no such allocation was made or the figure differs materially.

civility.statement: To simply say, “Oh, for example, here’s a few we found” is actually either lazy or misleading.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust about the drafting, but 'lazy' characterises the effort of whoever drafted it rather than the text itself. It edges toward the person without landing on them — no attack on competence, character or intelligence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a shameful day for the rule of law when we let people go to court and win, and then when we don’t like what they’ve won, we take it off them.
civility.explanation: About as harsh as criticism of a legislative act can be, and it attacks no one. The target is the retrospective mechanism and its effect on litigants, not any member's character. Under the re-anchored scale this is near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
civility.explanation: 'Thank the member for his history lesson' is a sneer at the preceding speech rather than an engagement with it — condescension aimed at the member, though brief and unaccompanied by any attack on his character. Sits just above the 0.5 failure line because the rest of the answer does engage the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: See, with this raupatu legislation that’s coming through the House, they will not be able to get entitlement, when any type of CMT that they had is now going to be ripped away from them.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the named groups' existing CMT recognitions will be voided on commencement and that no compensation will follow. It is a prediction about the world's state after enactment, not a promise about her own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The status, after the Act commences, of the customary marine title recognition orders and interim judgments held by the groups she named (Wairarapa; Aotea Harbour — Ngāti Te Wehi, Ngāti Whakamarurangi, Waikato-Tainui; the Kāpiti Coast groups; Ngā Pōtiki and associated hapū; Ruapuke Island). True if those orders cease to have legal effect and no compensation is paid to those groups; false if any of them retains its CMT without rehearing, or receives compensation.

veracity.statement: The fact that no work was done in five years to address their financial situation was absolutely appalling.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no work at all was done on polytechnics' financial sustainability over the five years of the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC and Te Pūkenga board papers, annual reports and Ministry of Education advice 2018–2023 on financial-sustainability work for individual polytechnics; false if any such work is documented in that period, true if none is.

veracity.statement: I reflect back on 2018 when $20 million had to be injected into Whitireia and WelTec to keep the lights on so that they could continue to pay their staff and their bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly $20 million of Crown money was put into Whitireia and WelTec in 2018 to keep them operating.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / TEC records of Crown financial support to Whitireia and WelTec around 2018; true if approximately $20m was provided for operating solvency, false if the amount or the year is materially different.

veracity.statement: I understand from the first Budget bid that was leaked in October 2022 that that was to be $940 million – odd over 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Te Pūkenga Budget bid leaked in October 2022 sought about $940 million over ten years for digital systems.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The leaked Te Pūkenga Budget bid reported in October 2022 and contemporaneous Ministry of Education documents; true if it sought approximately $940m over ten years, false if the figure or the timing is materially different.

veracity.statement: They weren’t able to do that once the pastoral care code came in, which the Green Party brought in.
veracity.explanation: Attributes authorship of the tertiary pastoral care code to the Green Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the Education (Pastoral Care of Tertiary and International Learners) Code of Practice and its parent amendment Act — which party and Government introduced it; true if the Green Party introduced it, false if it was introduced by the Labour-led Government.

veracity.statement: It started recovering in 2023 and there’s been a continuation and acceleration of that trend during this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that international student numbers began recovering in 2023 and that the recovery accelerated under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education New Zealand / Immigration NZ international student enrolment counts 2022–2025; true if enrolments rose in 2023 and the annual rate of growth increased from 2024, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: They talked in their submission about how 38 percent of disabled people aged 15 years and over who were not currently in post-secondary education or training would like to do so in the future but face numerous barriers in accessing it.
veracity.explanation: Relays a statistic from the joint DPA/NDSA submission: 38 percent of disabled people aged 15+ not in post-secondary education would like to be.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Disabled Persons Assembly and the National Disabled Students’ Association
veracity.falsification_criterion: The joint DPA / National Disabled Students' Association submission on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill and the underlying Stats NZ disability survey; true if it reports 38 percent on that measure, false if the figure or the population differs.

veracity.statement: It’s a pity that the previous Government spent a billion dollars trying to solve a problem that was only about a few million at the time and didn’t create an enduring solution.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a spend of about a billion dollars on Te Pūkenga against an underlying problem worth only a few million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education and Te Pūkenga financial reports on total Crown funding appropriated and spent on Te Pūkenga's establishment, and the aggregate ITP operating deficits at the time of the merger; true if spend was of the order of $1bn against deficits of a few million, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: What can she say to claims locally that there is a privatisation agenda in tertiary education, because we have seen a mental health programme cut from Otago Polytechnic that is now suddenly appearing via a private provider in Dunedin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a mental health programme was cut from Otago Polytechnic and an equivalent has since appeared at a private provider in Dunedin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic programme closure records for 2024–25 and NZQA programme approvals for a comparable mental health qualification at a Dunedin private training establishment; true if the programme was discontinued and an equivalent is now offered privately, false if either half does not hold.

veracity.statement: Otago Polytechnic sadly have a debt of $16 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific debt figure for Otago Polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic / Te Pūkenga audited financial statements for the most recent reporting year; true if debt is approximately $16m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Perhaps it’s the fact that the polytech sector, under Te Pūkenga, did not get back to pre-COVID numbers, with internationals sitting at only a third, when the universities and the schools and the private training establishments were getting back.
veracity.explanation: Asserts ITP international enrolments sat at about a third of pre-COVID levels while universities, schools and PTEs recovered further.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts / Education New Zealand international enrolment data by sub-sector, 2019 baseline against 2023–24; true if ITP internationals were around one third of the 2019 level while the other three sub-sectors were materially closer to theirs, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: I believe that the polytech sector trains more Māori than any other part of the tertiary education sector—something that I am incredibly proud of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ITPs train more Māori learners than any other tertiary sub-sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts tertiary enrolment data by ethnicity and sub-sector for the most recent year; true if ITPs enrol more Māori learners than universities, wānanga or PTEs, false if any other sub-sector enrols more.

veracity.statement: But even worse than this, and I hope the member listens very carefully to this—this is one of the reasons why redundancies have had to be made there—under the previous Government, $6.5 million was clawed back by the Tertiary Education Commission because under the closure of their campus from the cyclone, they didn’t meet their targeted numbers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that TEC recovered $6.5 million from EIT under the previous Government because cyclone-related closure meant enrolment targets were missed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC funding recovery / wash-up records for EIT for 2023, and Ministry of Education advice on cyclone-affected enrolment relief; true if approximately $6.5m was recovered on that basis, false if no recovery occurred or the amount or reason differs.

veracity.statement: NorthTec’s qualification completion rate for Māori was fourth out of 16 ITPs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NorthTec ranks fourth of sixteen ITPs on Māori qualification completion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC educational performance indicators for ITPs for the year cited; true if NorthTec ranks 4th of 16 on Māori qualification completion, false if the rank differs.

specificity.statement: I reflect back on 2018 when $20 million had to be injected into Whitireia and WelTec to keep the lights on so that they could continue to pay their staff and their bills.
specificity.explanation: Names the institutions, the year and the amount — checkable without further detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They talked in their submission about how 38 percent of disabled people aged 15 years and over who were not currently in post-secondary education or training would like to do so in the future but face numerous barriers in accessing it.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the population, the age threshold and the percentage — a reader could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can this be ensured when areas like Tairāwhiti and EIT Tairāwhiti, who have a Māori population of 56 percent and a rangatahi population of 70.4 percent, have lost 40 academic and support roles?
specificity.explanation: Two population figures and a staffing loss count, all attached to a named campus.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, let me give her the opposite situation in SIT, who went into Te Pūkenga with $40 million in reserves. Only $15 million of that will be ring-fenced, so they will not come out with the full amount that they went in with.
specificity.explanation: Two figures and the mechanism (ring-fencing in the recapitalisation) applied to a named institution.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Six of the governing positions will be by industry and will be put there by industry; two will be put by the Minister, but the Minister can only appoint people that industry have nominated.
specificity.explanation: Exact composition of the board and the constraint on the ministerial appointments — checkable against the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, this has nothing to do with the bill that we are currently looking at, but I can give the member assurance that total funding of approximately $18.5 million has been allocated to Māori and Pasifika trades training, and the funding was fully allocated in 2024-25.
specificity.explanation: Named programme, dollar figure and funding year.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The member will be delighted to know—absolutely delighted to know, I am sure—that EIT will be getting $1.559 million under the strategic fund in the next two years.
specificity.explanation: Named institution, exact amount to three decimal places, named fund and timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, in terms of the overarching retention of Māori learners at NorthTec, it was second out of 16 ITPs.
specificity.explanation: A named measure, a named institution and a precise ranking against a defined comparator set.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to think of a plan whereby people are put at the centre of decision making instead of a balance sheet, because not all regions are the same, e tātou mā.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, threshold or figure: nothing here says what a people-centred criterion would actually be.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m hoping that they will be able to grow that again, and I consider that we are not going to be faced with the sort of question of additional $930 million – odd being needed over the following nine years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the new polytechnic system will not generate a funding demand of the order of $930 million over the next nine years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations and TEC/Ministry of Education funding bids for the vocational education system to 2034; false if a bid or appropriation of that order (roughly $900m+ over the period) is sought for the new system, true if none is.

rigor.statement: That is a decision that should be made by the council of that polytechnic because they should be engaged with their community, they should know what is needed in their community.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (local councils have the local knowledge) and it does support the conclusion, but the premise is stated as what councils 'should' do rather than evidence that they do, leaving a gap between the normative claim and the institutional one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does it mean the people on the board should live in the same place? Does it mean they should have brown hair or blue eyes?
rigor.explanation: A reductio: the underlying point about drafting vagueness is real, but the illustration treats an ordinary statutory phrase as literally unbounded, which overstates the gap rather than demonstrating it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Submissions noted in the Ministry of Education departmental report that there were alternative options—these were not adequately considered because of the ideological agenda of this Government and the Minister.
rigor.explanation: The premise (submissions raised alternative options) does not support the causal conclusion; motive is asserted as the explanation with nothing offered to connect the two — an appeal to imputed motive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does dilute Māori representation and therefore will directly impact on achieving Māori outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A 'therefore' spanning a large gap: nothing is offered linking a change in council composition wording to measured learner outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would expect that there would be virtually no community in this country that would not have a significant proportion of Māori in it, and therefore I would expect that that would be reflected in the council.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the presence of Māori in a community does not entail their presence on its polytechnic council, which is the very inference the deleted 'include Māori' requirement existed to secure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not always about financial viability; it can actually be for public good, because what’s good for Northland is good for all of Aotearoa New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a sweeping unsupported generalisation — that regional benefit automatically transfers to national benefit — with nothing offered to connect them.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why would you take out from the charter a vital piece of the machinery, like the industry skills boards, the obligation that a Treaty clause conveys to engage fully with Māori leadership and with mana whenua to ensure that the right services are being delivered?
focus.explanation: Names the specific mechanism (industry skills boards) and the specific provision removed; scrutiny of a drafting decision, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a pity that the previous Government spent a billion dollars trying to solve a problem that was only about a few million at the time and didn’t create an enduring solution.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (Te Pūkenga), a figure and an outcome, though the framing is squarely about the other party's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can this be ensured when areas like Tairāwhiti and EIT Tairāwhiti, who have a Māori population of 56 percent and a rangatahi population of 70.4 percent, have lost 40 academic and support roles?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names the statutory characteristic at issue, the institution, and the specific staffing outcome that tests it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour loves quotas.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other party with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named — the interjection carries no content about the clause under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: She has not explained why she chose to disestablish Te Pūkenga as opposed to tweaking some of the challenges that the structure and the sector still faced.
focus.explanation: Names the specific decision and the specific alternative not addressed — accountability for a policy choice, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is no clear rationale that has been explained to the people of the South as to why SIT gets treatment on one hand—including Cabinet investment under her Government—versus no funding and a requirement for the Otago Polytechnic to have a pathway to recovery, which the unions have described as a cost-cutting programme.
focus.explanation: Names two institutions and the differing funding decisions applied to each; scrutiny of a specific ministerial decision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have been thrown under the bus by their leader, because remember, this mess was set up by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins and followed on from the mess in the police and in health and in COVID.
focus.explanation: Beyond naming who set up Te Pūkenga, the weight is a sweep across unrelated portfolios characterising the other side's record; no measure, figure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to think of a plan whereby people are put at the centre of decision making instead of a balance sheet, because not all regions are the same, e tātou mā.
focus.explanation: Squarely about how polytechnic viability decisions are made — the measure before the House — rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What was that, expert on Māori representation?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery aimed at another member personally rather than at anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Across this piece of legislation, it is the emperor without clothes, if anyone knows those stories, because the Minister has been building this plane as it flies, because there is a lack of information.
civility.explanation: Mocking imagery directed at how the Minister personally has handled the bill; short of a direct insult, but it sneers rather than engaging the drafting.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to ask the Minister about an elephant in the room in the lower South, in terms of why she is tearing apart our region when it comes to tertiary education.
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister as personally setting out to damage a region — an imputation about her motives rather than a criticism of the decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m going to spell this out very clearly because I know that financial matters can be quite challenging for some members of the Labour Party, but let me make it very clear to you: there was no conflict of interest there.
civility.explanation: Condescension about the intellectual capacity of named opposing members, attached to what is otherwise a substantive answer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A wonderful polytechnic, Otago Polytechnic, that has been so damaged by Te Pūkenga and all she wants to do is put out misinformation.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the member personally — that her purpose is to spread misinformation — rather than contesting what she said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Pūkenga: what a failed experiment, what a dreadful example of going with form before function, what a dreadful way to try to solve a few specific problems in the sector by creating far, far more.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the policy and the institution; no person is attacked, so it meets the standard cleanly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They have been thrown under the bus by their leader, because remember, this mess was set up by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins and followed on from the mess in the police and in health and in COVID.
civility.explanation: Attributes a pattern of personal failure across portfolios to a named member — an attack on his competence rather than on any decision's merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It would be great to see him come to our meetings; they’re well advertised.
civility.explanation: A pointed implication that a named local MP does not turn up to community meetings; it edges toward the person without landing a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, if you look at the parent Act’s section 276, members of councils for the university sector, it has institutions which can be between eight to 12 council members.
specificity.explanation: Names the parent Act, the exact section, and the numeric range; anyone could open section 276 and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
specificity.explanation: Names the institution, an exact dollar figure, the duration and the purpose of the funding — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the Education and Training Act as it is currently, with the provisions in relation to Te Pūkenga which this bill removes, there is a change from including a specific clause relating to polytechnics—which in the current Act is, I understand, section 318—to, in this, with the Minister’s bill, in Part 1 on page 9, amended section 267—it essentially puts academic freedom back into the primary academic freedom clause that applies to wānanga and universities as well.
specificity.explanation: Names both the section being removed and the section replacing it, with the page of the bill and the precise legislative mechanism; falls short of 1.0 only for the hedged section reference.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What communications, if any, has she had with the Minister for social development since the select committee stage and would she see the need for voices within the workforce rather than just industry as part of that board and those respective areas noted in Schedule 6?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question to Schedule 6 and to a named portfolio, but the substance asked for — 'voices within the workforce' — carries no mechanism, threshold or figure that could be checked against.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if you look at the parent Act’s section 276, members of councils for the university sector, it has institutions which can be between eight to 12 council members.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the parent Act sets university council membership at between eight and twelve members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education and Training Act 2020, section 276 as currently in force: true if it provides for university councils of between 8 and 12 members, false if the range stated in the section differs.

veracity.statement: Although I do note that Opposition members, including the Leader of the Opposition, has already committed to not re-establishing it again, but it does create a legislative safeguard to prevent that.
veracity.explanation: Relays a commitment attributed to the Leader of the Opposition that a future Labour government would not re-establish Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by the Leader of the Opposition, Chris Hipkins, and Labour spokespeople on or before 14 October 2025: true if a commitment not to re-establish Te Pūkenga has been made publicly, false if no such commitment can be found.

veracity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a precise annual allocation to NorthTec and that it is the largest strategic-fund allocation to any polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission strategic/priority funding allocations by polytechnic for the two years from 2026: true if NorthTec receives $3.648 million per year and that is the largest allocation of any ITP, false if either the figure or the ranking differs.

veracity.statement: Nowhere is more important than in the Far North, where we’ve got the highest number of NEETs anywhere in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Far North has the country's highest count of young people not in employment, education or training.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MSD statistics on youth not in employment, education or training by region and territorial authority: true if Northland or the Far North records the highest NEET figure in the country on the measure stated, false if another region is higher. Note the claim says 'number' while regional comparisons are normally made on rate — check both.

veracity.statement: They said to the Education and Workforce Committee in their submission that at no point was anyone able to articulate the problem that the reforms solved.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim made by a submitter organisation about what it told the select committee; the checkable fact is what the submission says.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Civil Contractors New Zealand's written submission to the Education and Workforce Committee on this bill: true if it states that no one was able to articulate the problem the reforms are trying to solve, false if the submission contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: Only 11 percent of submitters support this legislation—11 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific proportion of submitters on the bill expressed support for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report and the departmental report summarising submissions on this bill: true if approximately 11% of submitters are recorded as supporting the bill, false if the recorded proportion is materially different.

veracity.statement: Under her watch, there have been thousands less apprentices enrolling in programmes, there’s thousands less graduating from the programmes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that apprenticeship enrolments and completions have each dropped by thousands since the Minister took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission industry training and apprenticeship data for 2023 to 2025: true if both new apprenticeship enrolments and completions fell by thousands over the period, false if either fell by materially less or rose.

rigor.statement: Essentially, if the Minister doesn’t strengthen the language around consultation and upgrade it to requiring the consent of the poytechnic, I think she’s, essentially, leaving the door open for Te Pūkenga to be re-established, which she said that she doesn’t want to do.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the drafting: consultation without consent does leave a future Minister free to re-designate polytechnics, and he supplies the mechanism (fold them into the federation, rename it). The final step — that this amounts to re-establishing Te Pūkenga — stretches beyond what the clause shows, so there is a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anywhere between six and eight is generally accepted as a good working board or council that will be able to represent the community but also be agile and nimble.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that six to eight is the right size rests entirely on an appeal to received wisdom — 'generally accepted' — with no evidence, source or reasoning offered for why that range produces the claimed agility.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, it is described as “may”, but it is, effectively, mandatory because the chair will be appointed.
rigor.explanation: Answers a question about permissive drafting by asserting the outcome will happen anyway. The reason given (a chair will be appointed) supports the practical claim but does not establish that a discretionary 'may' is 'effectively mandatory' — a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the cluster that you’ve established is the anchor polytechnic of the Open Polytechnic, who are the educational delivery partner—that is their core business. They are not the financial partner, as I understand it. So who, therefore, in that live example, is offering the fiscal advice to assist Otago Polytechnic to get to a place of sustainability as required by this legislation?
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: the stated problem is financial, the designated anchor's expertise is educational delivery, therefore the model leaves the financial problem unaddressed. Premises are offered, flagged as his understanding, and the conclusion tracks them.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In regard to the comments from Civil Contractors New Zealand, the CE of Civil Contractors New Zealand Alan Pollard—Alan has his own inimitable way of expressing himself and I enjoy conversations with him.
civility.explanation: Responds to a substantive submission by characterising the way its author expresses himself rather than the content — a gently condescending dismissal of the person. Short of a direct insult, but it edges past pointed into sneering at the messenger.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A number of submissions were made on that, and I wonder if the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins sometimes reflects and wishes he’d gone down that track.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal — it invites the House to picture a named member privately regretting his judgement — but the barb is tied to a policy decision rather than to his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I see that the Minister is not willing to answer that particular question.
civility.explanation: Imputes unwillingness rather than noting that no answer had yet been given — a mild attribution of bad faith to the Minister personally, though it stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m keen to know, in relation to section 314, why there is nothing in there, in the description of the characteristics, about the role that polytechs play in alleviating skills and workforce shortages.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at a named provision and a specific omission from it; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of my colleagues said to me, when she received the Library pack, that it’s quite easy to do a speech on this in opposition because there are so many negative stories that have come out as a result.
focus.explanation: Gestures at real consequences of the reform, but the weight of the remark is on how easy the politics of opposing it are rather than on any named policy, measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Speaking of regions served by the anchor polytech, how will the Minister ensure local autonomy in multi-region providers like UCOL Wairarapa?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the anchor-polytechnic model against a named institution and a named region; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It’s going to see the closure of its main campus in Whangārei, as an example, to be relocated somewhere else.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the closure and relocation of NorthTec's main Whangārei campus as a consequence of the reforms.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NorthTec / Tertiary Education Commission announcements and Northland news reporting: true if NorthTec's main Whangārei campus closes and its provision is relocated to another site, false if that campus remains NorthTec's main Whangārei campus.

divination.statement: Her timelines have ISBs to be established on 1 January 2026. That is not on track to be set up.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the industry skills boards will miss the Government's stated 1 January 2026 establishment date.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Gazette notices and Tertiary Education Commission announcements establishing the industry skills boards: true if the ISBs were not established and operating on 1 January 2026, false if they were established on that date as planned.

rigor.statement: It was only two weeks ago that the Education and Workforce Committee reported back; lo and behold, last week we had the second reading, and we have the committee of the whole House today, but very few amendments, which tells me that, despite a large number of submissions, the Minister hasn’t really taken those on board too much.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the process: from the small number of amendments he concludes submissions were not taken on board. The premise is offered and relevant, but the conclusion outruns it — submissions can be reflected in a bill without producing amendments at committee of the whole House, and the compressed timetable is a separate point. A genuine but under-supported inference, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, the reform that the Minister puts before the Chamber today doesn’t aid in offering any certainty or stability for the sector. It, in fact, offers more instability and more questions that remain unresolved.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to anecdote — what institutions say to him when he meets them — generalised into a claim about what the legislation itself delivers. No mechanism in the bill is identified that would produce the instability asserted, so there is a real gap between what was offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is because Māori figure so prominently in statistics that show they are getting the rough end of the employment market and the education system, and we have an obligation to take that seriously and to fix that.
rigor.explanation: A premise (disparities in Māori employment and education outcomes) is offered in support of a conclusion (that high-quality engagement with iwi Māori should sit at the heart of the vocational system). The premise is relevant and the inference is reasonable, but the connecting step — that council-level engagement requirements are what improves those outcomes — is assumed rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the title, I support Shanan Halbert’s amendment, because I believe the Minister has created more instability in the sector, and I ask and plead that we can do something to ensure the staff, the students, and the community can feel affirmed and stable in the future, going forward, of vocational education.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to anecdote (what he heard on one visit to WITT) plus a stated belief, with no provision of the bill identified as the source of the instability. He also acknowledges the previous reform caused upheaval, which cuts against attributing instability to this Minister without further argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some submitters were concerned that this could limit workers’ right to strike, but let me clarify: this only applies to the notification that unions must provide before conducting a strike. It does not limit workers’ rights to engage in lawful industrial action.
rigor.explanation: She states the objection accurately and answers it directly, which is more than most rebuttals here manage. But the conclusion follows only if a longer mandatory notice period counts as no constraint at all on the right — a definitional move rather than a demonstration, since the submitters' concern was precisely that lengthening notice restricts the practical exercise of the right.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was only two weeks ago that the Education and Workforce Committee reported back; lo and behold, last week we had the second reading, and we have the committee of the whole House today, but very few amendments, which tells me that, despite a large number of submissions, the Minister hasn’t really taken those on board too much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific parliamentary timeline for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: select committee report-back roughly two weeks before 14 October 2025, second reading the preceding week, committee of the whole House on the day of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if the Education and Workforce Committee reported back in the last days of September or first days of October 2025 (i.e. ~2 weeks before 14 Oct) and the second reading occurred in the week of 7 October 2025; false if either stage is materially outside that window.

veracity.statement: There was lots of opportunity there, but this Minister, under this legislation, has chosen to disestablish that successful model and re-establish a model with half the funding and more entities to manage, which just doesn’t make sense in any respect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable quantities about the replacement of workforce development councils with industry skills boards: that the funding for the new arrangement is about half that of the old, and that there will be more entities than there were WDCs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Tertiary Education / TEC appropriations and Ministry of Education transition documents: true if annual funding budgeted for industry skills boards is approximately half the funding previously appropriated to the six workforce development councils AND the number of established ISBs exceeds the number of WDCs; false if funding is materially closer to parity or the number of entities is the same or fewer.

veracity.statement: That’s simply because we’re going back to a model that was so expensive. We ended up with millions of dollars of debt. Consecutive Governments had to continue to bail institutions out, and that, in fact, is one of the primary reasons why we established Te Pūkenga.
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions about the pre-Te Pūkenga polytechnic sector: that institutes accumulated debt in the millions, that successive governments repeatedly provided financial rescue, and that this financial position was a primary stated rationale for creating Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
