veracity.falsification_criterion: Institute of Technology and Polytechnic annual reports and TEC financial monitoring for roughly 2015–2019, plus the 2019 Reform of Vocational Education Cabinet papers: true if multiple ITPs recorded multi-million dollar deficits, received Crown capital injections or deficit support in more than one year, and financial viability is named in the RoVE Cabinet papers as a principal driver for a single institution; false if the deficits or interventions did not occur or the official rationale rested on other grounds.

veracity.statement: We saw it in relation to new section 314(d); we saw it in relation to new section 318 removing the provision that a polytech council should, as reasonably practical, include Māori; new section 370(c) references to Te Tiriti removed; and in 314, around the characteristics of polytechs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that specific, named provisions of the bill remove references to Te Tiriti and remove a requirement that polytechnic councils include Māori membership where reasonably practicable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the bill as reported back (clause 23 and related clauses) against sections 314, 318 and 370 of the Education and Training Act 2020: true if the named provisions delete Te Tiriti references and the Māori-membership provision for polytechnic councils; false if those references are retained or merely relocated.

veracity.statement: I would have thought that at a time when we’re seeing significant issues—I mean, if I were to just look at disability unemployment rates, it’s gone up from 8.2 percent in 2022 to 14 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the unemployment rate for disabled people in New Zealand rose from 8.2 percent in 2022 to 14 percent by the time of speaking (October 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey disability labour market statistics: true if the unemployment rate for disabled people was approximately 8.2% in 2022 and approximately 14% in the most recent 2025 quarter; false if either figure differs materially (more than about one percentage point) from the published series.

veracity.statement: The Government has had to bail them out several times over the years in terms of financial viability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Western Institute of Technology at Taranaki (WITT), the institution he has just named, has received Crown financial rescue on multiple occasions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC and Ministry of Education records of Crown capital injections, deficit funding or bailout support to WITT: true if two or more separate financial interventions are recorded since roughly 2015; false if there was one or none.

veracity.statement: The committee received 714 submissions and heard 42 oral submissions, and the number and type of submissions showed that New Zealanders care deeply about our education system and the outcomes it delivers for learners, families, and communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two counts from the select committee process on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2): 714 written submissions received and 42 oral submissions heard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2): true if it records 714 written submissions and 42 submissions heard orally; false if either count differs.

specificity.statement: My second question for the Minister is: how will ISBs be enabled to deliver on their statutory functions from day one when, in some instances, only two or three roles from the workforce development councils to their corresponding ISBs have been identified for transfer via an expression of interest process?
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (expression of interest transfer process), a countable quantity (two or three roles), the bodies involved and the point at issue (statutory functions from commencement). A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer; only the missing identification of which ISBs holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reason for the need to often unpack whether the titles actually represent the intent of the bill is that I do think—unless you are studying law or unless someone who you know peruses the Parliament website often to go through legislation and the sort of the minutiae of it—it can be genuinely difficult to get a sense of whether titles reflect potential harm in our communities.
specificity.explanation: A general observation about public legibility of bill titles. It is trying to convey substance, but carries no figure, mechanism or named provision — nothing here could be checked or acted on beyond the sentiment that titles are hard for the public to interpret.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would have thought that at a time when we’re seeing significant issues—I mean, if I were to just look at disability unemployment rates, it’s gone up from 8.2 percent in 2022 to 14 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures on a named statistical measure — precise enough that anyone could go to the source series and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I note from the member Phil Twyford his suggestion of the alternate naming, which I think is entirely inappropriate because, as I answered five or maybe six times, the references here around the expectations and engagement and representation of Māori in new sections 314(d), 318(1), 321(c), 370(e), inserted by clause 23, and the overarching general duty in the main Act to acknowledge the Treaty.
specificity.explanation: Names four specific new sections, the clause inserting them, and the general duty in the principal Act — a reader can go to those provisions and check what they say. Held below the top because the sentence trails off without stating what those references actually provide.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Another key proposal in this bill is increasing the amount of days’ notice that unions must provide before they strike from three days to “no less than seven days”.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism with the before and after figures — three days to no less than seven. Anyone could locate the provision and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This Minister has no money. She’s put up a proposal that looks good politically but she hasn’t shown us the fiscals on how she is going to achieve that. That is not acceptable.
civility.explanation: Imputes a motive rather than engaging the case: the proposal is characterised as designed to look good politically. That is an attribution of bad faith to the Minister personally, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure — though it stops well short of a direct insult, and the accompanying complaint (no fiscals shown) is legitimate.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Minister has no money. She’s put up a proposal that looks good politically but she hasn’t shown us the fiscals on how she is going to achieve that. That is not acceptable.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — the absence of published financial information for the reform — but its weight is carried by framing about the Minister's political motives rather than by the fiscal detail itself.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That is going to make a huge difference to those polytechnics and industry skills boards.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the recapitalisation of the vocational education sector, once landed, will materially improve the position of polytechnics and industry skills boards. It is a prediction about an outcome in the sector, not a promise about her own action — the recapitalisation itself is the promised action; its effect is the forecast.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Published annual reports and TEC financial monitoring for the newly independent polytechnics for the 2026 and 2027 financial years: true if a majority return to operating surplus or materially reduce their deficits following the recapitalisation; false if a majority remain in deficit at similar or worse levels.

veracity.statement: We had violent crime up 33 percent, gang membership up 51 percent; we had a four-fold increase in ram raids, and a doubling of retail crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four specific changes in crime measures over the period of the previous government: violent crime +33%, gang membership +51%, ram raids up four-fold, retail crime doubled.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police victimisation statistics and the National Gang List for 2017-2023; true if violent crime victimisations rose about 33%, gang list membership about 51%, ram raid offences roughly quadrupled and retail crime roughly doubled over that period; false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m proud to say there are 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime; there’s a 16 percent reduction in serious youth offending.
veracity.explanation: Claims a reduction of 29,000 victims of serious violent crime and a 16 percent fall in serious youth offending under this government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Justice serious violent crime victimisation counts and youth offending statistics against the government's own target baseline; true if the fall is about 29,000 victims and about 16% for serious youth offending, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We didn't triple the debt to $180 billion, writing out a $9 billion interest rate bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous government debt tripled to $180 billion and that debt servicing now costs $9 billion a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown debt series 2017-2023 and the Budget 2025 finance costs line; true if debt approximately tripled to about $180b and annual interest is about $9b, false if either figure is materially off.

veracity.statement: Just yesterday, you would have seen 86 percent confidence in our tourism operators—our second biggest industry, at 7.5 percent of our total GDP.
veracity.explanation: Three assertions: an 86 percent confidence reading among tourism operators, tourism as New Zealand's second biggest industry, and tourism at 7.5 percent of GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Tourism Industry Aotearoa survey released the week of 13 October 2025 for the 86% figure, and Stats NZ Tourism Satellite Account for the GDP share and ranking; true if the survey reports about 86% confidence and tourism is about 7.5% of GDP, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We supported the initial pay equity legislation that came through the House, but that member took a paper to Cabinet and blew the cost from $3.5 billion up to $12 to $13 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Cabinet paper taken by the member raised the fiscal cost of the pay equity regime from $3.5 billion to $12-13 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Public Service Commission costings of the pay equity provisions and the released Cabinet paper; true if the costing moved from about $3.5b to about $12-13b as a result of that paper, false if the figures or the attribution do not match.

veracity.statement: But as my colleague Mr Bishop has said, over $60 billion has been put aside for infrastructure, including the construction sector, over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $60 billion is allocated to infrastructure over the coming four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 capital allowances and the National Infrastructure Pipeline four-year totals; true if committed infrastructure investment over the stated four years exceeds $60b, false if materially lower or if the figure covers a different period.

veracity.statement: Obviously, our contribution to global emissions is 0.17 percent—less than 1 percent! It is the height of conceit to imagine that somehow by closing down New Zealand industry we’re going to save the planet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's share of global greenhouse gas emissions is 0.17 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's gross emissions in the Greenhouse Gas Inventory as a share of global emissions per the Global Carbon Project / UNFCCC totals for the same year; true if about 0.17%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement in April this year that “We’ve been seeing green shoots across the economy.”, when at that time the economy was shrinking by almost 1 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at April 2025 the New Zealand economy was contracting by almost 1 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ GDP releases covering the quarters up to April 2025; true if the most recent published GDP change at that date showed a contraction approaching 1%, false if the economy was recorded as growing or the contraction was materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Half of teachers reported that students’ English and maths have improved compared to last year. Parents agree, with over three-quarters reporting better progress for their children in both English and maths, and so do our young people.
veracity.explanation: Reports two findings attributed to the Education Review Office evaluation released that day: half of teachers and over three-quarters of parents reporting improvement in English and maths.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report on implementation of the English and maths reforms released 15 October 2025; true if it reports approximately 50% of teachers and over 75% of parents reporting improvement, false if the proportions or the questions asked differ materially.

veracity.statement: Because under their watch, the number of young people that went on to benefit under the age of 25—the duration increased to 18 future years on welfare, a 49 percent increase since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the expected future lifetime on welfare for under-25 beneficiaries reached 18 years, a 49 percent rise since 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit system actuarial valuation reports covering 2017 onwards; true if average future years on benefit for under-25 recipients is about 18 years and about 49% higher than 2017, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: With respect to mining fossils, which is what four countries are doing—namely, China, USA, India, and Russia—and contributing to 60 percent of the emissions, what hope have we got to change that?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that China, the United States, India and Russia together account for 60 percent of global emissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Global Carbon Project / IEA national CO2 emissions shares for the most recent year; true if the four countries' combined share is about 60%, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We’ve got spending under control, inflation down to 2.7 percent, and mortgage rates cut eight times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual inflation of 2.7 percent and eight cuts to mortgage/official interest rates under this government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the most recent quarter published before 15 October 2025 for the 2.7% figure, and the RBNZ OCR decision record since the government took office for the count of cuts; true if the latest CPI print was about 2.7% and there have been eight OCR reductions, false if either is materially off.

veracity.statement: We’ve delivered 33 new cancer medicines, delivered the biggest funding boost for general practitioners, and just today announced an extension to breast screening, which, by the way, Labour promised in 2017 with their coalition agreement with New Zealand First but failed to deliver.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 33 new cancer medicines funded, the largest ever GP funding boost, and that the 2017 Labour-New Zealand First coalition agreement promised a breast screening extension that was not delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac funding decisions since 2024 for the medicines count, Health NZ/Budget documents for the GP funding claim, and the text of the 2017 Labour-NZ First coalition agreement plus the screening age range as at 2023; true if 33 cancer medicines were funded and the 2017 agreement contained a breast screening extension that was not implemented, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Now, David Seymour was the only guy in this entire precinct that voted against the zero carbon Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour was the sole member of Parliament to vote against the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill in November 2019; true if exactly one vote was recorded against and it was Seymour's, false if any other member voted against or if he did not.

veracity.statement: Farmers in rural New Zealand are worth almost $60 billion—60 billion—and Chris Hipkins knows this, as the leader of that party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that farming in rural New Zealand is worth almost $60 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre export revenue, or Stats NZ agricultural contribution to GDP, for the current year; true if the relevant measure is close to $60b, false if materially different — noting the claim's measure must be identified before checking.

veracity.statement: It’s a damnable shame that here we are and we are talking about a gas that decays back to carbon dioxide, and it is, factually, two parts per million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that methane breaks down into carbon dioxide and that its atmospheric concentration is two parts per million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NIWA or NOAA global atmospheric methane concentration measurements and standard atmospheric chemistry on methane oxidation; true if concentration is about 2 ppm and methane oxidises to CO2, false if the concentration is materially different from 2 ppm.

veracity.statement: Over the last 12 months, the strong wool indicator is up 32 percent, mid micron up 41 percent, and fine wool up 35 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific twelve-month price increases across the strong, mid micron and fine wool indicators.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand wool auction indicator series (PGG Wrightson / NZ Wool Services International) for October 2024 to October 2025; true if the three indicators rose about 32%, 41% and 35% respectively, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: We had violent crime up 33 percent, gang membership up 51 percent; we had a four-fold increase in ram raids, and a doubling of retail crime.
specificity.explanation: Four named measures each with a figure or multiple; anyone could go and check each one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We supported the initial pay equity legislation that came through the House, but that member took a paper to Cabinet and blew the cost from $3.5 billion up to $12 to $13 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (a Cabinet paper), the regime, and both cost figures — checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s actually about helping New Zealanders get ahead by lifting the collective living standards of all Kiwis. That’s what our Government’s focused on.
specificity.explanation: Asked to choose between orange roughy harvesting and marine ecosystem integrity, the answer offers only a generic statement of purpose — no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So why is he willing to accept a pay rise in line with inflation, claim a $50,000 housing allowance, and spend $44,000 on a helicopter ride so he could take a photograph for his Facebook, while his Government makes pay offers to workers like firefighters, nurses, and teachers that amount to pay cuts in real terms?
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, a named benefit, a named expense and a named set of workforces — every element is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If his Government is so supportive of pay equity, how many of the 33 active pay equity claims that were in the process when he became Prime Minister have been settled during his two years as Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: A precise question with a named figure (33 active claims) and a defined period; as checkable as any answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It has long been a rite of passage for Kiwis to venture overseas. The changes that we are making, both of a fiscal and a regulatory character, are both short term and medium term. Green shoots are emerging.
specificity.explanation: Attempts to convey substance about the government's programme but names no measure, figure, mechanism or date — 'fiscal and regulatory' changes and 'green shoots' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But as my colleague Mr Bishop has said, over $60 billion has been put aside for infrastructure, including the construction sector, over the next four years.
specificity.explanation: A named amount and a named timeframe, though no breakdown of what it buys or when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The hope is we will dig our own coal up, starting with 200,000-plus tonnes to reduce our reliance on imported Indonesian coal. The hope is that with the $200 million allocated in the Budget, we will accelerate the development of the oil and gas industry.
specificity.explanation: A tonnage, a Budget appropriation and two named mechanisms; missing only timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did he say to New Zealanders that there will be more people wearing hi-vis and hard hats when there has been, under his watch, $2.9 billion less spent on infrastructure and when his Government has cut Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealand, and 760 construction firms have gone under, under his watch?
specificity.explanation: Four checkable elements — a dollar shortfall, a named scheme cut, a job-count change and a company-failure count.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These include Altum in Wellington, a school focused on classical education; Aotearoa Infinite Academy, a school focused on remote education; and Te Aratika High School, a school in Hawke’s Bay focused on giving vocational pathways to Māori and Pacific students who have been disengaged from education.
specificity.explanation: Three named schools with locations and stated educational focus — concrete and verifiable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How does cutting fishing industry levies, enabling ring-net fishing in high protection areas, and blocking our own proposal to restrict bottom trawling show that his Government is protecting our oceans in the interests of all New Zealanders, rather than the interests of the commercial fishing industry?
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete measures and the regulatory context; no figures, but each element is identifiable and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why I have substantively accepted the recommendations of the Science System Advisory Group and am creating a single, independent board, Research Funding New Zealand, which will replace the complex bureaucracy that researchers currently have to navigate.
specificity.explanation: Names the advisory group, the new body and the change it makes, but gives no timeframe, funding figure or transition detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Once fully rolled out, around 130,000 additional women will be eligible for free screening every two years.
specificity.explanation: A named population size and screening interval for a defined programme; the 'once fully rolled out' qualifier leaves the timing open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got spending under control, inflation down to 2.7 percent, and mortgage rates cut eight times.
specificity.explanation: Two checkable figures alongside one general claim about spending.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the last 12 months, the strong wool indicator is up 32 percent, mid micron up 41 percent, and fine wool up 35 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three named market indicators, each with a percentage change over a defined period.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I consider that the member who was the education Minister for 5½ years did a pretty bad job, actually, making sure that over half our kids weren't at school regularly and that half of them couldn't read at the standard they needed to be going into high school, and 80 percent weren’t at the standard they needed in maths.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the record is supported with figures, but 'did a pretty bad job' lands on the named individual's competence rather than on the policy — pointed and condescending toward the person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And just look at the front bench across the road. Do you think there are any economically literate people in that front bench? It's unbelievable.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the intelligence and competence of the members opposite rather than on any argument they have made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know you might be worried about your union mates, but actually we're not worried about your unions.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the questioner a captured motive — that his concern is for 'union mates' rather than the issue — which is a sneer at his good faith rather than an engagement with the question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Not surprising—can't do math, so not a surprise, but we're actually making it workable given the complexities around that regime, and it's still available for people today, and we encourage unions and members to make claims under the pay equity legislation that's there.
civility.explanation: 'can't do math' is a clear personal jibe at the questioner's competence, attached to an otherwise substantive answer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So why is he willing to accept a pay rise in line with inflation, claim a $50,000 housing allowance, and spend $44,000 on a helicopter ride so he could take a photograph for his Facebook, while his Government makes pay offers to workers like firefighters, nurses, and teachers that amount to pay cuts in real terms?
civility.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a public office-holder's expenses, but 'so he could take a photograph for his Facebook' is a sneer at the person's motive rather than a point about the spending.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And therein lies the lesson for that particular member as she struggles to understand economics.
civility.explanation: A direct condescension about the questioner's grasp of the subject — an attack on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Sadly, we are unlikely to see unanimity until the former Minister disappears from Parliament.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe suggesting a named colleague's departure from Parliament is the precondition for agreement — aimed at the individual rather than at any position they hold.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, either that man doesn’t know how to count, being a former Minister of Education, or, quite simply, Mr Hipkins is so committed to trying to do a deal that he’ll do anything to try to get into Government.
civility.explanation: A dilemma constructed entirely out of attacks on a named individual — his numeracy on one horn and his willingness to abandon principle on the other.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That side of the House eviscerated rural New Zealand. Damien O’Connor and his thugging mate of David Parker were beating up rural New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and characterises them as thugs 'beating up' rural New Zealand — an attack on the people rather than on the policies they made.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And just look at the front bench across the road. Do you think there are any economically literate people in that front bench? It's unbelievable.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know you might be worried about your union mates, but actually we're not worried about your unions.
focus.explanation: A jibe about the other side's allegiances; the pay negotiations at issue are not addressed in this sentence at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If his Government is so supportive of pay equity, how many of the 33 active pay equity claims that were in the process when he became Prime Minister have been settled during his two years as Prime Minister?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy regime and asks for a specific outcome under it — accountability for a stated commitment, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, given that the size of our economy is $440-odd billion, it takes a while to turn the super-tanker around. We are not only very focused on the right navigational bearings but we’re leaving the storm and hurricane of destruction that was left to us by the last regime.
focus.explanation: Asked who else is to blame, the answer is metaphor plus attribution of blame to the previous government; a single GDP figure aside, no policy, measure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did he say to New Zealanders that there will be more people wearing hi-vis and hard hats when there has been, under his watch, $2.9 billion less spent on infrastructure and when his Government has cut Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealand, and 760 construction firms have gone under, under his watch?
focus.explanation: Holds the government to a stated commitment using named policies and measured outcomes; scrutiny of a specific promise, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That was an education secretary under a Labour Minister, Peter Fraser, and I would love to see the Labour Party fulfil that kind of aspiration for the students of New Zealand rather than cuddle up to the unions.
focus.explanation: There is an educational aspiration in the sentence, but its weight falls on characterising the other party's loyalties rather than on any measure, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she think it is reasonable to cut jobseeker for young people when over 218 applications for one role at a Tank Juice bar show that there are simply no jobs available?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the named policy change and its effect on the people it applies to.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does cutting fishing industry levies, enabling ring-net fishing in high protection areas, and blocking our own proposal to restrict bottom trawling show that his Government is protecting our oceans in the interests of all New Zealanders, rather than the interests of the commercial fishing industry?
focus.explanation: Three named policy decisions tested against a stated government commitment — precisely the scrutiny role, with no content-free party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you want to see what happens when ideology trumps competence, when virtue signalling replaces governing, and when chaos becomes policy, then look no further than the unholy alliance of the Labour - Greens - Te Pāti Māori.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other parties; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named anywhere in the statement.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We're now growing now; we're expected to grow even further in quarter four.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the economy is currently expanding and that growth will be stronger again in the December 2025 quarter.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases; true if the December 2025 quarter records positive real GDP growth exceeding the September 2025 quarter, false if the December quarter contracts or grows less than the preceding quarter.

divination.statement: Whether it’s a savings tax, whether it’s a property tax, whether it’s a death tax, New Zealanders can be guaranteed that, behind the scenes, that’s what they’re cooking up to take to the next election.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori will campaign at the next general election on one or more of a savings tax, a property tax or an estate/death tax.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The published tax policies of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pāti Māori for the 2026 general election; true if any of the three parties campaigns on a savings tax, a property/wealth tax or an estate duty, false if none of those appear in their election tax policies.

rigor.statement: As is the case with statistics, they’re so backward looking. The actual truth of the matter is that with the reduction and the improvement in terms of monetary policy, more liquidity is coming into the economy, banks are more confident, and the market is talking about yet another further reduction in monetary policy standards from 2.5 percent to some other figure.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference — contemporaneous monetary conditions, not lagging GDP prints, are the better guide to present momentum — but the conclusion leans on market talk of a future OCR cut, and dismissing the contrary data as 'backward looking' sidesteps rather than answers it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Obviously, our contribution to global emissions is 0.17 percent—less than 1 percent! It is the height of conceit to imagine that somehow by closing down New Zealand industry we’re going to save the planet.
rigor.explanation: Two defects in the inference: a small national share does not by itself establish that domestic action is futile (fallacy of division / appeal to insignificance), and the position rebutted — 'closing down New Zealand industry' to 'save the planet' — is a strawman of the question asked about fossil fuel drilling.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But to suggest that a single Minister or a Government or 5.2 million people at the distant end of the South Pacific can effect change when larger climate change emitters are doing zero is fanciful.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on a strawman: no one suggested New Zealand alone would 'effect change' globally, and the premise that larger emitters are 'doing zero' is asserted rather than shown, so the conclusion of futility is not supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’re both correct, because what we do know is that we have a higher aspiration for young people, clearly, than the Opposition do.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was which of two conflicting factual claims about job availability is correct, and the reason offered — a comparison of aspirations between the parties — cannot establish that both are true.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she think it is reasonable to cut jobseeker for young people when over 218 applications for one role at a Tank Juice bar show that there are simply no jobs available?
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a single vacancy's application count is offered as showing 'there are simply no jobs available' nationally — the anecdote cannot carry that conclusion, even though the underlying policy point is real.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Increasing unemployment; an economy that’s shrinking; more kids living in poverty; more people homeless and living on the streets; the construction sector—remember, they were going to get things done and get things building again—is at its lowest point in seven years, two years into this Government’s leadership; $3 billion less spending on building stuff in the last year compared to when they became the Government.
veracity.explanation: A bundle of factual assertions about the record since October 2023: unemployment rising, GDP contracting, child poverty and homelessness rising, construction activity at a seven-year low, and $3 billion less capital spending on building in the last year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate Q4 2023 vs mid-2025; Stats NZ quarterly GDP; Stats NZ child poverty statistics and the housing register/emergency housing counts; Stats NZ building work put in place (volume) — true if construction volume is the lowest since 2018; Treasury/Budget capital expenditure on buildings — true if approximately $3bn lower than 2023.

veracity.statement: There is one thing the Government has broken records on, and that is the number of New Zealanders giving up and leaving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that departures of New Zealanders are at a record high — i.e. the highest in the recorded series, not merely elevated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration series, departures of New Zealand citizens for the year to mid-2025; true if that annual figure is the highest on record, false if any earlier year exceeds it.

veracity.statement: Every time a member on the opposite side of the House gets on a plane to fly to Auckland or to Christchurch, I want them to think of one thing: the number of people on that plane is the equivalent number of people who are permanently leaving the country every day—every day—under their Government’s leadership.
veracity.explanation: A quantitative comparison dressed as an image: the daily number of permanent departures equals a domestic jet-load of passengers (roughly 150–200 people).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ migration data — daily average of permanent/long-term departures over the most recent year, compared with the seat capacity of aircraft on main-trunk domestic routes (A320/B737, ~165–180 seats); true if the daily figure falls within that capacity range, false if it is materially below or above.

veracity.statement: Instead you left us with an utter mess and you left house owners in a terrible situation, paying interest rates they shouldn’t have been paying, because of your behaviour as the Government that then sat around spending New Zealanders’ money, borrowing money for New Zealanders to pay so that New Zealand is now paying interest every single year that is more than Corrections, Police, and Defence, and our fire service all together because of him and his former Government.
veracity.explanation: The checkable core is the comparison: annual finance costs on Crown debt now exceed the combined annual appropriations for Corrections, Police, Defence and Fire and Emergency New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Treasury financial statements: core Crown finance costs for the year, compared against the sum of Vote Corrections, Vote Police, Vote Defence plus Vote Defence Force, and FENZ appropriations for the same year; true if finance costs exceed that sum, false if they do not.

veracity.statement: They’re not going to work as baristas; they’re going to work in the mines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealanders emigrating to Australia are predominantly going into mining work rather than low-wage service jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian Bureau of Statistics / Department of Home Affairs data on the occupations and industries of recent New Zealand arrivals; true if mining is the leading destination industry for that cohort, false if it is a small share relative to health care, construction or hospitality.

veracity.statement: Despite what the left say, we have the fourth largest search and rescue area in the world.
veracity.explanation: A ranking claim about the size of New Zealand's search and rescue region relative to other countries' declared regions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand / RCCNZ published extent of New Zealand's search and rescue region (~30 million km²), ranked against other states' ICAO/IMO-declared SAR regions; true if New Zealand's is fourth largest, false if the ranking differs.

veracity.statement: It is Luxon’s fault that a visit in New Zealand now to the GP, a standard adult visit to the GP, can cost nearly $100.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a standard adult GP consultation in New Zealand can now cost close to $100.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published fee schedules of New Zealand general practices in 2025 (and Health NZ's annual fee-increase approvals); true if standard adult consultation fees of approximately $90 or more are being charged at practices, false if the top of the range is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Now one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor.
veracity.explanation: A survey-based prevalence claim: approximately 17 percent of New Zealanders report unmet need for GP care because of cost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey (or the Health NZ/Ministry of Health unmet-need series) for the most recent year: proportion of adults reporting they did not visit a GP due to cost; true if approximately one in six, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Exports in one year are up from $500 million to around $750 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand game-development export revenue rose from about $500 million to about $750 million in a single year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual industry survey, export revenue figures for consecutive years; true if the series shows roughly $500m rising to roughly $750m year on year, false if the levels or the growth differ materially.

veracity.statement: The same people in this coalition Government who crashed the economy leading to 36,000 fewer jobs the day that they took office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific employment loss — 36,000 fewer jobs — under the current Government since it took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs (Employment Indicators) or HLFS employment level, change between December 2023 and the most recent quarter before October 2025; true if the fall is approximately 36,000, false if materially different or if employment rose.

veracity.statement: Earlier this year, 142 jobs were lost from Carter Holt Harvey’s Eves Valley sawmill. Another 59 jobs are on the line at Sealord, after 79 were axed recently.
veracity.explanation: Three specific job-loss figures at two named Nelson-region employers during 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company announcements and contemporaneous news reports for the Carter Holt Harvey Eves Valley sawmill closure and Sealord's 2025 restructurings; true if the numbers match approximately 142, 59 and 79, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: In fact, when I asked Nicola Willis in the House last week what she was doing about this, she claimed Nelson should be happy with the Government because they’re giving us half a hospital.
veracity.explanation: An account of what the Minister of Finance said in the House the previous week — specifically that Nelson should be satisfied because it is receiving a partial hospital rebuild.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the relevant question to the Minister of Finance in the week of 6 October 2025; true if the Minister's answer bears that meaning, false if the characterisation is not supported by the transcript.

veracity.statement: That’s why, in Budget 2025, the Government committed $250,000 to support rural New Zealand’s grassroots work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $250,000 Budget 2025 commitment directed at grassroots rural community work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 appropriations / Vote Agriculture, Biosecurity, Fisheries and Food Safety and associated Ministry for Primary Industries announcements; true if a $250,000 allocation for rural grassroots/rural women's organisations appears, false if no such appropriation exists.

veracity.statement: Some 73,900 New Zealanders are hearing that message and have left—200 New Zealanders every day with no plan to get them back.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 73,900 departures of New Zealanders over the reference year, equivalent to about 200 a day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, departures of New Zealand citizens for the year to the most recent month before October 2025; true if approximately 73,900 (and therefore ~202 per day), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: They’re also not being upfront with things like the pricing rules, which they say is going to be a big market intervention on those large corporates, those monopolistic large corporates that they say they are going to focus on when in fact they have picked the one pricing intervention which makes it illegal to drop prices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's announced pricing rules would make it unlawful for prices to fall — i.e. that the intervention prohibits price reductions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Government's announced pricing/Commerce Act changes and the accompanying Cabinet paper or regulatory impact statement; true if the rules prohibit reducing prices generally, false if they instead target predatory or below-cost pricing by dominant firms.

veracity.statement: It's been two years since the election, and when you are focused on managing a merger like they are, you can’t actually get things done, but let me tell you what we’ve done in the last two years since the election: in law and order, we’ve reduced violent crime—29,000 victims less than on election day; ram raids are down 85 percent; police patrols are up 40 percent; bans on gang patches.
veracity.explanation: Four law-and-order claims: 29,000 fewer victims of violent crime than at the 2023 election, ram raids down 85 percent, police patrols up 40 percent, and a gang patch ban in force.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey victims-of-violent-crime estimates for 2023 vs 2025; NZ Police ram-raid offence statistics for the same period; Police beat/patrol reporting; and the commencement of the Gangs Act patch prohibition. True if each figure matches within its stated margin, false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that many councils recorded turnout below 40 percent in the October 2025 local elections, and some in the 30s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Council-published and DIA-collated 2025 local authority election turnout figures; true if a substantial number of territorial authorities recorded turnout under 40 percent with several in the 30–39 percent band, false if turnout was generally above 40 percent.

veracity.statement: This directly contradicts the Prime Minister in Monday’s post-Cabinet press conference saying he’s discussing the Electoral Commission running the local elections with Minister Watts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister said on 13 October 2025 that he is discussing having the Electoral Commission run local elections, and that this conflicts with the Minister of Local Government's answer given in September.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transcript/recording of the post-Cabinet press conference of Monday 13 October 2025, and the September question and answer to the Minister of Local Government; true if the two statements are inconsistent on that point, false if the Prime Minister said nothing of the kind or the positions are reconcilable.

veracity.statement: Despite the attacks on te reo, Te Tiriti, and Māori customary rights by the coalition partners, a strong majority across the country—as of today, 520,113 voters—voted to keep Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 520,113 voters nationally voted to retain Māori wards, and that this constituted a majority across the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregated results of the 2025 Māori ward polls as reported by the councils holding them; true if the national total voting to retain is approximately 520,113 and exceeds the total voting to disestablish, false if the aggregate favoured disestablishment or the count differs materially.

veracity.statement: Only 13 percent supported this bill in its totality—13 percent out of hundreds of submissions that were received.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only 13 percent of the several hundred submissions to the select committee supported the bill in full.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's departmental report on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2), submission analysis section; true if it records approximately 13 percent full support out of the submissions received, false if the proportion differs materially.

specificity.statement: Increasing unemployment; an economy that’s shrinking; more kids living in poverty; more people homeless and living on the streets; the construction sector—remember, they were going to get things done and get things building again—is at its lowest point in seven years, two years into this Government’s leadership; $3 billion less spending on building stuff in the last year compared to when they became the Government.
specificity.explanation: Names sectors, a seven-year comparison point and a dollar figure; someone could go and check each limb. Falls short of 1.0 because most of the list is directional ("increasing", "more") without magnitudes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will be focused on jobs, on health, on homes, on real action on the cost of living—not more broken promises, more blame, and more excuses, which is all this Government has to offer.
specificity.explanation: A list of policy areas with no mechanism, no amount and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on; the surrounding speech supplies no detail for these commitments either.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve released this defence industry strategy, so our New Zealand businesses like Syos, like Dawn Aerospace, like Kea Aerospace, like all the businesses up and down the country who are currently manufacturing for people like Rocket Lab and others, so that they are actually going to be able to work with the Defence Force to help provide aerial drones, land drones, and sea drones for our New Zealand Defence Force.
specificity.explanation: Names the published strategy, four specific firms and the concrete capability classes being sought. Short of 1.0 because no amounts, contract volumes or dates are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour can fix this. We will make care more affordable and make it easier to see a doctor and nurse when you need one in your community.
specificity.explanation: After several minutes of detailed fee examples, the remedy is stated as a direction with no funding figure, no mechanism and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked against later.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve merged seven Crown research institutes (CRIs) into three public research organisations (PROs), creating some of the biggest research and development thematic institutions in the world.
specificity.explanation: A named structural change with exact counts of the institutions merged and created; checkable against the reform documents. Not 1.0 because no dates, budgets or headcounts accompany it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Earlier this year, 142 jobs were lost from Carter Holt Harvey’s Eves Valley sawmill. Another 59 jobs are on the line at Sealord, after 79 were axed recently.
specificity.explanation: Named employers, named sites, exact headcounts and a timeframe. Directly checkable, and the sort of detail an MP could easily have left as "hundreds of jobs".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why, in Budget 2025, the Government committed $250,000 to support rural New Zealand’s grassroots work.
specificity.explanation: A named Budget, an exact amount and a stated purpose — checkable against the Budget documents. Short of 1.0 because the delivery mechanism and period are not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It's been two years since the election, and when you are focused on managing a merger like they are, you can’t actually get things done, but let me tell you what we’ve done in the last two years since the election: in law and order, we’ve reduced violent crime—29,000 victims less than on election day; ram raids are down 85 percent; police patrols are up 40 percent; bans on gang patches.
specificity.explanation: Four quantified outcomes with a stated baseline (election day) and a named legislative change. Not 1.0 because the sources and measurement periods behind each figure are left unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Out of the 136 submitters that opposed this, they mainly focused on the unnecessary nature of the changes, the risks to academic freedom and erosion of university autonomy, concerns about safety and impacts on marginalised communities, and views that the changes were contrary to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
specificity.explanation: An exact submitter count and a four-way itemisation of the grounds of opposition, sourced to the departmental report — checkable against that document.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It shows that they have no plan. They know they can’t defend their own record; they know they don’t know how to fix the mess that they have been creating; all they can do is scaremonger and attack, because they don’t know how to turn things around.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is "really like" — their motives, their inability, their tactics. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named anywhere in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s also practically a miracle this week—you think it’s the Middle East? No, no, the miracle is that the Green Party has actually asked some questions on conservation of the environment.
focus.explanation: Wholly about what another party is supposedly like; no measure, figure, policy or outcome is named. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly — this is exactly the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, this game is clearly an homage to the current Opposition parties, with the game described as a dark, grim fantasy world where people are exiled to a place which is filled with monsters, political intrigue, and a constant struggle for survival.
focus.explanation: An extended joke whose entire content is what the Opposition parties are like. No policy, figure or outcome is engaged; strip the party framing and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: National are tone deaf and out of touch and they just don’t care.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other party's attitude with no policy, figure or outcome attached. No individual is insulted, so this passes Civility; it is pure party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead, they’ve got policy announcements like the surcharge ban, which sounds good and is, in fact, policy that is supported all around this House. But instead of being clear with consumers about who will bear the cost of that, they have lumped it on to small businesses.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure, concedes cross-House support for it, and identifies a specific incidence problem — who bears the cost. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They tried to merge Te Pūkenga: it was an abject failure. They tried to merge Health New Zealand; they tried to merge three waters; and now they’re trying to merge Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori. New Zealand would bear the cost of that.
focus.explanation: Names real past reforms, but only as set-up for a point about the Opposition parties' internal arrangements. The weight of the passage is on who might govern with whom rather than on any measure, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill removes some of the key parts of the Act that aim to promote and protect the rights of our tamariki and young people, such as those rights under Te Tiriti o Waitangi and under the National Education and Learning Priorities.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly, identifying which provisions of the Education and Training Act the bill removes. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Instead you left us with an utter mess and you left house owners in a terrible situation, paying interest rates they shouldn’t have been paying, because of your behaviour as the Government that then sat around spending New Zealanders’ money, borrowing money for New Zealanders to pay so that New Zealand is now paying interest every single year that is more than Corrections, Police, and Defence, and our fire service all together because of him and his former Government.
civility.explanation: Aimed at a named opponent and sliding from his record to his conduct — "sat around spending New Zealanders’ money" imputes idleness and profligacy to the person rather than arguing about the fiscal choices. Short of a direct insult, but past civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve no idea why that woman keeps shouting.
civility.explanation: A dismissive personal reference to another member — "that woman" — engaging nothing she said. It targets the person, not any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Winston Peters and Shane Jones on the other side of the House gloat about ruining our oceans and our soils and our air and telling our people that this is the only way forward.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and imputes to them a motive — taking pleasure in environmental ruin. That is an attack on character rather than on the policy they advance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Over in the National Party we have our environment Minister destroying the name of her job, sitting outside of Cabinet for the first time in 50 years, providing no input—none—on fast-track projects that will destroy our taio and our moana.
civility.explanation: "Destroying the name of her job" turns from the portfolio decisions to the individual minister's worth in the role. Pointed criticism of the Cabinet ranking would have been civil; this lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Do you want Erica Stanford, who delivers results in education, or Willow-Jean Prime, who can’t manage her emails?
civility.explanation: A named member's basic competence is made the punchline. The jibe engages nothing she has argued or done in policy terms.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why they’re going because New Zealand, in the last six years of the Labour Government, decided to cut the mines.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause inference: emigration to Australia is attributed wholly to the previous government's mining consent policy. Nothing is offered to connect the two, and the obvious competing explanations (wage differentials, the labour market, the exchange rate) are not addressed. This engages a real policy, so it is a reasoning failure rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is Luxon’s fault that a visit in New Zealand now to the GP, a standard adult visit to the GP, can cost nearly $100.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered (underfunding of general practice, so practices raise fees or close), but the conclusion asserted is sole personal fault for a nationwide price level, which the chain does not support: wage costs, workforce shortages and pre-existing fee trends are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government say fast tracking environmental destruction is going to create jobs.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the Government's position is characterised as advocating "environmental destruction" rather than as a consenting-process reform, so what is rebutted afterwards is not the position actually held. The argument engages the fast-track policy, so the defect is in the reasoning, not the topic.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Fuel and transport costs keep going up, not because of global events but because this Government has added on fees that are administrative costs to keep moving around your city and your region, and this Government won’t own up.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: global factors are ruled out by assertion and the entire increase attributed to domestic administrative fees, with no evidence offered for the split. The statement is squarely on the policy — the failure is in the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You see, you’d have to choose: do you want a National-led Government, as a country, that got inflation down from 75 percent into the twos, or a Labour - Greens - Te Pāti Māori-plus that would give us another $100 billion - plus of debt?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: the electorate is offered exactly two packages, with the opposing one's consequence ($100 billion of extra debt) simply asserted rather than derived from any published policy. The inflation figure is an obvious speech slip and is not what makes the reasoning weak.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that low turnout reflects a confusing and outdated voting system — is drawn from the turnout figure alone. Nothing is offered to exclude the competing explanations (disengagement, candidate information, long-run decline), so the inference outruns the evidence given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Most concerning: when I asked the Minister if she had come across any examples, any evidence that validated this particular change, that validated the time that we used in this wonderful Parliament of ours, the only example that Minister Stanford could offer me was Don Brash—Don Brash from Hobson’s Pledge and the ex-leader of the National Party. So that’s probably the influence on this Government—Don Brash pushing through legislation in this House that isn’t asked for and isn’t necessary.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that a single example was cited in answer to a question does not establish that the person in the example is the driving influence behind the legislation. The premise supports only that the evidence base offered was thin.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We see New Zealand businesses getting a bit more confidence, and that will help them to employ more people.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that improving business confidence will translate into rising employment — an outcome in the labour market, not a promise about the Government's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs: change in total employment over the four quarters following October 2025; true if employment rises materially, false if it is flat or falls.

veracity.statement: You don’t need to believe me; you can just look at the Government’s own statistics of child poverty to see that more children are projected to not have their basic needs being met as a result of Government decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official government child poverty statistics/projections show more children falling below material-needs thresholds as a consequence of government policy decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Budget 2025 child poverty forecasts and the Stats NZ Child Poverty Related Indicators / material hardship series: true if official projections published by the Government show the material hardship or below-50%-median rate rising over the forecast period, false if they project a fall or no change.

veracity.statement: We are seeing more and more evidence of this, particularly with the removal of kupu Māori from children’s books.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that te reo Māori words have been removed from children's books used in schools.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education decisions and publisher records for the Ready to Read Phonics Plus series: true if te reo Māori words present in earlier editions were removed or excluded from the school-supplied readers, false if no such removal occurred.

veracity.statement: For all students, only 23 percent were at the level that they were supposed to be—23 percent; 62 percent were at least a year behind where they should be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the 2025 year 8 maths achievement data, 23 percent of all students were at curriculum level and 62 percent were at least a year behind.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education curriculum-benchmarking / year 8 maths achievement results released in 2025: true if the at-level figure is 23% and the at-least-a-year-behind figure is 62% within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In 2023, it was 47 percent who did, 53 percent who didn’t; in 2024, 53 percent did, 47 percent didn’t; and 2025 it’s up to 58 percent plays 42.
veracity.explanation: Asserts term 2 regular attendance rates (students present more than 90 percent of the time) of 47% in 2023, 53% in 2024 and 58% in 2025. ('plays 42' is a spoken slip for 'to 42'.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education term 2 regular attendance statistics for 2023, 2024 and 2025: true if the published regular-attendance rates match 47%, 53% and 58% within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the select committee stage, I asked questions of the Minister about how many universities in 2024 had actually restricted speakers from their campuses. The Minister’s answer was zero.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that when asked at select committee how many universities restricted speakers from campus in 2024, the Minister answered zero.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's record of evidence on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2): true if the Minister's answer to that question is recorded as zero or none, false if a figure above zero or no such exchange is recorded.

veracity.statement: They want the Government to be focused on the real issues, like rising cost of living, like the economy that is shrinking, and like the 73,000 New Zealanders who have left under their watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that the economy is contracting, and that 73,000 New Zealanders have left the country during this Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for net departures of New Zealand citizens over the period since November 2023, and the Stats NZ quarterly GDP series: true if the net citizen departure figure is approximately 73,000 and the most recent GDP prints show contraction, false if either is materially different.

rigor.statement: Because, on the one hand, they’re creating all these additional layers of bureaucracy around attendance management plans and then, on the other hand, quite happily allow material hardship for children to go up on their watch.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: requiring schools to address underlying causes of absence while the speaker says government policy worsens those causes. The tension is genuine but the claimed contradiction is not established — requiring attendance plans is not strictly inconsistent with hardship rising, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Hon David Seymour has been working really hard to improve attendance of students at schools and we have seen some really good results because of that hard work.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: attributes improved attendance results to one minister's effort with nothing offered to connect the two beyond their co-occurrence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member, the Green Party member who spoke before me, instead of supporting that, he was actually providing excuses for students to not attend school.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The preceding speaker argued that material hardship causes absence and that the Government should address it; that is recast as excusing non-attendance, and the rebuttal is then aimed at the recast version.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of those things are good, but all of those things are still in the bill.
rigor.explanation: A direct and valid rebuttal: the Opposition's objection was that safety, rights and Te Tiriti obligations are being lost, and the reply is that they remain in the bill and only their ranking changes. The conclusion follows from what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Initiatives like the provisions in this bill are an attempt to break down the gates of academia and use the power of the State to force independent academic institutions to give platforms to the pedlars of hate speech—white supremacists, Islamophobes, racists, anti-trans activists, and Holocaust deniers—in order to give their views respectability by giving them access to independent academic institutions.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. Nothing is offered connecting a requirement that universities adopt a freedom-of-expression statement and a complaints procedure to the conclusion that institutions will be forced to platform Holocaust deniers and white supremacists; the imputed purpose does the work the argument does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that was the opinion of the Free Speech Union, who claim authorship for large parts of the bill and who received a resounding “Hear, hear” from ACT Party member Simon Court in the House, so you can give that submission the kudos that those clues might deserve.
rigor.explanation: Largely a genetic fallacy — the submission is discounted by reference to who wrote it and who cheered it rather than by anything it says. The conflict-of-interest point is legitimate as far as it goes, which keeps this above the floor, but it is offered as a substitute for engaging the substance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we heard from Labour and the Greens is their contention that hearing different opinions is akin to some kind of violence.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The Opposition speakers argued about institutional autonomy and the absence of an evidenced problem; that is recast as a claim that hearing opinions is violence, and the recast version is what gets rebutted.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is due to the changes in clause 9 and clause 23, which subsequently were recommended to be changed to be a bit more workable.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clauses at issue, which is checkable, but conveys nothing about what the changes actually do or what 'more workable' amounts to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For all students, only 23 percent were at the level that they were supposed to be—23 percent; 62 percent were at least a year behind where they should be.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages tied to a named cohort and subject (year 8 maths achievement data). Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s what the schools should be focusing on to ensure that every child learns, progresses, and succeeds, and this bill is about lifting student achievement, improving attendance, and making sure that every young New Zealander gets the best possible start in life.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic aspirations about the bill — no figures, mechanisms, clauses or timeframes. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Again, all that we will see is our universities continuing to drop in some of those international rankings when it comes to how they’re perceived internationally.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand universities will continue to fall in international university rankings. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: QS World University Rankings and Times Higher Education World University Rankings editions published after this statement: true if a majority of New Zealand's eight universities sit lower than their positions in the edition current at the time of speaking, false if a majority hold or improve their positions.

divination.statement: Now, this is something that we know that ultimately is going to be looked at and is going to be removed.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Te Tiriti o Waitangi school-board objective (section 127(2)(e) as inserted by clause 8) will be removed, either through the wider Treaty-clause review or sooner. A prediction about a legislative outcome, not a promise of the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Education and Training Act 2020 as amended: true if the Te Tiriti o Waitangi school-board objective is repealed by an Act in force by the resolve-by date, false if it remains on the statute book in any form.

focus.statement: So, again, it’s really concerning that this Government just wants to punch down.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other side's general disposition. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in the statement itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the moment, what is happening because of those members sitting on the other side, our universities have been hijacked by the ideology, and we want to rescue universities from that, and that is why I am really pleased with this provision in this legislation.
focus.explanation: Gestures at the provision but the weight of the statement is a general characterisation of what the other side has supposedly done to universities; no mechanism, case or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a distracted and out-of-touch Government that is obsessed with imported culture wars.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side's disposition. No specific policy, provision or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I mean, what has this Government got? One trick: bust the unions; bust the teachers’ unions; bust the universities.
focus.explanation: A summary judgement of the other side's motives with no clause, cost, mechanism or outcome named — the surrounding policy detail is dropped in favour of party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is another piece of legislation that proves and shows why National is more trusted in education compared to that lot these days, and so I commend this bill.
focus.explanation: Purely a comparison between parties. Nothing in the bill — no provision, figure or outcome — is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have sat here and listened to about seven speeches from the other sides, and do you know what? I have not heard—I have not heard—about lifting the educational achievements of our children, and that is absolutely shameful.
focus.explanation: The content is a judgement about what the other side did and did not say, rather than about any provision of the bill. It gestures at educational achievement but names no measure, figure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is an absolute joke of a bill.
civility.explanation: A brutal dismissal aimed entirely at the legislation. No person is attacked, no bad faith is imputed to an individual — under the re-anchored scale, harsh criticism of a measure is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's not actually about protecting free speech, it’s about crushing dissent from universities and setting them up to be Government-controlled commissariats, controlled by David Seymour, who will be prescribing his vision of ideology on what free speech actually should be.
civility.explanation: Imputes a concealed authoritarian motive to a named minister personally — that he intends to crush dissent and prescribe his own ideology. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person's good faith rather than on the provision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just to acknowledge, at the top of my contribution, that the member Cameron Brewer took only 25 seconds to claim to be more trusted in education but was unable to make an argument longer than 30 seconds to convince, which would suggest to me it’s not an argument he’s confident in and neither is it an argument he’s prepared to make on the record in the House.
civility.explanation: Turns on a named member personally, imputing that he lacks confidence in his own position and is unwilling to defend it on the record, rather than engaging what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The most frightening thing I’ve ever seen Don Brash try and do is get into a speedway car or try to walk down a gangplank and get on a boat.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named individual's physical bearing, used in place of engaging the argument about why a university declined the booking. Light-hearted rather than contemptuous, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These 10 will stand alone on 1 January 2026, with two of them expected to be in the federation.
