specificity.explanation: A count, a commencement date and a named structural arrangement — checkable and actionable. Scored only on detail carried, not on whether the plan is sound.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is important because this is about local needs, this is about local jobs, and it’s about ensuring that local industries have a stronger voice.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — local needs, local jobs, a stronger voice — with no mechanism, figure or named provision. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over 10 years of delivery of Māori-Pacific trade training; in December 2024, the door was shut on Te Matarau Education Trust and they were evicted from the building in NorthTec.
specificity.explanation: Names the organisation, the institution, the month and the concrete event — someone could go and check it. Precision is scored here regardless of whether it turns out to be accurate.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s about time sensibility returned to polytechs and vocational training that we all knew worked and delivered.
specificity.explanation: A slogan: 'sensibility', something that 'worked and delivered'. No figure, mechanism, provision or timeframe — nothing a listener could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I got that round the wrong way deliberately because I believe “M” always comes before “N”, but that has had $23 million that went into Te Pūkenga and they’re going to come out with $11.7 million.
specificity.explanation: Names the institution and two precise dollar figures for a defined before-and-after. Whether the figures are right is Veracity's question; the statement is checkable, which is what is scored here.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I am confident they will complete this work and that decisions will be able to be made about their establishment in the new year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the polytechnics remaining inside Te Pūkenga will finish building financial sustainability and that establishment decisions for them will be taken during 2026. Not a promise about her own action — the completion depends on the institutions.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and Orders in Council during calendar 2026 establishing the polytechnics not in the initial group of 10 as stand-alone institutions; true if establishment decisions for the remaining polytechnics are made within 2026, false if they are deferred beyond 2026 or abandoned.

divination.statement: Well, the good news is that by the time that person leaves school, this Government will be history.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current National-led coalition will have left office before the intermediate-aged student he describes finishes secondary school — roughly five to six years from the statement.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The composition of the New Zealand Government following the 2026 and 2029 general elections; true if the National–ACT–New Zealand First coalition formed in 2023 is out of office at any point before the end of 2031, false if it is continuously in government through that period.

divination.statement: Given the Government’s apparent unwillingness to invest in the new politics, the inevitable result will be fewer courses, fewer trainees, and fewer jobs in the system.
divination.explanation: Forecasts contraction across three measurable dimensions of the ITP sector — course offerings, trainee numbers and staff numbers — as the consequence of the new funding settings. ('new politics' is a transcription slip for 'new polytechs'; quoted as it appears.)
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Education Counts data for the ITP sector, 2025 baseline compared with 2028: programme offerings, industry-training and ITP enrolments, and staff FTE; true if all three fall, false if enrolments and staffing hold or rise.

civility.statement: I don’t know if anyone else in this room today thought that that sounded somewhat like a valedictory speech, Minister, when you go around thanking every single person in this House.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at the Minister personally — a sneer implying she is on her way out — rather than at anything in the bill. Short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She knows that this doesn’t create better outcomes for learners, it’s not financially viable, and that, most of all, she has let industry down in the promise that she made back in the last election.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith: not that the Minister is mistaken, but that she knows the policy fails and is proceeding anyway. That is an attack on her honesty rather than on the design.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In that case, I’m very happy to let those members across the other side of the House who are hanging on every word know that whilst I can see from the looks on their faces they have struggled to keep up to this point, I will now speak a lot slower.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at other members' comprehension — an attack on the people opposite rather than on any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At this point, I can’t help but think that the result is a victory for political hubris over evidence, stakeholder opinions clearly articulated, and common sense.
civility.explanation: 'Hubris' attributes a character flaw to the Minister rather than a defect to the policy — imputing ego as the motive. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m not sure whose it was, but I think the technical term is “projection”.
civility.explanation: Insinuates that another member did not write his own speech, and labels him psychologically. Aimed at the man, not at anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know why that is: it’s because the promise that the National Government sold last election—to reintroduce regional autonomy for polytechnics—this bill does not achieve that.
focus.explanation: Names a specific election commitment (regional autonomy for polytechnics) and measures the bill against it. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing, and scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have realised that there were issues with the vocational education and training system, but when they were in Government they didn’t realise that they didn’t ask those kind of questions.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposition parties' past conduct and consistency; no policy, mechanism or figure is named. Nothing emitted for Rigor — strip out the part about the other side and there is no argument left, only a characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister knows that the reports and the advice that she has had is that she needs at least $200 million to stand up 16 polytechnics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice to the Minister put the cost of standing up 16 polytechnics at $200 million or more, against the $20 million she has announced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission advice to the Minister on the bill (regulatory impact statement, or briefings released under the OIA); true if that advice states a capitalisation/transition requirement of at least $200 million for 16 institutions, false if the advice contains no such figure or a materially smaller one.

veracity.statement: We know that, under this Government, thousands and thousands less apprentices are graduating under their watch—thousands.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall of several thousand in apprenticeship completions since the change of government in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Education Counts industry training and apprenticeship completion data, 2023 compared with 2025; true if completions fell by thousands, false if they were flat or rose.

veracity.statement: It’s hard to see that all this pain is being suffered with the ultimate conclusion of the Treasury that the viability of the new institutions would be the same, if not worse.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury advised the financial viability of the new stand-alone polytechnics would be no better, and possibly worse, than under Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published advice and the regulatory impact statement on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if Treasury concluded viability would be the same or worse, false if Treasury reached no such conclusion or concluded viability improves.

veracity.statement: Over 10 years of delivery of Māori-Pacific trade training; in December 2024, the door was shut on Te Matarau Education Trust and they were evicted from the building in NorthTec.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Matarau Education Trust, after roughly a decade delivering Māori-Pacific trade training, was ended and evicted from NorthTec premises in December 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NorthTec / Te Pūkenga records of the Te Matarau Education Trust arrangement and contemporaneous reporting; true if the partnership and tenancy ended in or about December 2024, false if the trust remained in place or the arrangement ended at a materially different time.

veracity.statement: It is something that submitters have very much opposed or opposed in part in their submissions—I believe only 11 percent were completely in support of the changes—and therefore we oppose this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only about 11 percent of submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee fully supported the changes in the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report / summary of submissions on the bill prepared for the Education and Workforce Committee; true if the share of submissions recorded as fully supportive is about 11 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We still haven’t seen a cost-benefit analysis that would justify the policy design and the architecture of the system that the Minister has chosen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no cost-benefit analysis supporting the chosen system design has been produced or released during the bill's passage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and supporting papers published for the bill, plus documents provided to the Education and Workforce Committee; true if none contains a cost-benefit analysis of the chosen model, false if such an analysis was published or provided to the committee.

veracity.statement: I got that round the wrong way deliberately because I believe “M” always comes before “N”, but that has had $23 million that went into Te Pūkenga and they’re going to come out with $11.7 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Nelson Marlborough institute entered Te Pūkenga with $23 million and will emerge with $11.7 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology / Te Pūkenga annual reports and the division-level financial statements at merger (2020) and at separation (2025–26); true if the institute's reserves fell from about $23m to about $11.7m, false if the figures differ materially.

rigor.statement: If the federation model was going to be so successful, then, logically, polytechs would want to be a part of it, and they wouldn’t need to be forced to be part of it.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but it leans on an unstated premise that institutions accurately judge their own interests — the very premise the Minister disputed (that some polytechs 'don't know they're drowning'). Reasonable point, real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you have a car that’s lost one-seventh of its functions, of its parts, or of its essence, how is that going to be a more viable car going forward?
rigor.explanation: False analogy: an institution shedding staff is not a machine missing parts, and nothing is offered to connect headcount loss to financial viability — reduced cost could as easily improve it. The conclusion rides entirely on the image.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister said that it was not necessary to include provisions to require exit clauses for anchor polytechnics, because they’re being established by Order in Council, but ISBs are also being established by Order in Council.
rigor.explanation: A valid parallel-case argument: the Minister's stated reason for omitting exit provisions applies equally to bodies for which the bill does provide disestablishment machinery, so the reason does not support the omission.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One other thing I would say in that area is that if you are a long way away from your polytech, the drop-out rate and the inability to complete is much, much higher than it is if you live in the area very, very close, in the town that is there, so there is an extra need not only for extra resource or maybe hybrid models but also for extra pastoral care.
rigor.explanation: A premise about completion rates by distance, and a conclusion about resourcing and pastoral care that follows from it. Whether the premise is true is Veracity's question; the inference itself is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first questions I have are around the number of dwellings that we might expect from this change: 13,000 units was a number that was raised with committee by our officials in the committee’s proceedings.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure (13,000 units) and names where it came from (officials, in committee proceedings), so it can be checked against the committee record. Not a full 1.0 because the timeframe is only supplied in the following sentences.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need density, and we need density done well, but we also, I think, owe it to those people who put us here to be able to change the way that people’s neighbourhoods feel, to be able to account for that.
specificity.explanation: A statement of principle with no figures, mechanism, or named accountability process: 'density done well' and 'account for that' commit to nothing checkable. This is the high-focus/low-specificity pair — the vagueness is a specificity failing, not a focus one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I should say that the building code standards still remain applicable, but the relevant qualified trade professionals—for example, licensed building practitioners, registered plumbers, drain layers, electricians, and so on—will be conducting the work and certifying it.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism replacing the consent (professional certification), names the categories of professional who will certify, and states what continues to apply (the building code). Someone could check the bill against this description. No figures or timeframes, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Until recently, we had the 30 square metre rule, where you didn’t need a consent at all as long as it complied.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure and the mechanism it attaches to — a floor-area threshold below which no building consent is required, conditional on compliance. Precise enough to be looked up in the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first questions I have are around the number of dwellings that we might expect from this change: 13,000 units was a number that was raised with committee by our officials in the committee’s proceedings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as a matter of record, that officials gave the committee a figure of 13,000 units arising from these changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee evidence and the departmental/supplementary analysis for the small stand-alone dwellings bill: true if officials advised the committee that roughly 13,000 additional units would result over about 10 years, false if the advised figure was materially different or no such advice was given.

veracity.statement: However, I would say there are tens of thousands—probably hundreds of thousands—of dwellings in this country that do not have consents at the moment. They were built before the current regime. Typically, that’s not a reason for them not to be insured.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions of present fact: that a large share of New Zealand's housing stock predates the consent regime and lacks consents, and that this absence does not typically prevent those dwellings being insured.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Insurer and Insurance Council of New Zealand underwriting practice for pre-1991 dwellings lacking consent documentation: true if such dwellings are routinely insured as a matter of standard practice, false if absence of a consent record is typically a bar to, or a specific exclusion in, house insurance. The dwelling-count element resolves against building-stock estimates for pre-Building Act 1991 housing.

veracity.statement: As for the second category of question, I think we’ve covered insurance tolerably well except to say that the Insurance Council of New Zealand, I understand, did indicate their approval with the natural hazard provisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named industry body signalled approval of a specific part of the bill — the natural hazard provisions — during its passage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Insurance Council of New Zealand's written submission to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee on this bill, and any subsequent ICNZ statement on it: true if ICNZ expressed support for the natural hazard information provisions, false if it opposed them or raised unresolved objections to them.

veracity.statement: Until recently, we had the 30 square metre rule, where you didn’t need a consent at all as long as it complied.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that a 30 square metre no-consent threshold existed, and — through 'until recently' — that it is no longer the position. The second element is the load-bearing one; the Minister's reply in the same exchange refers to the 30 square metre exemption as an existing one in Schedule 1.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Schedule 1 of the Building Act 2004 and its amendments: true if a consent exemption for detached buildings up to 30 square metres existed and has since been removed or superseded, false if that exemption remains in force at the date of the statement.

focus.statement: We need density, and we need density done well, but we also, I think, owe it to those people who put us here to be able to change the way that people’s neighbourhoods feel, to be able to account for that.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy question before the committee — density and who is accountable for its effects on neighbourhoods. No party framing and no reference to opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So allowing for one of these to be built at marae doesn’t seem to create any problems that are foreseeable around the infrastructure that is at those marae. The plumbing is there.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: marae already have ablution and kitchen facilities, therefore the infrastructure objection to siting these dwellings there does not bite. The premise supports the conclusion, but the conclusion generalises further than the premise ('any problems that are foreseeable' from plumbing alone), leaving a gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course, the rating base for a council will increase according to the increase of the property value in each individual case, and the number of residents, frankly, is a relevant factor there too. It’s not as though councils will be left short changed.
rigor.explanation: The premise (rating revenue rises with property value and residents) is offered in support of the conclusion that councils are not left short changed, but nothing is offered comparing that extra revenue with the extra cost councils bear. The conclusion needs a net position and only the revenue side is shown — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s relatively little extra risk associated with that. Yes, it’s slightly larger, but, in fact, the relatively risky areas are those wet areas, so-called—kitchenettes and bathrooms—and particular provision’s been made to mitigate the risk associated with those.
rigor.explanation: A genuine mechanism-based inference: risk is concentrated in wet areas rather than distributed by floor area, so a 60-to-70 square metre increase adds little risk. The conclusion tracks the premise; it is short of 1.0 only because the claim that risk concentrates in wet areas is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I know of builders who have had buildings that have just been given a flat no, when there are processes and ways to mitigate that issue with the project which haven’t been accepted by the council.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the evidential basis for the claim that councils obstruct buildable projects, but it rests entirely on an unnamed personal anecdote — an appeal to anecdote. No number of cases, no council named, and no basis given for treating these instances as typical of council behaviour.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don't blame any homeowner that builds or buys in an area that they are told they are allowed to. If there's one lesson, after all the recent severe weather events, surely it is that there are certain areas of the country that shouldn't have residential dwellings on them, because of the tendency to have severe weather or natural hazard events. If people are told they're allowed to, then of course they're going to.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument: people build where they are permitted to build, so permission itself does the work of siting houses in hazard-prone areas, and the responsibility sits with the rule-maker rather than the homeowner. The weak link is 'surely it is' — the central premise about which areas should not be built on is asserted as self-evident from recent events rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I’m coming at this particularly from a seniors perspective, because one of the things that we do see in terms of granny flats is that, if there isn’t proper insulation, that’s going to lead to damper granny flats, which would then lead on to additional health issues.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain offered in support of a conclusion — no insulation requirement leads to damp dwellings, which leads to health harm, which matters more for the older occupants these dwellings are aimed at. Each step follows from the last; it falls short of the top because the chain is asserted rather than backed with any evidence, which is precisely the gap his own follow-up question about studies acknowledges.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He turned down a knighthood on leaving Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger was offered and declined a knighthood when he left Parliament in 1998.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary reporting and Bolger's own published interviews/biography on honours declined, plus the New Zealand honours lists 1998-1999. True if he was offered and declined a knighthood; false if no offer was made or if he accepted one.

veracity.statement: I do want to acknowledge Winston Peters today, the only remaining member of the House who served in Government with Jim Bolger during the time that he was Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of all MPs sitting in October 2025, Winston Peters is the only one who held a position in government during Bolger's premiership (1990-1997).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Library register of current members' service dates cross-referenced against ministerial lists for the 1990-1997 Bolger ministries. True if Peters is the sole current MP appearing in those ministerial lists; false if any other sitting MP also served in government in that period.

veracity.statement: There has been one member of Parliament between Jim Bolger and myself, and that was Shane Ardern.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an unbroken succession in the Taranaki-King Country electorate: Bolger, then Shane Ardern, then Kuriger, with no other member in between.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission results for the Taranaki-King Country electorate from the 1998 by-election onward. True if Shane Ardern is the sole member between Bolger's 1998 departure and Kuriger's 2014 election; false if any other person held the seat in that period.

veracity.statement: I’m going to miss “Sir Jim”, and I know he wasn’t a fan of knighthoods, but when we met, I told him he’d been Prime Minister for seven years and I was going to call him “Sir”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger served seven years as Prime Minister of New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official record of Bolger's term as Prime Minister (Parliament/DPMC list of NZ Prime Ministers); true if the span from his taking office to leaving office rounds to about seven years, false if it is materially shorter or longer (e.g. five or nine years).

rigor.statement: If we were in the business of failing to provide consents, or even to require them where they otherwise wouldn’t be required, on the basis that there might be hazards of which we’re unaware, then, simply, we’d be very hidebound and have an even greater issue of productivity and affordability, in terms of housing in this country, than we already do.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: from 'we cannot know unknown hazards' to 'requiring consents against unknown hazards would worsen housing affordability'. The step is plausible but the cost side is asserted rather than shown, and it edges toward a reductio without establishing that the alternative is as absolute as described.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To be able to change the requirements for the small stand-alone dwellings, in terms of the detail of clause 2 within new Schedule 1A, is a good thing, but it’s not an unlimited power, because it’s still subject to clause 1, which can’t be changed by Order in Council.
rigor.explanation: Direct rebuttal to the 'it could be a castle' argument: if clause 1 sets the envelope and is outside the Order in Council power, the regulation-making power is bounded. The conclusion follows from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the point around return of a development contribution or some land that had been set aside where that has taken place in consideration for providing or enabling the development to take place: if the development doesn't take place, then the development contribution which is used to support funding infrastructure isn't needed anymore for that purpose.
rigor.explanation: A straightforward conditional: the contribution is levied to fund infrastructure for a development, so if the development does not proceed the purpose lapses and the contribution is returned. The conclusion tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Every time I’ve seen the word “non-consent”, it automatically makes me think that that’s a bad and naughty thing. I think that this amendment is quite sensible and to the point.
rigor.explanation: An argument from her own reaction to the drafting: because the term reads to her as pejorative, the clarifying amendment is warranted. It is a real inference about the statute's wording, but it rests on a single personal impression — an appeal to anecdote — with nothing offered about how other readers would take it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It can be the size, so 70 metres squared. It could be just to build a mansion. It could have several bathrooms, it could be large, it could be many floors, it could be a castle, it could be a swimming pool—it could be absolutely anything.
rigor.explanation: Escalates from a breadth-of-power premise to mansions, castles and swimming pools without establishing that clause 1's constraints fall within the power. A slippery slope: the final step, 'absolutely anything', is asserted rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It makes sense to use that sort of “must” in the context where the council was after a development contribution, because there is an end point to that; the council are after money, so they’re incentivised to pursue that.
rigor.explanation: A sound incentive argument: a statutory 'must' works where the obliged party has a self-interested reason to act, and the contrast case (an obligation with no payoff and no recourse) is what her question is built on. The conclusion follows from the mechanism she sets out.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re not in favour of broad exemptions, which some people have argued for. We are going to have some narrow exemptions, but the whole point at some level is to make sure that people actually face a price signal. The more people you exempt, the less effectiveness there is of the price signal.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows directly from the stated mechanism: the scheme works by exposing drivers to a price signal, so each exemption removes someone from that signal and weakens it. Premise and conclusion are properly connected, and the position taken (narrow but not zero exemptions) is consistent with it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yeah, 55,000, but they could have three representatives on a scheme board, and Wellington City with 200,000 people could have one.
rigor.explanation: A concrete disproportionality argument: population figures set against possible board seats, supporting the conclusion that the scheme board provisions can over-represent councils outside the charging area. The inference is sound, but it depends on an unevidenced assumption that the neighbouring councils would in fact hold three seats to Wellington's one — she elsewhere concedes it may be a worst case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t make sense to use revenue from a congestion charging scheme to build additional capacity on a motorway. That completely defeats the purpose, because, when you put the congestion charge in place, that reduces the demand for the roads, and it increases the demand for the other forms of transportation.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument: the charge shifts demand off the roads and onto alternatives, so spending the proceeds on road capacity funds the mode whose demand has fallen while starving the one whose demand has risen. The conclusion follows, though the 'completely defeats the purpose' step is stronger than the premises strictly support.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Therefore, it’s relevant to say that homes must meet the building code, including that they mustn’t worsen natural hazards and, in fact, must also actively mitigate natural hazards where present.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that building code compliance already carries two natural-hazard duties — a negative duty not to worsen a hazard and a positive duty to mitigate one that is present — independently of whether a council officer or a licensed practitioner certifies the work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Building Act 2004 (ss 71–74, land subject to natural hazards) and the New Zealand Building Code: true if the Code/Act require that building work not accelerate or worsen a natural hazard AND require active mitigation where a hazard is present; false if the requirement is limited to not worsening the hazard, with no positive duty to mitigate.

veracity.statement: It can be the size, so 70 metres squared. It could be just to build a mansion. It could have several bathrooms, it could be large, it could be many floors, it could be a castle, it could be a swimming pool—it could be absolutely anything.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the regulation-making power is broad enough to bring buildings of any size, height or configuration within the non-consented exemption. The Minister's reply directly contradicts this, so the bill text settles it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 14 of the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill read with clauses 1 and 2 of new Schedule 1A: true if the Order in Council power extends to the stand-alone / 70 m² / single-storey limits, so that a dwelling of unbounded size or storeys could be brought within the exemption; false if clause 1 is not amendable by Order in Council.

veracity.statement: A recent estimate—and there’s been a range—suggests Auckland could face an annual cost of $2.6 billion by 2026.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a recent published estimate places the annual cost of Auckland congestion at around $2.6 billion by 2026. What is checkable is whether such an estimate exists at that magnitude and date, not whether the cost is 'really' that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates of the annual economic cost of Auckland congestion (NZIER 2017, the Congestion Question programme, Auckland Council / NZTA modelling): true if a recent published estimate puts the annual cost at about $2.6 billion by 2026; false if no such estimate exists or the published range is materially different.

veracity.statement: Traffic dropped by 7 percent—over 7 percent. Travel times improved by up to 40 percent in peak hours.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims about the observed effect of New York's congestion charge in its first year: a fall of over 7 percent in traffic and peak travel-time improvements of up to 40 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA and NYC DOT reporting on Manhattan's congestion relief zone, introduced January 2025: true if vehicle entries into the zone fell by roughly 7 percent or more and peak-hour travel times improved by up to about 40 percent; false if either figure is materially lower than stated.

veracity.statement: It will be a momentous day when that happens, because the first economic study into congestion charging, or time of use pricing, whatever you want to call it—I think I’m right in saying—was in 1994.
veracity.explanation: Dates the first economic study of congestion charging in New Zealand to 1994, i.e. 31 years before the bill. He hedges with 'I think I'm right in saying', but the date is a definite, checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand road-pricing literature and Ministry of Transport / Auckland regional transport study records: true if a published economic study of congestion or time-of-use charging in New Zealand dates from 1994; false if the earliest such study is materially later.

veracity.statement: It causes approximately $10 billion in social costs each year, including 3,000 cases of childhood asthma.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims about the annual health burden of motor-vehicle air pollution in New Zealand: roughly $10 billion in social costs, and roughly 3,000 childhood asthma cases. Both come from a specific published study and can be checked against it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The HAPINZ 3.0 (Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand) study: true if the social cost of motor-vehicle air pollution is about $10 billion a year and childhood asthma cases attributed to it are about 3,000; false if either figure is materially different from the published estimate.

veracity.statement: We have higher fares, on average, than every city in Australia for public transport. In Brisbane, they set up a 50c fare to anywhere recently.
veracity.explanation: A universal comparative claim — NZ average public transport fares are higher than those in every Australian city — plus a specific supporting fact about Brisbane's flat 50c fare. The universal quantifier is what makes it falsifiable by a single counterexample.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparison of average adult public transport fares in New Zealand cities against every Australian capital and major city (Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Perth, Adelaide, Canberra, Hobart), plus Queensland government records of the 50c flat fare: true if NZ average fares exceed those of every Australian city and Brisbane introduced a 50c flat fare; false if any Australian city has higher average fares or the Brisbane fare is not as described.

veracity.statement: Public transportation is very expensive; it’s got more expensive under this Government because of the policies of Simeon Brown, and I’m hoping that the current Minister will see fit to ensure that more of the budget can be used for transportation fares.
veracity.explanation: A claim about a named predecessor Minister's record: that public transport fares increased under this Government as a result of his policy decisions. Checkable on both limbs — that fares rose, and that the identified policy changes were made.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport and regional council fare data since late 2023, alongside the transport policy decisions of the then Minister (ending half-price public transport fares and narrowing the Community Connect concessions): true if average public transport fares rose following those decisions; false if fares were flat or fell over the period.

specificity.statement: To be able to change the requirements for the small stand-alone dwellings, in terms of the detail of clause 2 within new Schedule 1A, is a good thing, but it’s not an unlimited power, because it’s still subject to clause 1, which can’t be changed by Order in Council.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact instruments — clause 2 versus clause 1 of new Schedule 1A, and the Order in Council mechanism. Someone could open the bill and check the boundary he describes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A recent estimate—and there’s been a range—suggests Auckland could face an annual cost of $2.6 billion by 2026.
specificity.explanation: A named city, a dollar figure and a year, offered as the quantified case for the bill. Someone could go and find the estimate. He also flags that there is a range rather than presenting one number as settled.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yeah, 55,000, but they could have three representatives on a scheme board, and Wellington City with 200,000 people could have one.
specificity.explanation: Names the populations (200,000 and 55,000), the specific councils involved and the exact mechanism — seats on a scheme board — rather than asserting unfairness in the abstract.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It can be the size, so 70 metres squared. It could be just to build a mansion. It could have several bathrooms, it could be large, it could be many floors, it could be a castle, it could be a swimming pool—it could be absolutely anything.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the scope of the clause 14 regulation-making power and what it may alter in Schedule 1A. No party framing at all; the target is the drafting.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That name change would be at least clearer with people about what is happening here and what the effect of this will be: 13,000 of these dwellings around the country.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the national uptake of the new non-consented small stand-alone dwelling pathway at 13,000 dwellings, unevenly distributed across the country. This is an outcome in the world, not a commitment by the speaker, and it rests on the officials' estimate she cites earlier.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE building consent / project information memorandum records and Stats NZ dwelling data for small stand-alone dwellings built under this exemption: true if the national total reaches approximately 13,000 dwellings, false if the total is materially lower (or materially higher).

civility.statement: Well, I’m looking forward to hearing what will no doubt be a very passionate contribution from the Hon Julie Anne Genter, because, if nothing else, there’s always enthusiasm.
civility.explanation: 'If nothing else' is the sting — a backhanded compliment to a named member that credits her with enthusiasm while implying there is nothing else of value in her contribution. It lands on the person's manner and worth as a contributor rather than on any argument, though it stops short of open abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So far, agencies have paid over $11 million in top-up payments to over 900 survivors, at an average amount of almost $12,000.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete figures — total paid, number of survivors, average payment — all checkable against agency reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This includes 42 offences that are on the most serious end of the violent and sexual offending spectrum and that attract a maximum sentence of between seven and 20 years.
specificity.explanation: Names the count of offences and the maximum-sentence band, tied to a nameable schedule; a reader could go and check the scope.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The process will apply to all new claims made from 9 May 2025, and we expect that it will apply to around 100 claims a year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a commencement date and a quantified expected caseload.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the month, and exact counts (85 of 207) across two named reports — precisely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One in three children placed in residential care by the State ends up in prison later in life. That number is 42 percent for mokopuna Māori.
specificity.explanation: Two precise rates attached to a defined population; someone could locate the source and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They save about $12,500 if the person stands by the presumption, and that is inappropriate.
specificity.explanation: Puts a figure on the fiscal saving per excluded claimant, but does not say over what period, across how many claims, or where the figure comes from.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Actually, this doesn’t apply to most people. Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the affected share of claimants with a stated range; the second clause is looser but the headline figure is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So far, agencies have paid over $11 million in top-up payments to over 900 survivors, at an average amount of almost $12,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that agencies have paid more than $11m in top-up redress payments to more than 900 survivors under the common payments framework, averaging close to $12,000 each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Response Unit / MSD historic claims reporting on top-up payments made under the common payments framework as at October 2025; true if the cumulative total exceeds $11m across more than 900 survivors with a mean near $12,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: The royal commission found that most survivors do not receive apologies that they feel are genuine or personal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific finding of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care about survivors' experience of apologies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The royal commission's final report (Whanaketia) sections on redress and apologies; true if it records that a majority of survivors found apologies received were not genuine or personal, false if it makes no such finding or finds the opposite.

veracity.statement: There was widespread support for this change during the select committee process, and no person or organisation submitted against it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no submitter opposed the children's workers safety regime change to the Children's Act during select committee consideration of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Services and Community Committee's report and published submissions on the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill; true if no submission opposes the children's worker vetting change, false if any submitter opposed it.

veracity.statement: The royal commission explicitly recommended that all survivors be able to access redress, including those in prison or with a criminal record.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the royal commission recommended redress eligibility extend to survivors who are imprisoned or have criminal convictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The redress recommendations in He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu and Whanaketia; true if a recommendation expressly extends eligibility to survivors in prison or with a criminal record, false if no such recommendation exists.

veracity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's May 2025 response either declined or had not begun considering 85 of 207 royal commission recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown's May 2025 response to the royal commission's recommendations; true if the count of recommendations marked 'not accepted' plus 'not yet considered' equals about 85 out of 207, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Poi McIntyre would not be able to access redress through what we’re proposing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a survivor with a long serious-offending history and 23 years' imprisonment would be unable to access redress under the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced; true if a person with such convictions is barred from redress, false if the bill creates only a rebuttable presumption against financial payment with an application route to a redress officer and retains apology, records and wellbeing redress.

veracity.statement: This redress system, as it’s been characterised in this House, is not depriving anyone of redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill removes no one's access to redress, only routes some claimants through a different process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced; true if in-scope claimants retain access to apology, records, counselling and a route to financial redress via the redress officer, false if any claimant is absolutely barred from all forms of redress.

veracity.statement: One in three children placed in residential care by the State ends up in prison later in life. That number is 42 percent for mokopuna Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about a third of children placed in State residential care are later imprisoned, rising to 42 percent for Māori children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal commission (Whanaketia) and Oranga Tamariki / Corrections longitudinal data on imprisonment rates for former State residential care residents; true if the overall rate is near one in three and the Māori rate near 42 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It undermines Aotearoa’s obligation under international human rights law, including the convention against torture and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, both of which require the State to provide redress to all victims of institutional abuse, without discrimination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that UNCAT and UNCROC each impose an obligation to provide redress to all victims of institutional abuse without discrimination, and that the bill is inconsistent with it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Article 14 of the Convention against Torture, the Committee against Torture's General Comment No. 3, and the relevant UNCROC provisions, plus any NZ Bill of Rights vet or Human Rights Commission analysis of this bill; true if those instruments are read as requiring non-discriminatory redress to all victims, false if the obligation does not extend as stated.

veracity.statement: Actually, this doesn’t apply to most people. Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only 5–6 percent of redress claimants fall within the serious-offender presumption and that most of those have not created further victims.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Departmental advice / regulatory impact statement for the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill giving the estimated proportion of claimants in scope; true if the estimate is in the 5–6 percent range, false if materially higher or lower.

divination.statement: The process will apply to all new claims made from 9 May 2025, and we expect that it will apply to around 100 claims a year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that roughly 100 redress claims a year will fall within the serious-offender presumption. Not a promise about the Government's own action but a prediction about claim volumes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Annual reporting by the redress agencies (or the redress officer) on the number of claims referred into the serious-offender process; true if the first full year falls in the range 70–130, false if materially outside it.

focus.statement: And we have not seen a great deal of action from this Government, so perhaps they have been distracted—unless you call kicking the can down the road “action”.
focus.explanation: A general jibe about the Government being distracted and delaying; no measure, figure or named commitment is engaged, so the weight sits on party characterisation rather than policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is morally bereft. It is cynical. It is a dog whistle to their base.
focus.explanation: Nominally about the bill, but the content is motive attribution to the governing parties and their voter base; no clause, mechanism or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to take responsibility as the Government on what has occurred and not try to change the deck chairs and retain the power within the Crown, and acknowledge that independence is required because how do you assess, how do you critique, and how do you improve a system when it’s yourself looking at yourself?
rigor.explanation: A real conflict-of-interest inference: an agency assessing claims against itself cannot be an impartial assessor, therefore independence is needed. The inference holds but is carried by a rhetorical question rather than any evidence that self-assessment has in fact distorted outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it does not do the victims of those crimes any justice to know that, potentially, their abuser may now be getting financial compensation.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to the feelings of a third party, and a non sequitur: that a crime victim would be aggrieved does not establish that the State owes less redress for a separate wrong it committed against the offender. The two harms are not offset in the argument, merely juxtaposed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Even if you were sodomised, does that give you the right to go and do that to another person? A hundred percent it doesn’t.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing case is that abuse in State care warrants redress irrespective of later offending, not that abuse confers a right to offend. The conclusion is drawn against a claim nobody made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I myself have worked in criminal courts and prisons around New Zealand, and I do know that the victims often become the victimisers.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal experience: professional exposure is offered as the sole warrant for a general empirical claim about offending pathways, with no data cited and no link drawn between the claim and the presumption the bill creates.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just think it’s really unfortunate that when we heckle in this House, when we hurl abuse at each other as we’re making speeches, we are not presenting this House in a proper light.
civility.explanation: Mid-debate, after pointed interjections aimed at her side, she criticises the conduct collectively including herself in the 'we' rather than naming or attacking any member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It makes a mockery of the apology from the Prime Minister, which I accept was sincere on the day.
civility.explanation: A harsh judgement of the bill's effect on the Crown apology, while expressly conceding the Prime Minister's personal sincerity — the criticism lands on the policy, not the man.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yesterday, Stats New Zealand released the latest figures for the Consumers Price Index—the CPI—which showed annual CPI inflation increasing slightly, from 2.7 percent in the June quarter, to 3 percent in September, but remaining within the Reserve Bank’s target 1 to 3 percent band.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific CPI annual inflation rates for the June and September 2025 quarters and that the September figure sits inside the RBNZ's 1-3 percent target band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the September 2025 quarter; true if annual CPI inflation was 2.7% in the June 2025 quarter and 3.0% in the September 2025 quarter, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Let me remind members that inflation in the four quarters of 2022 was 6.9 percent in the March quarter, then 7.3 percent, then 7.2 percent, and then 7.2 percent in the December quarter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four specific annual CPI inflation rates for the four quarters of 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series for the March, June, September and December 2022 quarters; true if the rates were 6.9%, 7.3%, 7.2% and 7.2% respectively, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Non-tradeables inflation—that is, for goods and services not exposed to international competition—fell to 3.5 percent, which is the lowest rate since mid-2021.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: that non-tradeables inflation was 3.5 percent in the September 2025 quarter, and that this was the lowest print since mid-2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI non-tradeables annual inflation series; true if the September 2025 quarter print was 3.5% and no quarter between mid-2021 and then was lower, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: Local authority rates rose 8.8 percent in the year to September, and that’s why we are clear, in Government, in our call for councils to focus on the basics and to keep rates under control.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual increase in the local authority rates component of the CPI to September 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI local authority rates and payments subgroup, annual change to the September 2025 quarter; true if approximately 8.8%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Clearly, the Reserve Bank is not concerned about lingering inflation, as it reduced the official cash rate by half a percent earlier this month, and financial markets are fully expecting the bank to make another 25 basis point reduction at the next opportunity in November.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Reserve Bank cut the OCR by 50 basis points in October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025; true if the OCR was reduced by 0.50 percentage points, false if by a different amount or not at all.

veracity.statement: What I can tell the member is that it’s not 7.3 percent, which is what it was under his Government because he had an 84 percent increase in Government spending, he drove inflation up to 7.3 percent, and then what he ended up doing was actually tripling our debt as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an 84 percent increase in government spending and a tripling of debt under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses and net core Crown debt series, 2017/18 to 2023/24; true if nominal core Crown expenses rose approximately 84% and net core Crown debt approximately tripled over that period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Electricity prices are about 11 percent of the growth we’ve seen in the last quarter, and, actually, council rates are the other 9 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that electricity and council rates account for about 11 percent and 9 percent respectively of the recent inflation increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI September 2025 quarter contribution analysis; true if electricity contributed roughly 11% and local authority rates roughly 9% of the annual increase, false if the contributions differ materially or if the figures are in fact the price increases rather than contributions.

veracity.statement: What I can say is that isn’t it fantastic that this is a Government that, through excellent economic management and getting a grip on Government spending, has been able to lower domestic inflation from 3.7 percent to 3.5 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that domestic (non-tradeables) inflation fell from 3.7 percent to 3.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI non-tradeables annual inflation for the June and September 2025 quarters; true if the series moved from 3.7% to 3.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Is he still laser focused on the cost of living; if so, why do basic staples cost more than ever, with bread now 50 percent more expensive than it was just one year ago?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the price of bread rose 50 percent in the year to September 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index, bread subgroup, annual change to September 2025; true if approximately a 50% increase, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Why have rents increased by 2.6 percent over the last year, according to the Consumers Price Index figures released yesterday, when he said his $3 billion tax cut for landlords was going to lower rents?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2.6 percent annual rent increase in the latest CPI and a $3 billion cost for the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI rentals for housing, annual change to September 2025, and Treasury/IRD costings for the interest deductibility change; true if rents rose approximately 2.6% and the measure is costed at approximately $3 billion, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: One is, actually, for new rents prices have lowered, and for existing rents, prices have gone up slightly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a divergence between new-tenancy rents (falling) and existing-tenancy rents (rising slightly).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services bond data on new tenancy median rents versus Stats NZ CPI rentals for housing (which tracks existing tenancies), year to September 2025; true if new-tenancy rents fell and existing rents rose, false if both moved the same way.

veracity.statement: But what was incredibly tragic was that in a period of low unemployment—about 3.2 percent—60,000 more people got consigned to benefits and jobseeker benefits; it increased by 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker beneficiary numbers rose by 60,000 (a 50 percent increase) during a period when unemployment was around 3.2 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets, Jobseeker Support recipient counts 2017-2023, alongside Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate; true if recipients rose by approximately 60,000 and about 50% over a period when unemployment was near 3.2%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his claim from five months ago, that “Unemployment is just almost peaking and about to come down.”; if so, how does he explain the fact that it has continued to increase and is now at its highest number, in terms of job seekers, since 2012?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker numbers have continued to increase and are now at their highest level since 2012.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Jobseeker Support recipient series; true if the September 2025 count exceeds every quarterly count back to 2012, false if a higher count occurred in the interim.

veracity.statement: Why should New Zealanders believe him now when he confidently predicted unemployment had peaked, yet it's still going up; he said, over a year ago, that the economy had “turned the corner”, when it's shrunk since then; he said his Government was going to increase infrastructure investment, but instead has cut it by $2.9 billion, putting thousands of people out of work?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the economy has shrunk since the 'turned the corner' remark and that infrastructure investment has been cut by $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series from mid-2024 to September 2025, and Treasury/Infrastructure Commission capital expenditure figures; true if real GDP is lower than at the reference point and capital investment fell by approximately $2.9 billion, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Today, I am pleased to announce we have not only achieved but surpassed the Government target of a 15 percent reduction in serious and persistent youth offending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's 15 percent reduction target for serious and persistent youth offending has been met and exceeded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Targets quarterly dashboard measure for serious and persistent youth offending; true if the reported reduction against the baseline exceeds 15%, false if it is at or below 15%.

veracity.statement: Oranga Tamariki has faced a sharp increase in reports of concern recently—up 44 percent overall.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 44 percent overall increase in reports of concern received by Oranga Tamariki.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki quarterly safety of children in care / reports of concern statistics; true if reports of concern rose approximately 44% over the stated recent period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Mokopuna Ora initiative has seen 98 percent of children that they engage with successfully remain out of State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 98 percent rate of children engaged by the Waikato-Tainui Mokopuna Ora initiative remaining out of State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Mokopuna Ora / Waikato-Tainui programme reporting or Oranga Tamariki partnership evaluation; true if approximately 98% of engaged children did not enter State care, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, the ultimate measure of affordability in the economy is whether wages are rising faster than inflation, which they are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wage growth currently exceeds inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Labour Cost Index (salary and wage rates) or average ordinary time hourly earnings annual growth versus CPI annual inflation for the September 2025 quarter; true if wage growth exceeds 3.0% CPI, false if it is at or below it.

veracity.statement: Teachers are not getting a pay cut. They’ve been made a reasonable offer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the offer to teachers does not constitute a pay cut. The disputed sense is nominal versus real, which the criterion has to fix.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The terms of the Government's 2025 collective offer to NZEI/PPTA members; true if the offered nominal pay rates are not lower than existing rates, false if any offered rate is nominally lower. (A real-terms fall below CPI does not, on this criterion, make it false.)

veracity.statement: The Government agrees, which is why in Budget 2025, we made the single largest investment in learning support in a generation of over $700 million for a range of incredibly important initiatives to provide better support for kids who need it most.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Budget 2025 learning support package of over $700 million and that it is the largest such investment in a generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 Vote Education documents; true if the learning support package totals over $700 million and no larger single learning support investment appears in the past ~25 years, false if the figure is materially lower or a larger prior investment exists.

veracity.statement: We’ve got 6,000 patients who are going to be disrupted, after Labour ran the wait-list up 30 times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government increased a health waiting list thirtyfold, and that 6,000 patients face disruption from the strike.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Ministry of Health planned care waiting list counts for 2017 and 2023; true if the relevant list grew by a factor of about 30, false if the growth factor is materially smaller. The 6,000 figure checks against Health NZ's published strike deferral count.

veracity.statement: They got a 2.5 percent increase immediately. They get a 2.1 percent increase in October. Within 12 months, they’re up 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific terms of the Primary Principals Collective Bargaining Union settlement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ratified PPCBU collective agreement terms as published by the Ministry of Education; true if it provides a 2.5% immediate increase and a further 2.1% in October, false if the rates or timing differ.

veracity.statement: So far, we've delivered over $4 million in PLD for teachers to support students with complex needs using the Expanded New Zealand Curriculum, and nearly 3,000 teachers and countless students have benefited already.
veracity.explanation: Asserts over $4 million of professional learning and development spend and nearly 3,000 teachers reached.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education PLD expenditure and participation reporting for the Expanded New Zealand Curriculum programme; true if spend exceeds $4 million and participating teachers number close to 3,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: How are our teachers and healthcare workers meant to feed their whānau when pay offers continue to lag behind growing inflation while fruit and vegetable prices have increased by 7.4 percent in the last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 7.4 percent annual increase in fruit and vegetable prices — a claim the Prime Minister immediately denied, making it worth resolving.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index, fruit and vegetables subgroup, annual change to September 2025; true if approximately 7.4%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, that’s why I’d encourage the member to get in behind and support Fast-track, because there’s 25 renewable energy projects that will increase electricity generation in this country by 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 25 renewable energy projects in the fast-track process would lift New Zealand's electricity generation by 40 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The renewable energy projects listed in the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 schedule and their stated capacities, against current national generation (Electricity Authority / MBIE energy statistics); true if the listed renewable projects total roughly 40% of current annual generation, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: Does the fact that two-thirds of rivers and half of groundwater bores are contaminated by E. coli, nitrogen, and other contaminants, while two-thirds of lakes are in poor or very poor condition demonstrates good Government stewardship?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific freshwater quality proportions: two-thirds of rivers and half of groundwater bores contaminated, and two-thirds of lakes in poor or very poor condition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Stats NZ 'Our freshwater' environmental reporting; true if the reported proportions are approximately two-thirds of monitored river sites, half of monitored groundwater bores and two-thirds of monitored lakes, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: As a result of the industry’s hard work, talent, and creativity and the Government’s continued support, the game development sector has seen strong growth, with a 38 percent increase in pre-tax income over the last financial year and a 29 percent increase in employment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 38 percent increase in the game development sector's pre-tax income and a 29 percent increase in its employment over the last financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual industry survey for 2025; true if pre-tax income rose approximately 38% and employment approximately 29%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How many game development jobs will end up overseas as a result of the decision not to increase the funding cap when 200 Kiwis a day are already leaving the country to find work overseas?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 200 New Zealanders a day are leaving the country for work overseas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, departures of New Zealand citizens for the year to mid-2025; true if the annual figure is approximately 73,000 (about 200/day), false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In May, the Government announced a significant investment of $533 million to improve the current State redress system as quickly as possible for survivors of abuse in care, investing in changes that have a direct impact for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $533 million package announced in May 2025 for the State redress system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents and the Government's May 2025 abuse in care redress announcement; true if the announced figure is $533 million, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, Stats New Zealand released the latest figures for the Consumers Price Index—the CPI—which showed annual CPI inflation increasing slightly, from 2.7 percent in the June quarter, to 3 percent in September, but remaining within the Reserve Bank’s target 1 to 3 percent band.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named index, two dated figures and the target band — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why have rents increased by 2.6 percent over the last year, according to the Consumers Price Index figures released yesterday, when he said his $3 billion tax cut for landlords was going to lower rents?
specificity.explanation: Two figures, a named data release and a named policy — an opposition question as checkable as any answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today, I am pleased to announce we have not only achieved but surpassed the Government target of a 15 percent reduction in serious and persistent youth offending.
specificity.explanation: A named target, a numeric threshold and a stated timeframe against the deadline.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government agrees, which is why in Budget 2025, we made the single largest investment in learning support in a generation of over $700 million for a range of incredibly important initiatives to provide better support for kids who need it most.
specificity.explanation: Names the Budget and a figure, but the 'range of incredibly important initiatives' is left unenumerated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They got a 2.5 percent increase immediately. They get a 2.1 percent increase in October. Within 12 months, they’re up 4.7 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three figures with timing, and a compounding total — fully checkable against the settlement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of this combined funding of $1.2 billion, $675 million is for consenting, design, route protection, site investigations, and some early works, and $515 million is for property acquisition, to get under way on these projects.
specificity.explanation: A total broken into two named tranches with the work categories each covers — someone could check it against the NZTA board decision.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to make sure that we protect our natural environment but also this Government is unapologetically focused on economic growth, as well—as well as also lifting the immunisation rates for young Māori under the age of two.
specificity.explanation: Two general commitments and one unrelated named indicator; no target, figure or mechanism attaches to the water quality issue being asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the fact that two-thirds of rivers and half of groundwater bores are contaminated by E. coli, nitrogen, and other contaminants, while two-thirds of lakes are in poor or very poor condition demonstrates good Government stewardship?
specificity.explanation: Three named measures with proportions and named contaminants — checkable against published environmental reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a Government that’s actually making sure we advance New Zealand economically and we protect our environment, and we’ll continue to do that.
specificity.explanation: Two generic virtues and a promise to keep doing them. No measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a result of the industry’s hard work, talent, and creativity and the Government’s continued support, the game development sector has seen strong growth, with a 38 percent increase in pre-tax income over the last financial year and a 29 percent increase in employment.
specificity.explanation: Two figures tied to a named sector and a stated period.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The industry has earned $513 million in 2024 and is projected to surpass $750 million this year.
specificity.explanation: A base figure, a projected figure and the years each applies to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With the passing of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, 10 regional polytechnics will be stood up by 1 January 2026, with four to be considered early next year, and eight industry skills boards will also be established on 1 January 2026.
specificity.explanation: Named legislation, counts of institutions and boards, and a dated commencement — precise enough to check on the day.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In May, the Government announced a significant investment of $533 million to improve the current State redress system as quickly as possible for survivors of abuse in care, investing in changes that have a direct impact for them.
specificity.explanation: A dated announcement, a total figure, and in the surrounding sentences the payment levels it funds.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Looking ahead, commodity export prices have levelled off, and so food inflation is expected to ease and inflation is expected to fall to somewhere near the mid-point target of 2 percent early next year, easing pressure on households and businesses.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that annual CPI inflation falls to around the 2 percent mid-point of the target band in early 2026, with food inflation easing.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the March 2026 and June 2026 quarters; true if a print in that window is at or near 2.0% (roughly 1.8-2.4%), false if inflation remains at or above about 2.7% through mid-2026.

divination.statement: We expect that that will start to trend down, as the economy is growing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that unemployment, having peaked, will begin to fall.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate; true if the rate is lower in the June 2026 quarter than the peak quarter of late 2025, false if it is the same or higher.

divination.statement: We have a projection for the next two years that we’ll grow faster than Australia.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand's economic growth will exceed Australia's over the two years following October 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ and ABS annual real GDP growth for calendar 2026 and 2027; true if New Zealand's growth exceeds Australia's in both years (or cumulatively over the period), false if Australia matches or exceeds New Zealand.

divination.statement: The industry has earned $513 million in 2024 and is projected to surpass $750 million this year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that game development sector revenue will exceed $750 million in the current year, up from $513 million in 2024.
