divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual survey reporting sector revenue for the 2025/26 year; true if reported revenue exceeds $750 million, false if it comes in below.

rigor.statement: Clearly, the Reserve Bank is not concerned about lingering inflation, as it reduced the official cash rate by half a percent earlier this month, and financial markets are fully expecting the bank to make another 25 basis point reduction at the next opportunity in November.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — inferring the Reserve Bank's assessment from its rate decision is reasonable — but the leap from one cut to 'clearly not concerned' overstates what a single decision shows, and market pricing is offered as corroboration rather than evidence of the Bank's view.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I can tell the member is that it’s not 7.3 percent, which is what it was under his Government because he had an 84 percent increase in Government spending, he drove inflation up to 7.3 percent, and then what he ended up doing was actually tripling our debt as well.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: the 84 percent spending figure is asserted as the cause of 7.3 percent inflation with nothing offered to connect them, and no account taken of the global inflation shock of the same period.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I can say is that isn’t it fantastic that this is a Government that, through excellent economic management and getting a grip on Government spending, has been able to lower domestic inflation from 3.7 percent to 3.5 percent?
rigor.explanation: Claims sole credit for a 0.2 percentage point move with nothing offered to link the government's spending decisions to that particular change — a post hoc attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I said that last month because three years ago inflation was 7.3 percent and now it’s 3 percent.
rigor.explanation: The question was why inflation is 'under control' when it has risen for four consecutive quarters; the answer establishes only that it is lower than three years ago, which does not support the conclusion about the recent trend. A real inference about the policy, and a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Ultimately, the ultimate measure of affordability in the economy is whether wages are rising faster than inflation, which they are.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument — real wage growth is a defensible affordability benchmark and the conclusion follows from it — but it leans on a single chosen measure to answer a question about the level of specific staple prices.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Nurses don’t have to strike. What I would encourage them to do is to get back around the bargaining table because it’s not possible to have a conversation in a strike.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a false dichotomy: striking and negotiating are treated as mutually exclusive, when industrial action routinely runs alongside bargaining. Nothing is offered to support the exclusive premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These are tough economic times, and we need to acknowledge that any Government spending, including the money to fund public sector salaries, comes from the taxes of other working Kiwis.
rigor.explanation: A sound and explicitly-stated premise-to-conclusion step about the fiscal source of public sector pay; the gap is that it establishes a constraint exists without connecting it to the level of any particular offer.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, and I also believe that they see that the improvement in Māori literacy rates for new entrants is also giving them great trust in what this Government is doing, as well.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was whether the Government's stewardship of harbours and rivers inspires public confidence, and the answer offers literacy results as support. Nothing connects the two domains.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We want to make sure that we protect our natural environment but also this Government is unapologetically focused on economic growth, as well—as well as also lifting the immunisation rates for young Māori under the age of two.
rigor.explanation: Asked whether contaminated rivers, bores and lakes demonstrate good stewardship, the reply offers immunisation rates. There is no inference connecting the evidence raised to the conclusion implied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are performing better than Australia and actually have a better scheme than Australia, so why would they go when they get a better offer here?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that developers will not leave — treats the rebate scheme as the only factor in relocation decisions, and the rhetorical question substitutes for evidence. A real inference about the policy, but a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s more important to the Government: keeping well-paid, high-tech jobs in a growing sector in New Zealand, or giving hundreds of millions of dollars in tax cuts to tobacco companies?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the two policies are presented as mutually exclusive alternatives when nothing offered shows the game development rebate was traded against the tobacco excise decision.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m delighted to say that Alan Pollard has been very keen to be involved in the reforms and has made himself available to be a board member of the infrastructure industry skills board to help drive these reforms.
rigor.explanation: The implied conclusion — that the criticism ('it is not about training but about cutting costs') is unfounded — rests on the critic's willingness to serve on a board, which bears on his engagement, not on whether the reform saves money at training's expense. A relevance gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I can tell the member is that it’s not 7.3 percent, which is what it was under his Government because he had an 84 percent increase in Government spending, he drove inflation up to 7.3 percent, and then what he ended up doing was actually tripling our debt as well.
focus.explanation: Named figures and a named outcome give it real policy content, but the weight of the answer is the previous government's record rather than the inflation question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he still laser focused on the cost of living; if so, why do basic staples cost more than ever, with bread now 50 percent more expensive than it was just one year ago?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named government commitment against a named commodity and a figure — squarely on the policy question, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why have rents increased by 2.6 percent over the last year, according to the Consumers Price Index figures released yesterday, when he said his $3 billion tax cut for landlords was going to lower rents?
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure, its stated purpose and the measured outcome. Textbook accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, good economic management from this coalition Government; a senior team that actually understands economics and can deal with numbers, unlike what we’ve seen in the great New Zealand Future Fund documental pamphlet.
focus.explanation: Asked what steps the Government took, the answer names none. It is a claim of general competence set against mockery of the Opposition's document — no mechanism, measure or figure appears.

focus.statement: Does he stand by his claim from five months ago, that “Unemployment is just almost peaking and about to come down.”; if so, how does he explain the fact that it has continued to increase and is now at its highest number, in terms of job seekers, since 2012?
focus.explanation: Holds the Prime Minister to a specific prior statement against a specific measured outcome. Scrutiny with a named claim and a named series.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why should New Zealanders believe him now when he confidently predicted unemployment had peaked, yet it's still going up; he said, over a year ago, that the economy had “turned the corner”, when it's shrunk since then; he said his Government was going to increase infrastructure investment, but instead has cut it by $2.9 billion, putting thousands of people out of work?
focus.explanation: Three named commitments each set against a named outcome. This is the accountability case, not party-bashing.

focus.statement: Yes, including my statement that I put more effort into my Uber Eats order than that member put into her policy brain fart yesterday.
focus.explanation: Nothing about any policy, mechanism, figure or outcome — the entire content is a jibe at the other side's document.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I encourage the Labour members to go fiscal literacy school; they need it.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is supposedly like. No policy, figure or measure appears.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yeah, well, you guys didn’t build any, so don’t come at me about building roads.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's record with no road, figure or timeframe named — party framing standing in for the policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How are our teachers and healthcare workers meant to feed their whānau when pay offers continue to lag behind growing inflation while fruit and vegetable prices have increased by 7.4 percent in the last year?
focus.explanation: Ties a named price series to the specific pay offers at issue — scrutiny with a figure attached, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, that’s just not true. I’d just encourage the member to encourage her friends in the unions to get them to get back to the bargaining table. That’s where this can be worked out.
focus.explanation: A bare denial with no counter-figure, followed by redirection to the unions. Nothing about the pay offers, the price series raised, or any mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, and I also believe that they see that the improvement in Māori literacy rates for new entrants is also giving them great trust in what this Government is doing, as well.
focus.explanation: Names a real policy area, but not the one at issue — the environmental stewardship question is left untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Prime Minister opposing iwi and hapū customary title over the foreshore and seabed because it limits his Government’s ability to approve seabed mining, bottom trawling, and deep-sea oil drilling?
focus.explanation: Names the customary title regime and three specific extractive activities — a real policy question, despite the motive framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yes, including my statement that I put more effort into my Uber Eats order than that member put into her policy brain fart yesterday.
civility.explanation: A direct personal belittlement of the questioner — ridicules her effort and her thinking rather than the policy's content. Contempt for the person, delivered as the opening answer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I encourage the Labour members to go fiscal literacy school; they need it.
civility.explanation: Mockery of opposing members' basic competence rather than of any position they hold — condescension aimed at the people, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I reject the characterisation in that question. I don’t know what she’s trying to get to. Probably teaching.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the questioner rather than the question — 'I don't know what she's trying to get to' implies she is unable to make a coherent point, and the trailing 'Probably teaching' is a shrug rather than an engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I understand a great many things, but one thing that I understand—that that member seems not to—is that in order to have a conversation with two parties negotiating, both parties need to be around a negotiating table.
civility.explanation: Constructed to say the questioner does not understand an obvious thing — the condescension is the point of the sentence, and it lands on the member rather than on her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister opposing iwi and hapū customary title over the foreshore and seabed because it limits his Government’s ability to approve seabed mining, bottom trawling, and deep-sea oil drilling?
civility.explanation: Probing motive is legitimate scrutiny, but the question is framed to assert rather than test an improper motive, which edges toward imputing bad faith to the person rather than contesting the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister find it curious that a member would sit in this House, but question its right to make laws?
civility.explanation: Aimed at the member's standing rather than her argument — it invites the House to find her presence inconsistent, which is a comment on the person, not on the customary rights question she raised.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m not sure that member has his ears on, because I have said that employment has grown 29 percent in the last year.
civility.explanation: 'Not sure that member has his ears on' is a jibe at the questioner's attentiveness rather than a response to what he asked — mockery, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 28 of the royal commission's 138 recommendations have been completed or had progress initiated as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown Response to the Abuse in Care Inquiry progress reporting on the Whanaketia report's 138 recommendations as at October 2025; true if the count completed or with work initiated is 28 (or rounds to it), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Look, we hear it quite a bit that these changes that are done have not been done in consultation with survivors, but what I would say is that there was six years of consultation with survivors: six years of an inquiry into the abuse in care, six years of listening to survivors, and six years of writing survivors’ stories, to be held and written for everybody to be able to read that going into the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the inquiry into abuse in care ran for six years and gathered survivors' accounts throughout.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's establishment date and final report date; true if the elapsed span is approximately six years, false if materially shorter or longer.

veracity.statement: They wanted to ban strip-searches of children, stop the treating of trauma with trauma. Kāo—missed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill fails to deliver a ban on strip-searching children in care, which survivors sought. Another member in the same debate states the opposite about the same bill, so the two accounts cannot both hold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill as passed: true if it leaves the power to strip-search children in care or youth justice residences intact, false if it prohibits or removes that power.

veracity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific proportion — one in five — of the current prison population were abused in State care, attributed to research before the royal commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission (Whanaketia) report and Department of Corrections prison-population data on the share of prisoners with a State care history involving abuse; true if the figure is about 20%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who’ve been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that expert advice was clearly against boot camps for this population and that the Government proceeded regardless.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki departmental advice, the regulatory impact material for the military-style academies pilot, and expert submissions; true if that advice advised against the approach on effectiveness grounds and the pilot proceeded anyway, false if the advice was supportive or equivocal.

veracity.statement: This is a legacy owed to the courageous nearly 2,400 survivors who provided their experience and shared their experience of abuse that has contributed to the commission’s work, which has now resulted in this additional step to improve the safety and wellbeing of children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to 2,400 survivors gave their accounts to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's own reported count of survivors engaged through private sessions, witness statements and hearings; true if the total is close to 2,400, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: As a result of that, all three coalition parties campaigned on a concept, similar to what is in this bill, known as the rule of two.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that all three governing parties — not one or two of them — took a 'rule of two' medicines-approval policy into the election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 election manifestos and published health policy of National, ACT and New Zealand First; true only if all three contain a policy allowing medicines consented in two other jurisdictions, false if any one of them did not campaign on it.

veracity.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence and size of an official estimate — roughly $90 million of economic benefit over ten years from allowing unapproved medicines to be marketed at medical conferences in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry for Regulation / MBIE analysis behind the proposed Amendment Paper to the Medicines Amendment Bill; true if it estimates about $90 million over ten years, false if no such estimate exists or the figure is materially different.

specificity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
specificity.explanation: Two hard figures against a named recommendation set — someone could go and check the count.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision and the clause inserting it, so the objection can be located in the bill; stops short of saying what the provision should say instead.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has worked tirelessly in the background, changing practice across the youth justice system and professionalising the youth justice system to make sure that our young people are actually cared for in a way that is appropriate.
specificity.explanation: Claims substantive activity but names no change, no mechanism, no timeframe and no measure — 'professionalising' and 'appropriate' carry nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill is a start. The bill is a process. Change needed to happen; more change will continue to need to happen.
specificity.explanation: Offered as a summing-up of what the bill does, but carries no provision, figure, mechanism or timeframe — it would be true of any bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
specificity.explanation: A single quantified proportion tied to a named population and attributed to research; no source, period or definition given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It simply says that if two other jurisdictions have consented a medication for an indication, then it can be used in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: States the operative rule precisely enough to apply: a threshold (two jurisdictions), the unit (a medication for an indication), and the consequence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, a timeframe and the mechanism producing it are all supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I leave that on the Hansard for that side of the House to have to live up to for decades—well, for ever now. It’s on the record. That’s what that side of the House has called for.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what 'that side of the House' is like and what it will have to answer for; no policy, measure or figure is engaged. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly — this is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who’ve been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
focus.explanation: Names a specific Government programme, the advice against it, and the decision to proceed. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By not recognising their harm and by minimising their harm, that is not the State taking accountability for its own violence; that is the State choosing to discriminate about who worthy survivors of violence are, and who deserves to have their violence recognised.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, and a weak one: it moves from 'the redress scheme has eligibility limits' to 'the State is deciding who counts as a worthy survivor', treating a scope criterion as a judgement about worth without offering anything to close that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, we hear it quite a bit that these changes that are done have not been done in consultation with survivors, but what I would say is that there was six years of consultation with survivors: six years of an inquiry into the abuse in care, six years of listening to survivors, and six years of writing survivors’ stories, to be held and written for everybody to be able to read that going into the future.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the criticism is that survivors were not consulted on this bill, and the rebuttal offers the royal commission's inquiry into past abuse instead. Evidence-gathering for an inquiry is not consultation on a legislative text, so the conclusion does not answer the premise it is aimed at.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are, unfortunately, many cases where people will use force against themselves or others, and reasonable force needs to be used to stop that, so let's have a responsible conversation as we continue this piece of work, ladies and gentlemen.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy before the House, resting on a single personal anecdote — an adult prisoner assaulting a visiting lawyer — generalised to the use of force on children in youth justice residences. Argument from anecdote, and from a materially different setting.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, how can we legitimately be against abuse in State care while still—and this is the point—allowing the State to use force, you know?
rigor.explanation: Squarely on the measure, but the inference collapses two different things: it treats any statutory use of force as equivalent to abuse, so the contradiction is manufactured by the equivocation rather than shown. A false dichotomy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s an incredibly important thing, because we know this is a place where violence grows—a relationship where somebody has no choice but to be there is a place where violence grows and there is predatory behaviour—so it’s really important that we make these amendments, and we change the system so that we’re checking overseas convictions.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks what is offered: a stated mechanism (captive relationships attract predatory behaviour) supports the specific remedy (more thorough vetting, including overseas convictions). The mechanism is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the only real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' contributions as 'rubbish... spouted' rather than engaging what was said — sneering, though short of a direct insult to a named member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Reasonable force is not about violence; reasonable force is done in good practice, with good training, to make sure that de-escalation does happen first, before reasonable force is used, and to say that that’s not going to happen is actually disingenuous.
civility.explanation: The substantive distinction is fine, but 'disingenuous' imputes bad faith to opponents rather than treating the disagreement as genuine — a real civility failure short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I think the sad thing is that if we had a Prime Minister who truly supported this apology, then he would have proved it, and this Government would have proved it in everything they did.
civility.explanation: Impugns the Prime Minister's sincerity in delivering the apology — an attack on the person's good faith rather than on the adequacy of the response.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I'm going to share one little story to say why these people should really wake up and live in the real world: a number of years ago, I was working as a lawyer, and I was contacted by a father of a young man who'd been accused of a very serious crime.
civility.explanation: 'These people should really wake up and live in the real world' is condescension aimed at the members opposite rather than at their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I’m trying to say, Mr Seymour, is that one of the calls from survivors was that the Treaty of Waitangi be respected and be part of this whole legislation, but Mr Seymour has got this weird sort of resentment to the Treaty and doesn’t understand that part of the Treaty process is that there is a special consultation process that has to be set up with Māori, that Mr Seymour disagrees with and refuses to be part of.
civility.explanation: Attributes a 'weird sort of resentment' to a named member and asserts he does not understand the subject — an attack on the person's motives and competence rather than on his stated position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t accept what Minister Chhour said when she said, “We have been engaging for six or seven years.” That is just not good enough.
civility.explanation: A flat, hard rejection of a named Minister's claim that stays entirely on what was said. The disagreement is sharp and no one is impugned — this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are such things as magnanimity and grace, but they take time to earn in the House, and some members clearly have not spent that much time here just yet, but we have hope for them, just as we have hope for all people.
civility.explanation: Answers a point of order with a dig at the member's inexperience and character rather than the substance of the objection — condescension dressed as generosity.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, it may be a great idea; however, it has come through the Ministry for Regulation, which, we know, is a creation from the ACT Party and is an interesting institution given that it's supposed to be about deregulating but is actually also being seen as a bit of an institution for fast tracking.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here about the provenance of a late amendment and about an agency's mandate, but the weight of the sentence is party framing — that the Ministry is 'a creation from the ACT Party'. A real point wrapped in the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we are now looking at the Medicines Classification Committee being a ministerial appointment, we don't think that is correct. It should be appointed by the director-general.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — a named provision, a named body, and the change sought. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It still requires a sponsor application. Companies need to see a commercial reason to apply in the first place, and the biggest barrier to that is going to be and will remain Pharmac funding, not necessarily Medsafe approval times.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill and its interaction with Pharmac funding. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can't help but reflect on the fact that National’s focus on cutting corners, on shifting control to Ministers rather than making the system work for patients, has been a step in the wrong direction.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent — the transfer of appointment powers to Ministers, which is actually in this bill — but it is framed as a characterisation of what National is like in general rather than as a claim about the provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
focus.explanation: Names a real and specific arrangement — the existing co-management of Ninety Mile Beach agreed by this House — which is genuine policy content, but the claim is anchored on an assertion about the Government's motives rather than on what the bill does to that arrangement.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, we don't also want to be like some foreign jurisdictions where we are seen as taking a silver bullet for every possible remedy, with relentless marketing on TV and with the big pharmaceuticals crowding out and basically medicalising other solutions for what could be lifestyle or other issues.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy from overseas direct-to-consumer advertising regimes to the likely effect here. The mechanism (marketing crowding out non-pharmaceutical treatment) is at least named, but nothing is offered to connect the proposed amendment to that outcome, so the step from 'other countries look like this' to 'we would too' is unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does seem a little bit strange that when there's been other countries of the same ilk who have approved medicines that we would have to have a long, drawn-out procedure before they could be used here in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: An argument from comparable jurisdictions to the redundancy of the domestic process. It has a real premise and conclusion about the policy, but the whole weight rests on an appeal to those regulators' authority — nothing is offered about why their assessments transfer, which is the contested step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It still requires a sponsor application. Companies need to see a commercial reason to apply in the first place, and the biggest barrier to that is going to be and will remain Pharmac funding, not necessarily Medsafe approval times.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal argument: the pathway is demand-led, sponsors are commercially motivated, therefore the binding constraint is funding rather than approval speed. The premises support the conclusion; the gap is that no evidence is offered for which barrier actually binds harder.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If a country has a medicine approved by two of those countries, then clearly it is appropriate for approval here.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to authority: the conclusion that domestic approval is appropriate rests entirely on the fact that two listed regulators approved it, with nothing offered about equivalence of standards or about New Zealand-specific factors. The word 'clearly' does the work that an argument should.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These kinds of loopholes in the law have caused huge tragedies and the ways that we structure our laws can make a huge difference, and so it’s really important.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the US opioid crisis to the importance of this bill's drafting, but the analogy is asserted rather than established — no link is drawn between the specific 'loopholes' in the US case and any provision here, so the conclusion outruns what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the bill is commended because the Government that made it is patient-focused, which is the very thing the bill was supposed to demonstrate. Nothing about the measure supports the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the bill has prospective effect only, it would be unfair to those applicants who, by way of scheduling, would be subject to a stricter restored test, while others retain awards under what Parliament regards as an incorrect interpretation of the legislation.
rigor.explanation: A valid consistency argument: if the test changes prospectively, otherwise identical applicants are treated differently on the accident of hearing date. The conclusion follows from the premise; it does not address the competing unfairness of unsettling decided cases, which is the obvious counter.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we are now looking at the Medicines Classification Committee being a ministerial appointment, we don't think that is correct. It should be appointed by the director-general.
specificity.explanation: Names the committee, the mechanism objected to (ministerial appointment) and the alternative sought (appointment by the Director-General). Concrete enough to act on, though no drafting or clause is cited.

specificity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
specificity.explanation: A named town, a number, and a stated timeframe ('right now') — checkable against enrolment data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It will allow the medicines to be approved for distribution in New Zealand when they've been approved by two other overseas jurisdictions.
specificity.explanation: States the operative mechanism and the threshold — approval by two recognised overseas regulators. No timeframes or criteria for which jurisdictions qualify, which is where the detail actually sits.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that families are paying more, they're waiting longer, and they're getting less.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical triad with no figure, no service, no timeframe and no comparison point. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are extremely skilled, they are well trained—they have four years of training, they have 300 clinical hours—and they are good people to extend that part of the Act to.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete training figures attached to a named group and a named legislative change, though the conclusion ('good people to extend that part of the Act to') carries no further detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. No mechanism, figure, timeframe or named provision — nothing that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
specificity.explanation: Named source document, named comparison set, a date range and a stated rank — fully checkable.

specificity.statement: The current wording of section 58 of the Act plainly states that in addition to holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga, the applicant groups need to have had exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
specificity.explanation: A named sum tied to a named purpose and an identified group. Checkable against the appropriation.

veracity.statement: I think nearly 200 submitters came before the select committee in writing and orally, and there were about 30-odd in terms of oral submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the volume of submissions on the Medicines Amendment Bill: close to 200 written and oral submitters in total, of whom roughly thirty appeared orally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill, which states the number of submissions received and the number of submitters heard. True if the totals are near 200 and near 30 respectively; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 3,000 families in Kaitāia currently have no access to a general practitioner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora primary care enrolment data for the Kaitāia catchment and reporting on closed books at Te Hiku Hauora and other Far North practices. veracity.statement: We heard 185 submissions and oral evidence from 32 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts exact submission counts for the Health Committee's consideration of the bill: 185 submissions received and 32 submitters heard orally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill, which records submissions received and submitters heard. True if the report states 185 and 32; false if either count differs.

veracity.statement: It doesn't include changes to existing drugs, new indications, formulations, or administration routes, and these actually make up a large share of the Medsafe applications.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the bill's new pathway is confined to new medicines and excludes changed indications, formulations and administration routes; and that such changes constitute a large proportion of Medsafe's application workload.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Medicines Amendment Bill as reported back, for the scope point; and Medsafe's published application statistics by application type, for the workload point. True if the pathway excludes those categories and they exceed a substantial share of applications; false if the pathway covers them or the share is small.

veracity.statement: Speaking of which, we know that, certainly under this Government's watch, it's become harder than ever to see a doctor or a nurse or a specialist.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that access to primary and specialist care has deteriorated to the worst point on record during the current Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey unmet-need-for-primary-care series and Health NZ planned care / first specialist assessment waiting-time data, compared across the full published series. True if the 2024/25 measures are the worst in the series; false if earlier periods were worse or the measures are flat.

veracity.statement: I find it is my obligation to remind the House that this Government is putting more money into health than ever before—ever before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that health funding under the current Government is at the highest level ever. The claim is unqualified as to whether it is nominal or real terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health appropriations in Budget 2025 compared with all previous Budgets, in both nominal and inflation-adjusted per-capita terms, per Treasury Estimates of Appropriations. True if the figure is a record on the measure a reasonable listener would take; false if earlier years were higher on that measure.

veracity.statement: They are extremely skilled, they are well trained—they have four years of training, they have 300 clinical hours—and they are good people to extend that part of the Act to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the training requirements for nurse practitioners: four years of training and 300 clinical hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nursing Council of New Zealand nurse practitioner scope and registration requirements, which specify the required qualification, years of practice and clinical practicum hours. True if the requirements amount to about four years and 300 clinical hours; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's regulatory impact statement cites research placing New Zealand last of 20 OECD countries for approval of modern medicines over 2011–2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Medicines Amendment Bill regulatory impact statement and the study it cites (the OECD comparison of new medicine registrations, 2011–2020). True if the RIS cites that research and New Zealand ranks last of the 20; false if the ranking, the country count or the period differ.

veracity.statement: This is, of course, something that the Labour Government introduced and that, in July this year, was removed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that free prescriptions were introduced by the previous Labour Government and that the policy was removed in July of 2025, the year of this statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac and Health New Zealand records of the $5 prescription co-payment: the date charges were removed under the previous Government and the date they were reinstated by the current one. True if reinstatement took effect in July 2025; false if it took effect in a different year.

veracity.statement: They have a new code of practice that was introduced in 2016, with updates in 2024, with a real understanding that for the public to trust these institutions, they need to know that they're independent, and they need to trust not only the individuals who are in those roles but the way in which they were appointed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the United Kingdom introduced a new code of practice governing public appointments in 2016 and updated it in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The UK Governance Code on Public Appointments and the Commissioner for Public Appointments' publication record. True if the code dates from 2016 and was revised in 2024; false if either date is wrong.

veracity.statement: The current wording of section 58 of the Act plainly states that in addition to holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga, the applicant groups need to have had exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 requires: holding in accordance with tikanga, plus exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. True if those elements appear as described; false if the section omits or qualifies any of them.

veracity.statement: Last year’s Supreme Court judgment in Re Edwards confirmed that the earlier judgments, particularly in the Court of Appeal, did not apply the test in line with Parliament’s intent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court's 2024 judgment in Re Edwards held that the Court of Appeal had misapplied the section 58 customary marine title test relative to Parliament's intent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment in Re Edwards (Te Whakatōhea No 2), November 2024. True if the Court held the Court of Appeal's approach departed from the statutory test as Parliament framed it; false if the Court substantially upheld the Court of Appeal's interpretation.

veracity.statement: During readings of this Act in the House back in 2011, the Hon Chris Finlayson and the Hon Tariana Turia both emphasised the Act was intended to recognise customary marine title in specific parts of the coastline.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what two named members said during the 2011 passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act about the intended geographic reach of customary marine title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the readings of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill in 2011. True if both Finlayson and Turia characterised the recognition as applying to specific parts of the coastline; false if either did not, or characterised it more broadly.

veracity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $15 million has been provided by the Government to meet applicants' costs of re-hearings arising from the amended test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations and Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti announcements on funding for takutai moana re-hearings. True if a $15 million allocation for that purpose exists; false if the amount or purpose differs.

veracity.statement: They work hard to make sure that they can fix those injustices of the past, and when we became Government in 2017, it was one of the first things the Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern did, in recognising that what Labour had done in 2004 was wrong and unjust. She publicly apologised for that particular matter, and we continue to work on our relationship to build that bridge again and build that relationship with the Māori people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on taking office in 2017 Jacinda Ardern publicly apologised for the previous Labour Government's 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act, and that this was among the first things she did.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The public record of statements by Jacinda Ardern as Prime Minister from October 2017, including Waitangi and Rātana addresses, for a formal apology relating to the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004. True if such an apology was made early in that term; false if no apology was made, or if it was made by another Labour leader or at a materially later time.

divination.statement: We see that strikes are coming up on 23 October, so clearly there are some issues within the health system.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that health sector industrial action will take place on 23 October 2025, two days after this statement.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora and health union (NZNO, ASMS) records and contemporaneous reporting for 23 October 2025. True if health sector strike action occurred on that date; false if it was withdrawn, settled or deferred.

divination.statement: So unless Pharmac can fund the medicine, companies simply aren't going to bother making those applications and applying in the first place.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that pharmaceutical sponsors will not lodge applications under the new pathway for medicines Pharmac does not fund, so uptake of the rule-of-two route will be limited.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Medsafe's record of new-medicine applications lodged under the recognised-overseas-regulator pathway in the first 12 months after commencement, cross-checked against Pharmac funding status. True if applications are overwhelmingly for funded or funding-application medicines and volumes remain near pre-reform levels; false if a material number of unfunded medicines are submitted through the new pathway.

civility.statement: It's unfortunate that on something that has wide support of the House, the member who just resumed her seat, Tracey McLellan, couldn't but help herself to take the opportunity to spread misinformation about what this Government is doing in the health sector.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and accuses her of spreading misinformation and of being unable to help herself — an imputation of bad faith and lack of self-control aimed at the person, not at what she argued. Past sneering, short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I recognise that this will be very disappointing to groups who have been through the process. Now, this is not something that we’ve done lightly, but there is a long way to go and much of our coastline still to be considered, and we believe, as a Government, that it’s important to get that right.
civility.explanation: On one of the most contested bills before the House, and following interruption, the speaker acknowledges the cost to those affected and states the reason for proceeding. No individual or group is disparaged.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hope that this Minister and this Government recognise, some time in the near future, the wrongs of this bill, and may find it in themselves to come back and apologise not just to the people of this House and of this Parliament but to the Māori people right around the country.
civility.explanation: A hard judgement on the legislation and an appeal directed at the Minister, but the criticism stays on the bill and its consequences. No attack on the Minister's character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker
